headings: Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency VBI / Vertebral Artery Dissection VAD
AHA/ASA Scientific Statement Biller et al., 2014
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Cervical Artery Dysfunction CAD encompasses pathological conditions of the vertebral arteries VA and internal carotid arteries ICA in the cervical region that may present with symptoms mimicking musculoskeletal neck pain or headache — and may be precipitated or exacerbated by cervical spine movement or manipulation. This is a critical safety topic for all physiotherapists performing cervical assessment and treatment. Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency VBI / Vertebral Artery Dissection VAD - Vertebral arteries VA : Arise from subclavian arteries; enter transverse foramina at C6, ascend through C6–C1, pierce dura, enter skull via foramen magnum, and unite to form basilar artery - Internal carotid arteries ICA : Ascend anterior to VA; enter petrous canal; supply anterior circulation - VA supplies posterior brain circulation: brainstem, cerebellum, occipital lobe, medial temporal lobe Pathology: 1. Atherosclerotic VBI : Progressive stenosis of VA/basilar artery; older patients >55 ; embolic or haemodynamic ischaemia; symptoms often positional but mechanical compression less important than atheroma/embolism 2. Vertebral Artery Dissection VAD : Intimal tear → intramural haematoma → stenosis, occlusion, or thromboembolism; may be spontaneous or trauma-related whiplash, manipulation, trivial trauma ; peak incidence 40s 3. Internal Carotid Artery Dissection ICAD : Similar mechanism; anterior circulation TIA/stroke; classically presents with neck pain + ipsilateral Horner's syndrome + contralateral focal deficit 4. Bow Hunter's Syndrome : Dynamic VA occlusion with head rotation, usually at C1/2 Risk factors for dissection: - Connective tissue disorders Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan's, fibromuscular dysplasia — strongest risk factors - Hypertension - Recent infection especially URTI — inflammatory arteriopathy - Oral contraceptive use - Migraine with aura - Prior dissection - Recent trauma whiplash, manipulation, trivial neck strain Incidence: - Spontaneous VAD: ~1–1.5 per 100,000/year - ICAD: ~2.6 per 100,000/year - Stroke associated with cervical manipulation: estimated 1–3 per 100,000 manipulations Cassidy et al., 2008 — controversial; observed association may represent consultation bias patients with prodromal dissection seek treatment - VAD accounts for ~20% of strokes in patients aged <45 years Dziewas et al., 2003 --- Special Tests Critical caveat: Pre-manipulative screening tests for CAD have poor diagnostic accuracy and should NOT be used as a sole safety screen. Clinical decision-making must be based on comprehensive history and risk assessment. Test Sensitivity Specificity Notes Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ------- ---------------- Vertebral Artery Test VAT / DeKleyn's Test 0.00–0.57 0.67–1.00 Unacceptably low sensitivity; FALSE NEGATIVE rate very high; DO NOT use to clear for manipulation Low Rivett et al., 1999; Kerry et al., 2008 Hautant's Test ~0.00–0.06 High No evidence base as safety screen; not recommended Very Low Hallpike-Dix Test Used for BPPV differentiation; not a CAD test — — Moderate for BPPV Sustained end-range rotation 10 seconds each way Very low sensitivity for CAD — Historical test; NOT recommended as safety screen Low Rancourt's Test sustained rotation in flexion No published data supporting diagnostic accuracy — — Very Low IFOMPT 2012 Consensus Statement updated 2017 : - Pre-manipulative testing for VBI VAT, Hautant's, DeKleyn's should not be used as a means of clearing patients for cervical manipulation — insufficient sensitivity/specificity - Comprehensive clinical history and risk factor analysis is the cornerstone of pre-treatment screening What TO use instead — IFOMPT Framework: History-taking red flags for CAD 5 D's + 3 N's + additional : Symptom Clinical Significance --------- ----------------------- Dizziness Vertebrobasilar ischaemia; differentiate from cervicogenic positional, brief, associated with neck movement Diplopia Brainstem ischaemia CN III, IV, VI involvement Dysarthria Bulbar ischaemia Dysphagia Medullary involvement Drop attacks Sudden loss of postural tone — vertebrobasilar Nausea Dorsal vagal complex ischaemia Numbness face/body Lateral medullary/trigeminal involvement Nystagmus Vestibulocerebellum ischaemia Ataxia Cerebellar ischaemia Headache new, severe, "thunderclap" Subarachnoid haemorrhage or arterial dissection Horner's Syndrome ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis ICA or VA dissection Neck pain new, severe, ipsilateral occipital Dissection prodrome --- Red Flags STOP — Do NOT proceed with manual therapy if: 1. New, severe, or unusual headache — especially "thunderclap" worst headache of life → Emergency 2. Bilateral or quadrilateral neurological symptoms → Urgent investigation 3. Ataxia or gait disturbance combined with neck pain 4. Diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia — brainstem signs 5. Drop attacks — sudden loss of postural tone 6. Horner's syndrome ipsilateral ptosis + miosis ± anhidrosis combined with neck pain → Suspected ICA/VA dissection → Emergency 7. Any positive cranial nerve finding in context of neck pain 8. Symptoms that worsen in sustained cervical rotation or extension 9. Recent trauma whiplash, blow to head, forceful neck manipulation with new neurological symptoms 10. Known connective tissue disorder EDS, Marfan's — relative contraindication to cervical HVLA Absolute contraindications to cervical HVLA: - Active or suspected arterial dissection - Confirmed cervical instability os odontoideum, AAI in RA/Down's/JIA - Vertebrobasilar symptoms provoked by cervical movement - Myelopathy signs - Fracture/dislocation - Malignancy at cervical level - Anticoagulation relative — not absolute; risk-benefit discussion - Osteoporosis with active vertebral fractures Signs of acute stroke/TIA — Call 999 FAST + BE-FAST : - B alance loss, E yes diplopia/vision loss , F ace drooping, A rm weakness, S peech difficulty, T ime to call 999 - Act FAST: do NOT delay by attempting physiotherapy assessment --- Clinical Frameworks IFOMPT International Framework 2012, updated 2017 The International Federation of Orthopaedic Manipulative Physical Therapists IFOMPT framework for management of CAD risk: Three-stage clinical decision process: 1. Stage 1 — Pre-examination screen: - Comprehensive history of dizziness, headache, neurological symptoms - CVD risk factors, connective tissue disorders, medications anticoagulants - Recent trauma 2. Stage 2 — Physical examination: - Assess provocation of symptoms with active ROM - Sustained positions assessment not VAT - VBI symptom onset ≥2 minutes sustained position more significant than <30 seconds - Neurological examination 3. Stage 3 — Decision: - If ANY concern → do NOT perform cervical HVLA; consider alternative techniques - Document reasoning - Share decision-making with patient informed consent including CAD risk AHA/ASA Scientific Statement Biller et al., 2014 - Clinicians should inform patients of the extremely small risk of stroke associated with cervical manipulation - Shared decision-making and informed consent required - Prefer cervical mobilisation over HVLA where risk factors present Differential Vertebrogenic Dizziness Framework Distinguish cervicogenic dizziness from vestibular causes: Feature Cervicogenic Dizziness Vestibular BPPV/Labyrinthitis VBI --------- ---------------------- -------------------------------- ----- Onset With neck movement Head position change Sustained rotation/extension Duration Proportional to neck movement Seconds BPPV or days labyrinthitis Seconds–minutes Associated Neck pain, stiffness Nausea, positional Hallpike positive Diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia Neurological None None Positive CNS signs --- Outcome Measures Primary goal: SAFETY — accurate identification and appropriate management of CAD risk Formal validated outcome measures for the management of CAD are limited — this is primarily a triage/screening condition rather than a primary physiotherapy treatment condition. Tools used in assessment: Dizziness Handicap Inventory DHI - 25 items; 0–100 0=no handicap, 100=maximum - Used for dizziness-related disability differentiate from cervicogenic vs. vestibular - MCID : 11 points Whitney et al., 2004 Neck Disability Index NDI - For associated neck pain disability tracking - MCID : 7.5/50 points NPRS 0–10 - For headache and neck pain severity - MCID : 2.1 points Neurological Examination Documentation - Serial documentation of cranial nerve findings, upper and lower limb neurology - Essential for monitoring improvement or deterioration --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Investigation of Suspected CAD: MRI + MRA Magnetic Resonance Angiography : - First-line investigation for suspected VA or ICA dissection - T1 fat-saturated axial images: intramural haematoma appears as crescentic hyperintensity surrounding lumen - MRA: demonstrates stenosis, occlusion, or "flame sign" of dissection - Sensitivity: ~84% for acute VAD within 48 hours CTA CT Angiography : - Faster than MRI; better availability in ED - Sensitivity: ~94–100% for arterial dissection Provenzale et al., 2003 - Higher radiation dose; may miss subacute dissection better seen on MRI Doppler Ultrasound: - Limited sensitivity for VA dissection poor vessel visualisation at skull base - Useful for ICA stenosis screening carotid atheromatous disease - Sensitivity for VAD: ~70%; not sufficient to exclude dissection Conventional DSA Digital Subtraction Angiography : - Historical gold standard; now reserved for intervention thrombolysis, stenting - Invasive; risk of stroke ~0.3–0.5% Clinical criteria for diagnosis Brandt criteria for VAD : 1. Local pain neck/occipital/periorbital 2. New neurological deficit 3. Imaging evidence of dissection --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- BPPV Positive Hallpike-Dix, brief <60 sec rotational vertigo, no brainstem signs Vestibular neuritis / Labyrinthitis Sustained vertigo, hearing loss labyrinthitis , no neck pain, normal MRI Cervicogenic dizziness Neck pain + dizziness proportional to cervical ROM, positive FRT, no brainstem signs Subarachnoid haemorrhage Thunderclap headache, worst of life, neck stiffness, photophobia, CT/LP Posterior fossa tumour Progressive headache, ataxia, cranial nerve deficit, MRI Migraine with aura Headache + aura visual, sensory , family history, no focal deficit, recurrent Multiple sclerosis Relapsing-remitting, MRI white matter lesions, young adult Brainstem TIA Transient <24h , multiple deficits, DWI-MRI, cardiac source Mechanical neck pain No neurological signs, ROM limited but symptoms peripheral, predictable Orthostatic hypotension Dizziness with positional change lying → standing , HR/BP response --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Suspected acute CAD/Dissection: - Call 999 / Transfer to ED IMMEDIATELY - Do NOT perform further cervical treatment - Administer no physical intervention that could extend or propagate dissection - Belfast stroke pathway : Royal Victoria Hospital / Antrim Area Hospital TIA / stroke assessment - TIA/Stroke thrombolysis window: 4.5 hours for IV tPA if ischaemic stroke - HSC Regional Stroke Network: all suspected stroke should go to nearest hyperacute stroke unit HASU Confirmed dissection — acute management medical team : - Anticoagulation vs. antiplatelet therapy: clinical equipoise; CADISS trial Markus et al., 2019 — no significant difference between aspirin and anticoagulation for VAD stroke prevention - Antiplatelet aspirin 300 mg loading, then 75 mg maintenance or anticoagulation depending on stroke risk profile - Haematology/vascular neurology input - Endovascular intervention: stenting for severe stenosis/pseudoaneurysm — specialist decision Physiotherapy role in confirmed CAD: - NEVER primary treatment provider for acute CAD - Post-acute rehabilitation post-stroke/TIA : multidisciplinary neurological rehabilitation - Subsequent neck pain post-dissection healing : gentle pain-free mobilisation, NO HVLA, NO traction - Minimum 3–6 months post-dissection before cervical manual therapy resumption; only with specialist clearance Preventing iatrogenic CAD: - Apply IFOMPT framework at EVERY new cervical spine assessment - Document pre-treatment screening - Obtain verbal informed consent including CVA risk prior to cervical HVLA - Consider thoracic manipulation as lower-risk alternative for most neck pain indications - Know your absolute contraindications Conservative Management For VBI from atherosclerosis stable, not acute dissection : - Medical management antiplatelet, statin, BP management is primary - Physiotherapy: avoid provocative cervical positions; treat associated neck pain with GENTLE Grade I–II mobilisation - Vestibular rehabilitation if chronic vertiginous symptoms with medical clearance For cervicogenic dizziness not VBI : - Manual therapy to C1/2 IFOMPT-compliant, non-HVLA technique - Proprioceptive retraining, gaze stability exercises - Cervical flexion-rotation test FRT to confirm C1/2 involvement Hall et al., 2010; Sens. 91%, Spec. 90% Post-dissection rehabilitation neurology/physio liaison : - Gradual return of cervical mobility pain-free range - No mobilisation of dissected segment until confirmed imaging resolution typically 3–6 months - Core, scapular, and peripheral strengthening safe from early stage - Address psychological impact anxiety, PTSD — dissection can be traumatic event Pharmacological Medical Team-Led - Antiplatelet : Aspirin 75–300 mg/day or clopidogrel 75 mg/day - Anticoagulation : Heparin → warfarin or DOAC — for dissection with high embolic risk - Statins : For atherosclerotic VBI; risk factor modification - Antihypertensives : ACE inhibitors, ARBs — risk factor management - Analgesics : Paracetamol/NSAIDs for associated neck pain if cleared for anticoagulation; avoid NSAIDs on anticoagulation - NICE NG128 Stroke : comprehensive stroke/TIA management guidance Onward Referral Criteria Emergency 999/ED immediately : - Any suspected acute dissection with neurological deficit - Thunderclap headache ± neck pain - New brainstem or cerebellar signs - Post-manipulation onset of neurological symptoms ↑ vigilance within 24 hours of cervical treatment Urgent same-day referral to neurovascular/stroke team : - New onset of 5 D's + 3 N's without resolution - Horner's syndrome with neck pain - Posterior circulation TIA Routine neurology/vascular: - Chronic VBI symptoms; atherosclerotic risk review - Post-dissection follow-up imaging review --- Key References 1. International framework for examination of the cervical region for potential of cervical arterial dysfunction prior to orthopaedic manual therapy intervention. 2012. Updated 2017. 3. Rivett DA, Sharples KJ, Milburn PD. Effect of premanipulative tests on vertebral artery and internal carotid artery blood flow: a pilot study. J Manipulative Physiol Ther . 1999;22 6 :368–375. 4. Dziewas R, Konrad C, Dräger B, et al. Cervical artery dissection — clinical features, risk factors, therapy and outcome in 126 patients. J Neurol . 2003;250 10 :1179–1184. 6. headings: AO Spine DCM Grading Research Framework
Modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association Scale mJOA
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Cervical myelopathy CM — more precisely degenerative cervical myelopathy DCM — is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults over 50 years, with an estimated prevalence of 60 per 100,000 in North America/Europe Nouri et al., 2015 . It is the leading cause of acquired spinal cord disability in adults worldwide. Pathophysiology: DCM results from progressive narrowing of the cervical spinal canal leading to spinal cord compression and ischaemia: - Static compression : osteophytes, hypertrophied ligamentum flavum especially in extension , ossification of posterior longitudinal ligament OPLL , degenerative disc bulges, facet joint hypertrophy - Dynamic compression : cord compression exacerbated by flexion/extension movement; cord is stretched over ventral osteophytes in flexion and folded by buckled ligamentum flavum in extension - Vascular compromise : compression of anterior spinal artery and intrinsic cord microvasculature → ischaemia → central grey matter necrosis - Congenital canal narrowing : canal diameter 45, gait deviation - +LR = 30.9 3 positive ; sensitivity 99% at threshold ≥1 sign Key examination findings: - Hoffman's Sign : flick middle finger distal phalanx — positive if IP flexion of thumb/index; indicates UMN dysfunction - Finger Escape Sign : patient holds fingers extended, adducted — ulnar 2–3 fingers spontaneously abduct/flex; positive in DCM - 10-Second Step Test : patient taps each foot alternately ≥20 times in 10 seconds — 40, rigid cervical spine with myelopathy → CT required --- Clinical Frameworks Severity Classification mJOA Scale The modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association mJOA scale is the most widely used tool for DCM severity: mJOA Score Severity ------------ ---------- 18 Normal 15–17 Mild 12–14 Moderate <12 Severe mJOA domains: Upper extremity motor function 0–5 , Lower extremity motor function 0–7 , Sensory 0–3 , Sphincter function 0–3 Maitland with significant caveats - Maitland mobilisation is NOT appropriate as primary treatment for confirmed DCM - Grade I–II soft tissue work to peripheral joints shoulder, elbow may be used if confirmed nerve root + cord involvement coexist — only under specialist physiotherapy with neurosurgical knowledge - Post-surgical rehabilitation: Maitland principles applicable once surgical clearance obtained AO Spine DCM Grading Research Framework - Grade 0: No signs/symptoms - Grade 1: Signs only, no symptoms - Grade 2: Symptoms but no functional limitation - Grade 3: Mild functional limitation — independent - Grade 4: Moderate functional limitation — requires some assistance - Grade 5: Severe — completely dependent Physiotherapy Role Post-Operatively ACDF/Laminoplasty/Laminectomy - 80% of patients improve post-decompression surgery Fehlings et al., 2013 - Post-op physiotherapy: gentle ROM, neurological recovery monitoring, functional gait retraining, ADL rehabilitation - Inpatient neuro-physio → community follow-up pathway --- Outcome Measures Modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association Scale mJOA - 18-point scale; MCID : 2.0 points Tetreault et al., 2015 - Most validated for surgical outcome measurement in DCM - Recovery rate = post-op mJOA − pre-op mJOA / 18 − pre-op mJOA × 100 Neck Disability Index NDI - MCID : 7.5/50 points 15% - Useful for tracking functional disability alongside neurological severity Nurick Grade - 0–5 functional walking classification; less sensitive to small changes - Grade 0: No root/cord signs; Grade 5: Chair-bound or bedridden European Myelopathy Score EMS - 5-domain, 5–18 scale; validated European alternative to mJOA - MCID : approximately 2 points Patient-Specific Functional Scale PSFS - MCID : 2.0 points average - Appropriate for post-surgical rehabilitation goal-setting GROC Global Rating of Change - 15-point scale; use at post-op physiotherapy review points --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis MRI gold standard : - T2 hyperintensity in spinal cord at level of compression = poor prognostic marker indicates myelomalacia - T1 hypointensity = cavitation/necrosis — even worse prognosis - STIR sequences for inflammatory/infective pathology - NICE NG59 / AO Spine: MRI should be obtained urgently for suspected CM CT Myelography: - Used when MRI contraindicated or inconclusive - Identifies bony compression, OPLL, calcified disc herniation with high resolution Electrodiagnostics: - Motor Evoked Potentials MEPs and Somatosensory Evoked Potentials SSEPs : sensitivity ~85% for functional cord conduction abnormalities - EMG/NCS to differentiate coexisting radiculopathy Clinical Diagnosis: - No single pathognomonic test; diagnosis requires combination of: 1. Consistent symptom profile 2. ≥2 UMN signs on examination 3. MRI evidence of cord compression ± signal change - Cook et al. 2009 : multivariable cluster achieves sensitivity approaching 99% — high clinical utility AO Spine / AOSpine North America Clinical Practice Guidelines Fehlings et al., 2017 : - Recommend surgery for moderate-severe DCM mJOA ≤14 - For mild DCM mJOA 15–17 : structured rehabilitation trial with watchful waiting; surgery if deterioration --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Multiple sclerosis Age <40, relapsing-remitting course, MRI white matter lesions, oligoclonal bands Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ALS/MND UMN + LMN mixed, bulbar involvement, no sensory deficit, EMG fasciculations Subacute combined degeneration B12 deficiency Posterior column signs, B12 low, macrocytic anaemia, no bony compression on MRI Normal pressure hydrocephalus Triad: gait apraxia, cognitive decline, urinary incontinence; no cervical compression Syringomyelia Cape distribution sensory loss, dissociated sensory deficit, often young adults Peripheral neuropathy No UMN signs, glove-stocking distribution, NCS abnormal Cervical radiculopathy Unilateral radicular symptoms, no UMN signs, no gait disturbance Parkinson's disease Tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, pill-rolling tremor; no cord compression Hereditary spastic paraplegia Family history, gradual onset, lower extremity predominant, genetic testing --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Confirmed or suspected DCM moderate/severe : - Urgent referral to Neurosurgery or Orthopaedic Spinal Surgery via GP - In NI: Regional Neurosurgery at Royal Victoria Hospital Belfast HSC Trust ; Orthopaedic Spine at Musgrave Park Hospital - For suspected acute deterioration → Emergency Department A&E with cervical spine imaging - Community physiotherapy: assess, recognise, refer — do NOT treat as primary condition Mild DCM with watchful waiting: - Structured physiotherapy programme with explicit safety boundaries: - No cervical HVLA manipulation - No cervical traction in confirmed cord compression - Functional rehabilitation, balance, UE fine motor retraining - Aquatic therapy: non-impact, offloads gravity - Serial neurological monitoring 3-monthly : grip strength, gait, bladder Post-surgical physiotherapy Trust-specific protocols : - Inpatient physiotherapy from post-op day 1 bed mobilisation, sitting balance - Discharge criteria: independent mobility, safe stairs - Community physiotherapy 6–12 weeks post-surgery for functional rehabilitation - Driving restriction post-ACDF: minimum 6 weeks; varies by surgeon Conservative Management Physiotherapy for mild DCM watchful waiting — Grade C evidence: - Cervical collar : Short-term rigid collar 4–8 weeks for symptomatic relief — limited evidence; may cause deconditioning - Balance and proprioceptive retraining : Standing balance, tandem stance, Wii Fit / perturbation training - Upper extremity fine motor retraining : Occupational therapy-led ADL retraining - Strengthening : Gentle scapular/shoulder stabilisation; avoid heavy loading through cervical spine - Gait retraining : Physiotherapy-led gait retraining with walking aids if required; referral to orthotics if foot drop - Neurological monitoring : Document serial mJOA, grip strength, 10-second step/grip-release test at each visit Post-surgical rehabilitation — Grade B evidence: - Most improvement in first 6 months post-decompression - Targeted: grip/pinch strength, fine motor retraining, gait normalisation, return to ADLs - Core stability and cervical muscle strengthening from 6–8 weeks post-fusion - 80% of patients gain ≥2 mJOA points Fehlings et al., 2013 Pharmacological - Neuropathic pain associated radiculopathy : Gabapentin/Pregabalin — NICE NG173 - NSAIDs : Short-term for pain; avoid long-term in elderly given GI/CV/renal risk - Corticosteroids : High-dose methylprednisolone for acute traumatic SCI; NOT recommended for degenerative CM Fehlings AANS 2013 - Baclofen/Tizanidine : For spasticity management in confirmed CM; specialist-initiated - Bladder management : Anticholinergics oxybutynin for urgency if confirmed; refer urology Onward Referral Criteria Emergency same-day via A&E : - Acute deterioration in myelopathy symptoms - New bladder/bowel dysfunction - Post-trauma with neurological deficit Urgent neurosurgical referral within 2 weeks : - Moderate/severe DCM mJOA ≤14 - Progressive neurological deterioration - Bilateral hand dysfunction affecting ADLs Routine surgical review: - Mild DCM with symptom worsening despite structured 3-month conservative management - Patient preference for surgical opinion --- Key References 1. Cook CE, Wilhelm M, Cook AE, Petrosino C, Isaacs R. Clinical tests for screening and diagnosis of cervical spine myelopathy: a systematic review. J Manipulative Physiol Ther . 2011;34 8 :539–546. 3. Efficacy and safety of surgical decompression in patients with cervical spondylotic myelopathy: results of the AOSpine North America prospective multi-centre study. Pathophysiology and natural history of cervical spondylotic myelopathy. Spine . 2013;38 22 Suppl 1 :S21–S36. 9. NICE. Neck pain — non-specific. Clinical Knowledge Summary. 2023. title: Cervical Radiculopathy
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Cervical radiculopathy CR is a clinical syndrome characterised by pain, neurological deficits, or both, caused by compression or irritation of a cervical nerve root. Annual incidence is approximately 83 per 100,000 population, with peak onset between 50–54 years of age Rad
headings: McKenzie / MDT Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Cervical radiculopathy CR is a clinical syndrome characterised by pain, neurological deficits, or both, caused by compression or irritation of a cervical nerve root. Annual incidence is approximately 83 per 100,000 population, with peak onset between 50–54 years of age Radhakrishnan et al., 1994 . Aetiology: - Disc herniation ~20–25% : acute onset, more common in younger patients 1 m, axial load to head, high-speed MVC, bicycle/motorised recreational vehicle collision - Paraesthesia in extremities - If high-risk feature present → X-ray/CT indicated; do NOT mobilise Malignancy: - History of malignancy, unexplained weight loss, night pain, age >50 with no prior neck history - Constant pain unrelated to posture or movement Infection: - Fever, immunosuppression, recent spinal procedure, IV drug use, neck rigidity - Spinal epidural abscess — urgent MRI Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency / Cervical Artery Dysfunction: - 5 D's + 3 N's: Dizziness, Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dysphagia, Drop attacks; Nausea, Numbness, Nystagmus - Screen before cervical manipulation — see cervical-artery-dysfunction.mdx Fracture indicators: - Severe trauma, inability to rotate 45° bilaterally, midline cervical tenderness - Apply Canadian C-Spine Rule; if positive, refer to ED --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Concept - Grade I–II oscillations for pain modulation in acute/irritable presentations - Grade III–IV for resistance-dominant presentations in subacute/chronic - Passive accessory intervertebral movements PAIVMs at C5/6, C6/7 to identify comparable signs - Passive physiological intervertebral movements PPIVMs to assess segmental mobility - Reassess neurological symptoms after each treatment — peripheralisation = contraindication to further technique McKenzie / MDT Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy - Repeated movement assessment: flexion/extension/lateral flexion/rotation in standing and supine - Identify directional preference: centralisation of radicular symptoms with repeated extension suggests disc pathology with good prognosis - Classification: Derangement most common, 80–90% , Dysfunction, Postural - Derangement: centralisation phenomenon guides treatment direction - MDT retraction ± extension exercises as first-line for Derangement syndrome - Centralisation as prognostic indicator: associated with better outcomes Werneke & Hart, 2003 Clinical Prediction Rules - Wainner CPR 2003 : see Special Tests above — for diagnosis - Fritz & Brennan 2007 CPR for manipulation benefit: ≥3 of 5 predictors associated with success 1. Symptom duration 10° 4. Pain with PA spring testing at C3–5 5. Not performing sedentary work --- Outcome Measures Neck Disability Index NDI - 10 items, 0–5 scale each, total 0–50 or 0–100% - Scoring: 0–8% = no disability; 10–28% = mild; 30–48% = moderate; 50–64% = severe; ≥64% = complete - MCID : 7.5/50 points 15% for CR Young et al., 2009 - Reliability: ICC 0.89–0.93; Strong validity for neck pain populations Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS - 0–10 NRS; MCID : 2.1 points for cervical radiculopathy Cleland et al., 2007 - Use for arm pain AND neck pain separately Patient-Specific Functional Scale PSFS - 3–5 patient-identified activities, scored 0–10 each 0=unable, 10=normal - MCID : 2.0 points per activity average for neck pain Cleland et al., 2006 - Responsive to clinically important change in CR Global Rating of Change GROC - 15-point scale −7 to +7 or 7-point Likert - +5 "quite a bit better" or greater = successful outcome - Use at 4 weeks and discharge Arm Pain NRS - Separate from neck NRS — important to track radicular symptom change - Reduction in arm pain more clinically significant than neck pain in CR --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic gold standard: Electrodiagnostic studies EMG/NCS and MRI MRI: - Preferred imaging for suspected CR - NICE NG59, 2016 : offer MRI if surgical opinion being sought or if red flags present - Do NOT routinely offer imaging in first 6 weeks of uncomplicated CR - MRI has high false positive rate — degenerative changes common in asymptomatic adults >50% over age 40 have disc bulges Electrodiagnostics: - EMG/NCS: sensitivity ~50–70%, specificity ~95% for radiculopathy - Most useful for confirming root level and ruling out peripheral entrapment carpal tunnel, cubital tunnel - Findings may lag clinical presentation by 3–4 weeks Clinical Prediction Rule Wainner 2003 : - 4/4 positive tests: +LR 30.3, probability of CR rises from 23% to ~90% - Most useful as a confirmatory cluster IASP Diagnostic Criteria for CR: - Unilateral arm pain in a dermatomal distribution - Corresponding sensory changes hypoaesthesia/paraesthesia - Motor deficit or reflex change at corresponding level - Positive provocative tests Spurling's, distraction - Imaging correlation but not required for clinical diagnosis --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Rotator cuff pathology Local shoulder pain, painful arc, negative Spurling's, positive Hawkins/Neer Thoracic outlet syndrome Provoked by arm elevation, positive Roos test, neurogenic/vascular Carpal tunnel syndrome Nocturnal wrist/hand pain, thenar wasting, positive Phalen/Tinel at wrist Cubital tunnel syndrome Medial elbow + ring/little finger symptoms, positive elbow flexion test Brachial neuritis Parsonage-Turner Acute severe shoulder pain followed by rapid weakness, no spinal correlation Peripheral neuropathy Bilateral, glove distribution, diabetes history Cervical myelopathy Bilateral symptoms, UMN signs, gait disturbance, bladder/bowel dysfunction Shoulder impingement Shoulder-localised pain, arc sign positive, negative neurodynamic tests Complex regional pain syndrome Autonomic changes, disproportionate pain, allodynia --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Community MSK: - First point of contact via GP referral or direct-access physiotherapy varies by Trust — Belfast, Northern, South Eastern, Southern, Western - Initial assessment within NICE recommended timeframes target: 18 weeks RTT - Triage: Urgent same-day/next-day onward referral if red flags present - Community MSK physiotherapy for uncomplicated CR with conservative management - If no meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks → discuss onward referral Secondary Care Pathway: - Refer to Orthopaedic Spine or Neurosurgery via GP if: - Progressive neurological deficit - Failure of 6–12 weeks conservative management with significant disability - Red flags present - Pain Clinic referral for chronic refractory radiculopathy consider epidural steroid injection, nerve root block - NICE NG59 2016 : Assessment and management of neck pain aligned with this guidance Waiting List Context: - HSC elective waits for orthopaedics significant in NI >52 weeks common ; use waiting time productively with ongoing conservative management and self-management education - Belfast Trust MSK interface service may offer earlier triage and physiotherapy-led assessment Conservative Management Exercise Therapy Grade A evidence : - Specific cervical and scapulothoracic strengthening reduces radicular symptoms - Deep neck flexor strengthening craniocervical flexion test biofeedback — CCFT protocol : Jull et al. 2009 - Neural mobilisation slider vs. tensioner techniques : Moderate evidence for symptom reduction - Median nerve slider: ULNT1-based; gentler, preferred in acute/irritable presentations - Radial nerve mobilisation for C6 root involvement - McKenzie-based exercises: centralisation protocol see Clinical Frameworks - Exercise alone equivalent to combined treatment at 12 months Ylinen et al., 2003 Manual Therapy Grade B evidence : - Cervical manipulation and mobilisation: Short-term pain relief; NCEPOD and NICE caution regarding serious adverse events — shared decision-making essential - Thoracic spine manipulation: Level B evidence for short-term reduction of neck pain and disability in CR Cleland et al., 2005 - HVLA to thoracic spine considered lower risk than cervical HVLA - Soft tissue techniques: Limited evidence as standalone; useful adjunct Education & Self-Management: - Pain neuroscience education PNE : addresses catastrophisation and kinesiophobia - Postural advice: ergonomic assessment desk/screen setup , pillow selection - Activity modification: avoid sustained cervical flexion, repetitive overhead loading - Reassurance regarding favourable natural history Traction: - Mechanical/intermittent cervical traction: Moderate evidence for CR Raney et al., 2009 - CPR for traction Raney et al. : ≥3 of 5 predictors: 1. Age ≥55 2. Positive shoulder abduction test 3. Positive ULNT1 4. Positive neck distraction test 5. Peripheralisation with lower cervical PA spring testing Pharmacological NICE-aligned - Analgesia: Paracetamol limited evidence for neuropathic component + NSAIDs short-term, consider GI/CV risk - Neuropathic pain: Gabapentin 300–1200 mg TDS or Pregabalin 75–300 mg BD — NICE NG173 first-line for neuropathic pain; monitor for sedation/dependence - Tricyclics: Amitriptyline 10–75 mg nocte — off-label for neuropathic pain; NICE NG173 endorsed - Oral corticosteroids: Short course e.g., Medrol dose pack may offer short-term relief; not routinely recommended - Muscle relaxants: Diazepam — short-term only for acute muscle spasm; addictive potential - Injections: Epidural steroid injection or transforaminal nerve root block — consider if conservative management failed at 6–12 weeks; refer to Pain Clinic/Spine service Onward Referral Criteria Urgent/Emergency same-day : - Progressive motor deficit new/worsening weakness - Signs of myelopathy bilateral UMN signs, bladder/bowel dysfunction - Suspected fracture, infection, or malignancy Routine Surgical Referral within 8–12 weeks : - Failure of 6–12 weeks conservative management with persistent severe radiculopathy - Significant or worsening neurological deficit - Severe radicular pain inadequately controlled Pain Clinic: - Chronic refractory radiculopathy >3 months - Consideration for nerve root blocks, epidural steroid injection, or spinal cord stimulation --- Key References 1. content: Cervicogenic Headache > Clinical Summary: Cervicogenic headache CGH is a secondary headache arising from structural pathology of the cervical spine, particularly the upper three cervical segments C1–C3 . It accounts for approximately 4–22% of all chronic headaches and is frequently misdiagnosed as migraine or tension-type headache. Accurate diagnosis and physiotherapy-led management significantly reduce headache burden. --- Overview & Pathophysiology Mechanism CGH arises from nociceptive input from the upper cervical spine structures joints, muscles, ligaments, dura mater that converges with trigeminal afferents within the trigeminocervical nucleus TCN in the brainstem. The TCN extends caudally from the trigeminal nucleus caudalis to approximately C3–C4. Afferents from: - C1 suboccipital / atlantoaxial — via the dorsal root of C1 where present and the spino-trigeminal tract - C2 atlantoaxial, C2-3 zygapophyseal joints, C2 dorsal root ganglion - C3 C2-3 and C3-4 zygapophyseal joints, third occipital nerve ...all converge with trigeminal afferents in the TCN. This anatomical convergence creates referred pain to the head and face from cervical structures — central sensitisation at the TCN level underpins the perceived headache. Primary pain generators include: - C1-2 and C2-3 zygapophyseal facet joints - Atlantoaxial and atlanto-occipital joints - Suboccipital muscles rectus capitis posterior minor/major, obliquus capitis inferior - C2-3 intervertebral disc - Upper cervical dura mater - Third occipital nerve branch of C3 dorsal ramus Prevalence - Population prevalence: 0.4–4% general population ; up to 17–20% in chronic headache clinic populations - Post-whiplash: up to 53% of whiplash patients develop CGH Bogduk & Govind, 2009 - Gender: female predominance F:M ≈ 4:1 - Age: peak 30–44 years; increases with age - Third occipital headache C2-3 facet-mediated accounts for ~27% of chronic post-whiplash headache Lord et al, 1994 Typical Clinical Presentation - Unilateral headache without side-shift though bilateral variants exist - Starts in the neck/suboccipital region, radiates to frontotemporal region, orbit, or vertex - Provoked or aggravated by neck movement or sustained neck posture - Reduced cervical range of motion particularly rotation - Ipsilateral shoulder/arm symptoms may coexist - Moderate, non-pulsating quality; not typically severe - Duration: hours to days episodic or continuous with fluctuation chronic --- Special Tests Sensitivity and specificity values are reported against the reference standard of diagnostic cervical medial branch blocks or IASP/Sjaastad diagnostic criteria as specified per study. Apply in clinical context alongside full assessment. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Reference Standard Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- -------------------- ---------------- Cervical Flexion-Rotation Test CFRT 91% 90% 9.1 0.10 Sjaastad CGH criteria Ogince et al, 2007 Cervical Flexion-Rotation Test CFRT 85% 83% 5.0 0.18 ICHD-2 criteria Hall et al, 2010 Reproduction of headache with C1-2 PAIVMT 80% 78% 3.6 0.26 Cervical nerve block Jull et al, 1988 Upper cervical segmental assessment C0-C3 combined 82% 79% 3.9 0.23 Sjaastad criteria Zito et al, 2006 Reproduction of headache with C-spine manual examination 87% 68% 2.7 0.19 Cervical joint blocks Jull et al, 1997 C2-3 manual segmental assessment 70% 100% ∞ 0.30 3rd occipital nerve block Aprill et al, 1992 CFRT The following features require immediate medical assessment and should not be attributed to cervicogenic headache without exclusion of sinister pathology. Red Flag Possible Cause Action ---------- ---------------- -------- Thunderclap headache severe, maximal within 60 seconds Subarachnoid haemorrhage SAH Emergency 999 / A&E immediately "Worst headache of my life" SAH, intracranial haemorrhage Emergency referral Meningism neck stiffness, photophobia, phonophobia, fever, rash Meningitis, encephalitis Emergency 999 Progressive focal neurological deficit Space-occupying lesion, intracranial bleed Urgent neurology Papilloedema / visual changes Raised intracranial pressure Same-day ophthalmology / neurology New onset headache >50 years Giant cell arteritis GCA , malignancy Urgent ESR/CRP; GP same day Temporal arteritis signs jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, ESR >50 Giant Cell Arteritis Urgent GP/rheumatology; do not delay steroids Postural headache worse standing, better lying Intracranial hypotension / CSF leak Urgent neurology Headache worse with Valsalva, cough, exertion Arnold-Chiari, raised ICP Urgent neuroimaging Immunocompromised / HIV / cancer history CNS malignancy, opportunistic infection Urgent medical assessment New onset headache post-head injury Subdural haematoma Urgent CT head Unsteady gait, diplopia, dysarthria with headache Vertebrobasilar insufficiency, posterior fossa pathology Emergency Vertebral Artery Insufficiency Prior to upper cervical manual therapy: - Conduct pre-manipulative screening IFOMPT framework 2012 - Document absence of: diplopia, dizziness/vertigo with neck movement, drop attacks, dysarthria, dysphagia, facial numbness - Sustained C1-2 rotation testing is no longer recommended as a single screen — clinical reasoning, history, and risk stratification are paramount --- Clinical Frameworks 1. Cervicogenic Headache International Study Group CHISG Criteria — Sjaastad et al, 1998 Major criteria one or more required : Group I — Symptoms/signs of neck involvement: - Ia: Precipitation of head pain by neck movement or sustained neck posture - Ib: Precipitation by external pressure over the upper cervical or occipital region - Ic: Unilateral head pain without side-shift - Id: Ipsilateral neck, shoulder, and arm pain of non-radicular character Group II — Confirmatory evidence: - IIa: Diagnostic blockade of cervical structures or their nerve supply abolishes pain This is the definitive confirmatory criterion Group III — Other characteristics: - IIIa: Moderate-severe, non-excruciating, non-throbbing, non-lancinating pain - IIIb: Headache starts in the neck - IIIc: Episodes of varying duration, or fluctuating continuous pain Exclusion: Migraine features aura, severe throbbing, nausea/vomiting, photophobia do not exclude CGH but should prompt differential diagnosis consideration. --- 2. ICHD-3 Criteria for Cervicogenic Headache 11.2.1 International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd Edition, 2018 A. Any headache fulfilling criterion C B. Clinical, laboratory, and/or imaging evidence of a disorder or lesion within the cervical spine or soft tissues of the neck known to be able to cause headache C. Evidence of causation demonstrated by at least two of the following: - 1. Headache has developed in temporal relation to onset of cervical disorder or lesion - 2. Headache has significantly improved or remitted in parallel with improvement or resolution of cervical disorder - 3. Cervical ROM is reduced, and headache is significantly worsened by provocative movements - 4. Headache is abolished following diagnostic blockade of a cervical structure or nerve supply D. Not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis --- 3. Jull's Assessment Approach Jull, 1997; Jull et al, 2007 A structured physiotherapy assessment framework: Phase 1 — Subjective assessment: - Headache characteristics frequency, intensity, duration, location, associated symptoms - Aggravating/easing factors — identify cervical mechanical contribution - Headache diary minimum 4-week baseline - Medication use and medication overuse screening - Psychosocial screening PHQ-4, pain catastrophising scale Phase 2 — Physical examination: - Active and passive cervical ROM CROM device preferred - CFRT detailed above - Upper cervical segmental examination C0-C3 PAIVM/PIVM - Cervicothoracic junction examination C4-T4 - Craniocervical flexion test CCF test — deep cervical flexor assessment - Postural assessment — forward head posture, thoracic kyphosis - Neurological screening Craniocervical Flexion Test CCFT : - Assesses neuromuscular control of deep cervical flexors longus colli, longus capitis - Using pressure biofeedback unit Stabilizer™ : baseline 20 mmHg; progressive target 22→30 mmHg - CGH patients typically show: reduced activation at lower pressure levels, increased activity of superficial flexors SCM, anterior scalene as compensation - Target: achieve and hold 22–26 mmHg without superficial muscle substitution Jull et al, 2008 --- Outcome Measures Measure Domain MCID Frequency Notes --------- -------- ------ ----------- ------- Headache Frequency days/month Primary ≥50% reduction clinically meaningful Headache diary, 4-week periods Gold standard for monitoring NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale Pain intensity 1.5–2.0 points Per episode or average weekly Validated in headache populations HDI — Headache Disability Inventory Disability/function 29 points total, 0–100 Baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months Emotional + functional subscales; Jacobson et al, 1994 NDI — Neck Disability Index Neck-related disability 7.5 points 0–50 scale Baseline, discharge 10 items; Vernon & Mior, 1991 Headache Duration hours/episode Primary No established MCID — track trend Headache diary Document alongside frequency Medication Use days/month Secondary Reduction to 33/44, address Relevant in chronic CGH Headache Diary Minimum 4-week prospective diary recommended at baseline: - Record: date, time of onset/offset, pain intensity 0–10 , location, medication taken, possible triggers - Digital options: Migraine Buddy, N1-Headache validated electronic diary - Required to establish baseline frequency and identify patterns before initiating treatment --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Cervical Flexion-Rotation Test as Primary Diagnostic Tool The CFRT is the most diagnostically accurate clinical test for CGH currently available: Study n Reference Standard Sn Sp +LR -LR ------- --- -------------------- ---- ---- ---- ----- Ogince et al, 2007 37 CGH + 37 controls Sjaastad CHISG criteria 91% 90% 9.1 0.10 Hall et al, 2010 31 CGH + 29 migraine + 31 controls ICHD-2 85% 83% 5.0 0.18 Hall et al, 2008 31 CGH + 31 controls ICHD-2 86% 87% 6.6 0.16 Arce-Leal et al, 2021 SR Meta-analysis Various criteria 87% pooled 85% pooled 5.8 0.15 Interpretation: - +LR of 9.1 = a positive CFRT makes CGH ~9× more likely - -LR of 0.10 = a negative CFRT substantially reduces probability of CGH - Both ROM restriction AND symptom reproduction should be present for a positive test Cervical Joint Blocks as Reference Standard The definitive diagnosis of CGH is anaesthetic blockade of cervical structures : - Third occipital nerve TON block — for C2-3 facet-mediated headache - C1-2 and C2-3 medial branch blocks - Diagnostic threshold: ≥50% or ≥80% for controlled blocks per International Spine Intervention Society - Available via: Pain Management/Neurology at Belfast City Hospital or Royal Victoria Hospital, Belfast Clinical physiotherapy diagnosis is made on the basis of clinical criteria Sjaastad/ICHD-3 in conjunction with CFRT and upper cervical examination. Diagnostic blocks are reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or pre-intervention confirmation. Differentiation from Migraine and Tension-Type Headache Feature Cervicogenic Headache Migraine without aura Tension-Type Headache --------- ---------------------- ------------------------- ----------------------- Laterality Unilateral consistent side Unilateral variable Bilateral Quality Dull, pressing, non-pulsating Pulsating/throbbing Pressing, tightening Severity Moderate Moderate–severe Mild–moderate Location Starts posterior/occipital → frontotemporal Frontotemporal ± orbital Band-like, vertex Cervical trigger Yes — consistent and reproducible Occasional trigger Occasional CFRT Positive 44° Normal or minimally reduced Nausea/vomiting Rarely Common Rare Photophobia/phonophobia Mild, if present Moderate–severe Mild Aura No Yes in 1/3 of migraineurs No Response to NSAIDs Partial Partial–good Good Response to triptans Poor Good No Response to cervical manual therapy Good No benefit Partial benefit Duration Hours–days variable 4–72 hours 30 min–7 days Physical activity May worsen Worsens Not worsened Overlap: ~50% of CGH patients have concurrent features meeting migraine diagnostic criteria Knackstedt et al, 2010 . Comorbid migraine does not exclude CGH and may require concurrent management. Use CFRT and cervical examination to identify the cervical contribution. --- Differential Diagnosis Headache Type Key Distinguishing Features CFRT Cervical Signs First-Line Management --------------- ---------------------------- ------ --------------- ----------------------- Cervicogenic Headache Unilateral, consistent side; cervical trigger; restricted CFRT; suboccipital onset Positive Present Cervical physio Migraine without aura Pulsating; nausea/vomiting; photophobia; 4–72h; worse with activity Negative Absent trapezius tenderness common but non-specific Triptans, preventive agents Tension-Type Headache Bilateral; pressing/tightening; mild–moderate; not worsened by activity Negative Pericranial tenderness not C0-C3 specific Analgesia, stress management Medication Overuse Headache MOH >15 headache days/month; analgesia use >10–15 days/month; worsens over time Variable Variable Medication withdrawal Cluster Headache Strictly unilateral; periorbital/temporal; severe/excruciating; autonomic features lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, ptosis ; 15–180 min; male predominance Negative Absent 100% O₂, sumatriptan SC, verapamil prophylaxis Occipital Neuralgia Paroxysmal shooting/electric-shock pain in distribution of GON/LON; scalp allodynia; positive Tinel's over occipital nerve; responds to nerve block May be reduced GON tender, not facet Nerve block, gabapentin Giant Cell Arteritis >50 years; temporal artery tenderness; jaw claudication; ESR >50; visual symptoms Negative Absent Urgent steroids prednisolone 40–60mg TMJ Dysfunction Pain at TMJ; jaw movement provocation; ear pain; clicking Negative Absent Dental/maxillofacial Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Obese female; pulsatile tinnitus; visual obscurations; papilloedema; worse lying Negative Absent Urgent neurology --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Self-referral to physiotherapy: Available in most HSC Trust areas Belfast, South Eastern, Western, Northern, Southern Trusts — patient contacts physiotherapy department directly without GP referral. Headache Clinics HSC NI : - Belfast City Hospital Neurology - Antrim Area Hospital - Altnagelvin Hospital Western Trust - Referral via GP; waiting times variable — 2026 targets: 18 weeks RTT --- Conservative Management Evidence Base Jull et al 2002 — Landmark RCT Spine, 27 17 : 1835–1843 - n=200; 4 groups: manual therapy MT alone, specific exercise alone, combined MT+exercise, control - Key finding: Combined MT + specific cervical exercise produced significantly better outcomes than either alone or control - 10-week intervention; outcomes at 12 months - Combined group: 76% had ≥50% reduction in headache frequency at 12 months - Manual therapy: targeted upper cervical manipulation and mobilisation - Exercise: specific craniocervical flexion training deep cervical flexors C1-2 SNAG Sustained Natural Apophyseal Glide — Mulligan Concept Technique: - Patient seated; therapist applies sustained posteroanterior glide to C1-2 on the symptomatic side using thumb/pisiform contact on the C2 spinous process / articular pillar - Patient performs active cervical rotation in direction of restriction whilst glide is sustained - If pain-free rotation improves → positive response, proceed with treatment - 3 sets × 10 repetitions; can be self-applied with towel home SNAG Evidence: - Hall et al 2007, 2008 : C1-2 SNAG significantly reduces headache frequency and intensity in CGH - Paungmali et al 2003 : SNAG produces hypoalgesic effect — pressure pain threshold increases - Significant improvement in CFRT range of motion following C1-2 SNAG Hall et al, 2007 Upper Cervical Mobilisation - Passive accessory intervertebral movements PAIVMs at C0-C1, C1-C2, C2-C3 - Grades III–IV Maitland grading to restricted, painful segments - May include: atlanto-occipital decompression, C1-2 rotation mobilisation in flexion - Dose: 3–5 sets of 30–60 second sustained holds or oscillatory grades; reassess after each set - Evidence: Jull et al 1997, 2002 ; Zito et al 2006 — upper cervical manual examination and mobilisation reliably identifies and treats CGH Specific Cervical Flexor Retraining Deep Cervical Flexor DCF Training Protocol Jull et al, 2008 : Stage 1 — Activation Weeks 1–2 : - Craniocervical flexion nodding in supine - Pressure biofeedback: target 22 mmHg; 10 × 10-second holds - Avoid SCM/anterior scalene substitution Stage 2 — Endurance Weeks 3–4 : - Progress biofeedback target: 24–26 mmHg - 10 × 10-second holds at each level; 3 levels progressed sequentially Stage 3 — Functional Integration Weeks 5–10 : - DCF activation during functional tasks - Sitting posture training - Progress to 28–30 mmHg as tolerated Stage 4 — Load/Strength Weeks 8–12 : - Resistance exercises: supine neck flexion with gravity resistance - Integration with cervical rotation and lateral flexion Postural Management - Identify and correct forward head posture FHP — increases loading on upper cervical joints and suboccipital muscles - Thoracic mobility: thoracic extension exercises, foam roller mobilisation T4–T8 - Workstation ergonomics assessment — screen height, chair position - Sleep posture: single pillow maintaining neutral cervical alignment; cervical pillow if indicated - Evidence: Ruivo et al 2017 — FHP correction reduces frequency of cervicogenic-type headache; correlation between FHP and CGH prevalence Exercise Prescription Summary Component Exercise Sets × Reps Frequency ----------- ---------- ------------- ----------- DCF activation CCF exercise biofeedback 3 × 10 × 10s holds Daily Cervical mobility CFRT self-mobilisation SNAG in flexion 3 × 10 Daily Suboccipital stretching Self-suboccipital release / chin tuck stretch 3 × 30s 2× daily Thoracic extension Foam roller extension T4-T8 3 × 60s Daily Scapular stabilisation Wall angels / low row 3 × 15 3×/week Postural re-education Chin tuck + retraction in sitting Hourly work breaks Daily --- Pharmacological Management Physiotherapy is the first-line recommended treatment for CGH. Pharmacological management is adjunctive and should be coordinated with the patient's GP. Analgesia NICE CG150 — Headaches in over 12s, 2012/Updated 2021 - Acute analgesia: Aspirin 900mg or Ibuprofen 400mg with food — first-line for acute CGH episodes - Paracetamol: 1g — alternative but less evidence in CGH specifically - Triptans: Not recommended for CGH mechanism differs from migraine; poor response rate - Opioids: Avoid in primary headache disorders; risk of medication overuse headache Nerve Blocks - Greater occipital nerve GON block: Methylprednisolone 40–80mg + lidocaine 1%; injection at occipital protuberance medial 1/3 of line from mastoid to protuberance - Evidence: Inan et al 2001 — GON block effective in CGH; duration of relief 4–8 weeks - Third occipital nerve TON block / C2-3 medial branch block: Diagnostic and therapeutic; available at Belfast City Hospital Pain Clinic - Referral for nerve block: Via GP or physio urgent recommendation if conservative management fails at 6–8 weeks Radiofrequency Neurotomy - Third occipital nerve RFN pulsed or conventional - Indication: Confirmed C2-3 facet-mediated CGH positive diagnostic block ; failed conservative management - Evidence: Lord et al 1996 — conventional RFN of TON: median pain-free period 297 days vs 8 days sham - Available via: Belfast City Hospital Pain Management / Neurosurgery Botulinum Toxin Botox - Limited evidence specifically for CGH stronger evidence base in chronic migraine - May be considered for refractory CGH via neurology/pain clinic - NICE TA260 2012 : Botox approved for chronic migraine ≥15 headache days/month ; not specifically for CGH - Use in CGH remains off-label / specialist decision Preventive Pharmacology for refractory/chronic CGH, via neurology - Amitriptyline 10–25mg nocte low-dose; not NICE approved for CGH specifically; pragmatic use - Gabapentin — particularly if occipital neuralgia component - NSAIDs regular, with PPI cover — short-term preventive role - All preventive medications: initiate via GP or neurology; monitor and review at 3–6 months --- Onward Referral Criteria Emergency referral 999 / A&E if: - Thunderclap headache / worst-ever headache - Signs of meningism neck stiffness + fever + photophobia - Focal neurological deficit with headache - Headache + altered consciousness Urgent GP same-day referral if: - New headache in patient >50 years - Suspected giant cell arteritis jaw claudication, temporal tenderness, visual symptoms - Postural headache positional; worse upright - Headache consistently worse with Valsalva/cough/straining - Accelerating headache pattern over weeks Routine neurology referral via GP if: - Failure to progress after 8–12 weeks of appropriate physiotherapy - Diagnostic uncertainty — atypical features - Consideration of botulinum toxin or preventive pharmacology - Sleep disturbance, significant psychological comorbidity requiring multidisciplinary input - Patient request or GP clinical judgement Pain Clinic / Interventional Referral via GP/neurology if: - Diagnostic cervical medial branch blocks required C2-3, TON - GON block indicated failed conservative management ≥3 months - Radiofrequency neurotomy consideration confirmed C2-3 CGH - Spinal cord stimulation intractable, multidisciplinary team decision Physiotherapy discharge / step-up criteria: - Step-up if: no ≥30% improvement in headache frequency after 4–6 sessions - Discharge if: headache frequency reduced ≥50%, patient self-managing, goals achieved - Provide written home programme and self-management plan at discharge --- Key References > All references are from peer-reviewed literature. title: Mechanical Neck Pain
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Mechanical neck pain MNP is the most prevalent cervical spine condition, with a point prevalence of ~14–15% globally and lifetime prevalence up to 67% Fejer et al., 2006 . content: Overview & Pathophysiology Mechanical neck pain MNP is the most prevalent cervical spine condition, with a point prevalence of ~14–15% globally and lifetime prevalence up to 67% Fejer et al., 2006 . It is the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide Hoy et al., 2014 . Annual incidence in UK primary care is approximately 15% of adult consultations involving neck-related complaints. Definition: Neck pain of musculoskeletal origin without neurological involvement, arising from cervical structures including intervertebral discs, facet joints, muscles, ligaments, and associated fasciae. Reproduced or modified by cervical movement and mechanical loading. Pathological sources: - Facet joints zygapophyseal joints : Most common identifiable pain source ~54% in chronic neck pain by Bogduk & McGuirk, 2006 ; intra-articular meniscoid inclusions, capsular strain, synovitis - Intervertebral disc discogenic pain : Annular tears, internal disc disruption; C5/6 and C6/7 most common - Muscles and myofascial tissue: Trapezius, levator scapulae, splenius capitis, suboccipitals — trigger points, postural overload - Ligaments: Posterior longitudinal, interspinous ligaments with repetitive strain - Atlantoaxial and atlanto-occipital joints: Particularly relevant in upper cervical pain Classification Guzman et al., 2008 — Bone and Joint Decade 2000–2010 Task Force : - Grade I: No signs of major pathology, does not interfere with daily activities - Grade II: No signs of major pathology, does interfere with daily activities - Grade III: Neck pain with neurological signs radiculopathy - Grade IV: Neck pain with signs of major structural pathology MNP broadly covers Grades I–II. Risk factors: - Sustained postures sedentary work, screen use >6 hours/day - Psychosocial: high job demands, low control, poor support, depression, anxiety - Previous neck pain episode strongest predictor of recurrence - Female sex RR ~1.4 - Age 45–54 years peak - Sleep disturbance Prognosis: Most acute MNP >50% resolves within 6 weeks; however, ~40–50% develop persistent or recurrent symptoms at 1 year Haldeman et al., 2008 . --- Special Tests Mechanical neck pain is primarily a diagnosis of exclusion — the primary role of clinical assessment is to rule out serious pathology and neurological involvement, then classify the mechanical presentation. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR −LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Spurling's negative — rules in MNP over radiculopathy 0.50–0.60 0.86–0.97 — — High ruling out radiculopathy Passive cervical rotation 10° 4. Pain with spring test at C3–5 5. Not performing sedentary work >50% of day Key assessments: - Active ROM goniometry or CROM device : flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation — establish baseline and monitor - PPIVMs : C2–7 intersegmental mobility - PAIVMs : posteroanterior pressure C1–7 — identify comparable sign pain provocation at symptomatic segment - Deep neck flexor endurance : CCFT or cranio-cervical flexion endurance test — assess neuromuscular control - Postural assessment : forward head posture, thoracic kyphosis, scapular position --- Red Flags Screening is essential at every new presentation and reassessment: NICE CKS Red Flags for Neck Pain: - Significant trauma consider fracture — Canadian C-Spine Rule - Malignancy: unexplained weight loss, previous cancer, thoracic pain, rest pain - Infection: fever, immunosuppression, recent spinal procedure - Inflammatory arthritis: morning stiffness >1 hour, bilateral joint involvement, systemic features - Myelopathy signs: bilateral neurological symptoms, gait disturbance, bladder/bowel dysfunction - Cauda equina equivalent very rare at cervical : bilateral upper limb weakness + bladder/bowel - Vertebrobasilar/cervical artery dysfunction: 5 D's + 3 N's see cervical-artery-dysfunction.mdx - Persistent severe headache with neck stiffness + photophobia → consider meningism Canadian C-Spine Rule Stiell et al., 2001 : No imaging required if ALL: age 29 work subscale predict poor return-to-work; inform targeted management --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis MNP is a clinical diagnosis — imaging rarely changes management in uncomplicated cases. Imaging guidelines: - NICE NG59 2016 : Do not routinely offer imaging for non-specific neck pain; MRI only if surgical referral or red flags - X-ray: low utility for soft tissue pathology; use if fracture suspected post-trauma, osteoporosis, malignancy - CT: bony anatomy, foraminal stenosis, OPLL when MRI contraindicated - Normal imaging does NOT exclude pain; degenerative changes are ubiquitous and poorly correlate with symptoms Key evidence: - Asymptomatic degenerative changes on MRI present in: 87% at age 70, 50% at age 40 Boden et al., 1990 - Imaging findings should be interpreted within clinical context — avoid iatrogenic nocebo - Systematic review Rubinstein & van Tulder, 2008 : clinical examination sufficient for diagnosis and management in non-complex cases Yellow Flag Screening STarT MSK : - Prognostic stratification improves outcomes vs. one-size-fits-all care Hill et al., 2011 — LBP evidence extrapolated to neck pain; Beneciuk et al., 2013 for cervical --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Cervical radiculopathy Radicular arm pain in dermatomal pattern, positive Spurling's, neurological deficit Cervicogenic headache Headache referral from C1–3, positive FRT, unilateral, occipital to frontotemporal Fibromyalgia Widespread pain, multiple tender points, fatigue, sleep disturbance Rheumatoid arthritis / inflammatory arthritis Morning stiffness, bilateral, systemic features, elevated ESR/CRP, ANA positive Ankylosing spondylitis Young male, sacroiliac involvement, HLA-B27, bamboo spine on X-ray Thoracic outlet syndrome Positional vascular/neurogenic symptoms with arm elevation Temporomandibular joint dysfunction Jaw pain, crepitus, bruxism, ear pain, limited mouth opening Occipital neuralgia Sharp, stabbing occipital pain, positive Tinel over GON, distinct from cervicogenic headache Whiplash associated disorder Mechanism of injury acceleration-deceleration , specific classification WAD grade Muscle tension headache Bilateral, pressure/band-like, no photophobia, not worsened by movement --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care: - GP can prescribe short-term analgesia and refer to community physiotherapy - Direct access physiotherapy available in some NI Trusts Belfast, Northern - Self-referral to community MSK services varies by Trust - First-contact physiotherapy FCP being rolled out in GP surgeries — appropriate for MNP triage Community MSK Physiotherapy: - Primary treatment setting for Grade I–II MNP - Stratified care based on STarT MSK risk: - Low: 2–3 sessions + self-management advice - Medium: 6–8 sessions with structured programme - High: 8–12 sessions + psychology/pain service liaison - NICE NG59: Offer exercise therapy, manual therapy, and psychological support as package - Consider group education/exercise cost-effective for low-medium risk Occupational Health / Work-Related Neck Pain: - Ergonomic assessment and workplace modification — coordinate with employer OH service - Fit notes Statement of Fitness for Work : physiotherapists can provide reports but not fit notes; liaise with GP Conservative Management Exercise Therapy Grade A — highest evidence for neck pain : - Deep neck flexor DNF strengthening : Craniocervical flexion test CCFT protocol — progressive pressure biofeedback 20–26–30 mmHg ; Jull et al. 2002, 2009 - Proven superior to general neck exercise for chronic neck pain - 8–10 week programme; 3–5 × per week - Cervical and scapulothoracic strengthening : Trapezius, rhomboids, serratus anterior — 3 × 10–15 RM, progressive - Aerobic exercise : Walking, swimming; reduces disability and pain catastrophising; NICE recommendation - Proprioceptive/sensorimotor training : Joint position error retraining; laser pointer head exercises; supports neuromuscular control deficits in chronic neck pain Revel et al., 1994 - Stretching : Suboccipital, levator scapulae, scalenes; limited standalone evidence but patient-valued and safe Manual Therapy Grade B–A : - Combined manipulation + exercise superior to either alone Hoving et al., 2002; Hurwitz et al., 2002 - Cervical mobilisation : Safe and effective; Maitland Grade III–IV PAIVMs/PPIVMs - Cervical HVLA manipulation : Short-term benefit for acute/subacute neck pain; requires informed consent, CAD screening IFOMPT 2012 framework ; contraindicated in red flags/myelopathy - Thoracic manipulation : Level A evidence adjunct for cervical pain Cleland et al., 2005, 2007 - Soft tissue therapy : Trigger point release, myofascial release — adjunct; limited standalone evidence Patient Education Grade A : - PNE: Explain pain as non-threatening; reassure re: natural history; de-medicalize - Postural advice: Ergonomic screen height, chair adjustment, monitor distance, pillow height cervical neutral - Activity modification: Avoid sustained end-range postures >20–30 minutes without movement break - Return to activity encouraged: "motion is lotion" messaging Dry Needling / Acupuncture: - Trigger point dry needling: Moderate evidence for short-term pain relief in myofascial neck pain Tough et al., 2009 - Acupuncture: NICE allows referral for chronic pain where appropriate NICE NG193, 2021 ; 10 sessions maximum via NHS Pharmacological NICE-aligned - Paracetamol : First-line; 1g QDS; limited evidence for musculoskeletal neck pain NICE NG59 - NSAIDs : Ibuprofen 400 mg TDS or Naproxen 500 mg BD with food; 2–4 weeks maximum; GI protection omeprazole if >45 years, smoker, or prior GI history NICE NG193 - Topical NSAIDs : Diclofenac gel — preferred in elderly for GI/CV risk reduction - Muscle relaxants : Diazepam 2 mg TDS acute muscle spasm only; 5–7 days maximum ; addictive potential — use sparingly - Amitriptyline 10–30 mg nocte : for sleep disturbance and chronic pain modulation; off-label - Avoid long-term opioids for mechanical neck pain NICE NG193 2021 — chronic primary pain: do not offer opioids Onward Referral Criteria Urgent same-day : - Red flags: suspected fracture, malignancy, infection, myelopathy - New bladder/bowel dysfunction Routine referral: - Failure to improve after 6–12 weeks of optimal physiotherapy - Suspected radiculopathy or myelopathy requiring imaging - Diagnostic uncertainty requiring specialist assessment - Persistent severe pain requiring Pain Clinic input - Significant psychosocial barriers → Psychology/CBT referral Occupational: - Inability to return to work after 4–6 weeks → Occupational health referral --- Key References 1. Hoy D, March L, Woolf A, et al. The global burden of neck pain: estimates from the global burden of disease 2010 study. Ann Rheum Dis . 2014;73 7 :1309–1315. 3. Jull G, Trott P, Potter H, et al. A randomized controlled trial of exercise and manipulative therapy for cervicogenic headache. Spine . 2002;27 17 :1835–1843. 4. Childs JD, Fritz JM, Flynn TW, et al. A clinical prediction rule to identify patients with low back pain most likely to benefit from spinal manipulation: a validation study. Ann Intern Med . 2004;141 12 :920–928. 5. Cleland JA, Childs JD, Fritz JM, Whitman JM, Eberhart SL. Development of a clinical prediction rule for guiding treatment of a subgroup of patients with neck pain: use of thoracic spine manipulation, exercise, and patient education. Phys Ther . 2007;87 1 :9–23. 6. Hoving JL, Koes BW, de Vet HC, et al. Manual therapy, physical therapy, or continued care by a general practitioner for patients with neck pain. Ann Intern Med . 2002;136 10 :713–722. 7. Pool JJ, Ostelo RW, Hoving JL, Bouter LM, de Vet HC. Minimal clinically important change of the neck disability index and the numerical rating scale for patients with neck pain. Spine . 2007;32 26 :3047–3051. 8. Hill JC, Whitehurst DG, Lewis M, et al.
