title: Whiplash Associated Disorders
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Whiplash Associated Disorders WAD is the term describing the constellation of symptoms following an acceleration-deceleration injury to the cervical spine, most commonly from motor vehicle collisions MVCs . The Québec Task Force QTF on Whiplash-Associated Disorders Spitzer
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Whiplash Associated Disorders WAD is the term describing the constellation of symptoms following an acceleration-deceleration injury to the cervical spine, most commonly from motor vehicle collisions MVCs . The Québec Task Force QTF on Whiplash-Associated Disorders Spitzer et al., 1995 provides the foundational classification framework. Epidemiology: - Annual incidence: 235–300 per 100,000 in Western countries - UK: ~250,000–300,000 per year; high rates linked to insurance claims CEGA/ABI data - Most common MVC injury type; estimated annual cost to NHS and insurance >£2 billion - Female:Male ratio ~1.4:1 - Peak incidence: 20–40 years Mechanism of Injury: - Rear-end collision most common: initial extension of lower cervical spine followed by rapid flexion of upper cervical spine S-curve deformation - This S-shaped motion is different from simple extension — it causes: - Stretching of anterior longitudinal ligament - Compression of posterior elements facet joints, nerve roots - Differential motion between segments with relative translation - Strain of zygapophyseal joint capsules most consistent pain source - Side-impact and frontal collisions also produce WAD with different biomechanics - No single lesion visible on standard imaging in most cases hence "soft tissue injury" Pathological pain sources: 1. Zygapophyseal facet joints — most consistently identified pain source; Barnsley et al. 1995 demonstrated by diagnostic nerve blocks that facet joint pain present in ~54% of chronic WAD 2. Intervertebral discs : Annular tears, especially C5/6 and C6/7 3. Musculature : Multifidus, semispinalis, suboccipitals — MRI evidence of fatty infiltration and atrophy in chronic WAD Elliott et al., 2006 4. Neural tissue : Dorsal root ganglia sensitisation; central sensitisation 5. Ligamentous injury : Alar, transverse, C2–3 ligaments rare but important in higher grades 6. Sympathetic nervous system involvement : autonomic dysregulation; links to widespread hypersensitivity Neurobiological Mechanisms: - Peripheral sensitisation: nociceptors in joint capsule, disc sensitised by mechanical and chemical stimuli - Central sensitisation: key driver of chronic WAD — explains widespread hypersensitivity, cold hyperalgesia, psychological distress seen in Grade III WAD - Psychosocial factors amplify and perpetuate sensitisation Québec Task Force Classification: Grade Clinical Presentation ------- ----------------------- WAD 0 No neck complaints, no physical signs WAD I Neck complaint pain, stiffness, tenderness , no physical signs WAD II Neck complaint + musculoskeletal signs reduced ROM, point tenderness WAD III Neck complaint + neurological signs reflex changes, weakness, sensory deficit WAD IV Neck complaint + fracture or dislocation WAD III is analogous to cervical radiculopathy following whiplash mechanism. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR −LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Cold Hyperalgesia cold pain threshold as predictor of chronicity 0.72 0.65 2.1 0.43 Moderate Chien et al., 2008 Widespread Pressure Pain Hyperalgesia PPT 0.68 0.64 1.9 0.50 Moderate Spurling's Test for WAD III/radiculopathy 0.50–0.60 0.86–0.97 3.5–6.1 0.47 High ULNT1 median nerve neurodynamic 0.72–0.97 0.22–0.33 1.1–1.3 0.12 Moderate Neck Distraction Test WAD III 0.44 0.90 4.4 0.62 Moderate Cervical ROM 1m height or 5 stairs; axial load to head; high-speed MVC >100 km/h; rollover; ejection; motorised recreational vehicle; bicycle collision - Paraesthesia in extremities Low-risk factors allow safe assessment — if any present AND no high-risk factors AND can rotate 45°, imaging not required : - Simple rear-end MVC - Sitting in ED - Ambulatory at any time since collision - Delayed onset of neck pain - Absence of midline cervical tenderness NEXUS Criteria alternative — imaging NOT needed if ALL 5 met : 1. No midline cervical tenderness 2. No focal neurological deficit 3. Normal alertness 4. No intoxication 5. No distracting painful injury WAD IV fracture/dislocation : - Do NOT mobilise cervical spine - Refer to ED/trauma team immediately - Cervical immobilisation until cleared Cervical Artery Dysfunction post-trauma : - Traumatic vertebral artery dissection can present as WAD - Symptoms: severe occipital/neck pain, unilateral facial numbness, Horner's syndrome, ataxia, brainstem signs - 5 D's + 3 N's - CTA/MRA required if suspected → Emergency Spinal cord injury indicators: - Bilateral paraesthesia, weakness - Bladder/bowel dysfunction - Hyperreflexia, Hoffman's sign - Lhermitte's sign --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Concept - Acute WAD 0–6 weeks : Grade I–II oscillatory techniques for pain modulation; gentle cervical mobilisation - Subacute/chronic >6 weeks : Progress to Grade III–IV techniques addressing stiffness; PAIVMs/PPIVMs - Comparable sign methodology: identify and track comparable pain response - Avoid techniques that peripheralise neurological symptoms WAD III McKenzie / MDT - Acute WAD: pain frequently multidirectional initially; retraction exercises as starting point - Look for directional preference may be slower to emerge than in disc pathology - If centralisation occurs → directional exercise - Education re: natural history and active recovery integral to MDT approach Graded Activity / Behavioural Approach - Evidence supports active management over passive rest in WAD I–II Rosenfeld et al., 2003 - Graded activity exposure: progressive increase in meaningful activities despite pain - Graded motor imagery GMI and mirror therapy: limited evidence; consider in complex chronic WAD Psychologically Informed Practice PiP - Critical in medium-high risk WAD IES-R ≥26, TSK ≥37 - Address fear-avoidance, catastrophising, catastrophic thinking about injury - CBT-based physiotherapy Linton & Andersson, 2000 principles - Link with psychology services for high-risk presentations Sterling's Risk-Stratified Approach 2010 - Low risk WAD I–II, low distress : Self-management advice, reassurance, brief physiotherapy - Moderate risk WAD II–III, moderate distress : 8–10 sessions physiotherapy + progressive exercise + psychological support - High risk high distress, widespread hyperalgesia : Intensive physiotherapy + psychology liaison + pharmacological management of central sensitisation --- Outcome Measures Neck Disability Index NDI - Primary outcome for WAD disability - MCID : 7.5 points 50-point scale ; chronic WAD: 8.5 points Jull et al., 2014 - Use at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 12 months - NDI ≥30% at 1 month predicts chronic disability Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS - 0–10; MCID : 2.1 points in WAD Sterling et al., 2010 - Measure arm pain if WAD III and neck pain separately Patient-Specific Functional Scale PSFS - Highly responsive to change; MCID : 2.0 points average - Functional activities specific to patient's life/work Impact of Event Scale-Revised IES-R - 22-item PTSD screening tool; score 0–88 - ≥26: moderate impact risk of PTSD ; ≥33: probable PTSD - Not an outcome measure per se but critical prognostic screener in WAD - Re-administer at 4 weeks if initially borderline Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia TSK - 17-item scale; 17–68; ≥37 = high kinesiophobia - MCID : 4 points; use alongside FABQ to guide psychosocial management GROC Global Rating of Change - 15-point scale; meaningful improvement ≥+5 - 6 weeks, 3 months, discharge Whiplash Disability Questionnaire WDQ - 13-item WAD-specific disability questionnaire; 0–130 - MCID : 13.3 points; validated specifically in whiplash populations Pinfold et al., 2004 --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis No imaging required for WAD 0–II without high-risk features Canadian C-Spine Rule . Imaging guidelines: - X-ray: rule out fracture/dislocation; dynamic X-rays flexion/extension for suspected instability — limited sensitivity - CT: preferred for high-energy trauma; superior bony detail; rule out fracture, SCIWORA - MRI: WAD III neurological signs or if neurological deterioration; assess disc, cord, nerve root; also for suspected ligamentous injury - CTA/MRA: Suspected traumatic vertebral or internal carotid artery dissection — urgent Prognostic factors strong evidence — Walton et al., 2013 systematic review : - High initial pain intensity NRS ≥5 : negative prognostic factor - High initial disability NDI ≥30% : negative prognostic factor - Cold hyperalgesia: negative prognostic factor central sensitisation marker - Psychological distress IES-R, anxiety : negative prognostic factor - Low self-efficacy: negative prognostic factor - Compensation claims in some jurisdictions: controversial; complex psychosocial interaction Active management vs. rest: - Rosenfeld et al. 2003 RCT: Active treatment early mobilisation superior to collar/rest at 6 months and 3 years - Söderlund & Lindberg 2001 : early activation combined with education reduces progression to chronicity --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Cervical fracture/dislocation WAD IV High-energy mechanism, midline tenderness, neurological deficit, X-ray/CT confirms Traumatic vertebral artery dissection Severe occipital headache, brainstem signs, Horner's, ataxia — CTA/MRI Traumatic disc herniation WAD III Radicular symptoms, positive Spurling's/distraction, MRI confirmation Concussion / mild TBI Associated head impact, cognitive symptoms, headache, vestibular signs TMJ injury post-MVC Jaw pain, crepitus, limited mouth opening, pain with chewing PTSD Psychological re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal — IES-R ≥33; requires psychology Shoulder injury rotator cuff Mechanism of arm bracing, shoulder-localised pain, arc test Thoracic outlet syndrome Vascular/neurogenic symptoms with arm elevation, positional SCIWORA Spinal cord injury without radiological abnormality — MRI required --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Acute WAD 0–12 weeks : - GP/ED → early physiotherapy referral target within 2–4 weeks of injury - Community MSK physiotherapy as primary treatment for WAD I–II - Evidence supports early active physiotherapy over collar/rest Rosenfeld et al., 2003 - Insurance/medico-legal context: Physiotherapists should document objectively; be aware of PSNI/motor insurer reporting norms - Immediate Access Physiotherapy at ED/MIU available in some NI ED departments for WAD I–II Subacute/Chronic WAD >12 weeks : - Continue community physiotherapy with biopsychosocial approach - Pain Clinic referral for persistent severe pain or suspected central sensitisation - Psychology referral for high IES-R, confirmed PTSD features - Spinal Surgery referral if WAD III with confirmed disc herniation/radiculopathy not responding to 12 weeks conservative management Medico-Legal Considerations NI specific : - Personal Injury Assessment Board PIAB / Compensation Recovery Unit processes - Whiplash Reform Programme England & Wales — different legislation applies; NI follows Civil Liability Contribution Act 1978 and common law - Standardised assessment and objective documentation essential Conservative Management Active Treatment — Grade A evidence: Exercise: - Early active mobilisation: gentle cervical ROM exercises from day 1 post-injury Rosenfeld et al., 2003 — significantly better outcomes than immobilisation - Progressive cervical and scapulothoracic strengthening — as per mechanical neck pain protocol - Deep neck flexor activation CCFT protocol — impaired in acute and chronic WAD Jull et al., 2008 - Proprioceptive/sensorimotor exercises: laser pointer gaze stability, joint position error retraining Manual Therapy — Grade B: - Cervical mobilisation: Maitland Grade I–II → III–IV as irritability settles - Thoracic manipulation: safer alternative to cervical HVLA; Grade A evidence as adjunct - Cervical HVLA: use with caution; screen for CAD IFOMPT 2012 ; informed consent mandatory; avoid in acute WAD with signs of instability or high IES-R Education — Grade A: - Most powerful single intervention for acute WAD with exercise - Reassurance: natural history is favourable in WAD I–II; >70% recover within 3 months - Pain neuroscience education: address sensitisation, avoid catastrophising - Activity continuation messaging: "keep moving, stay active" - Whiplash patient information booklet RACGP/Arthritis Australia evidence-based resources applicable to NI Physical Modalities: - Heat/ice: minimal evidence; low harm; patient-directed short-term use - TENS: limited evidence; may provide short-term pain relief - Ultrasound/laser: insufficient evidence; not recommended as primary treatment - Acupuncture: Moderate evidence for short-term pain relief in chronic neck pain; NICE allows referral Psychological Approaches High-Risk WAD : - CBT-based physiotherapy: fear-avoidance model - Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing EMDR : for confirmed PTSD — psychology-delivered - Acceptance and Commitment Therapy ACT principles incorporated into physiotherapy Pharmacological NICE-aligned Acute 6 weeks : - Neuropathic agents if sensory hypersensitivity features: Gabapentin/Pregabalin — NICE NG173 - Amitriptyline 10–30 mg nocte : sleep, pain modulation, low-dose - Avoid long-term opioids: NICE NG193 does not recommend for chronic primary pain Injections: - Medial branch blocks / radiofrequency neurotomy for confirmed facet joint pain Barnsley et al., 1995; Lord et al., 1996 : evidence-based for chronic WAD with confirmed facet pain; refer to Pain Clinic/Spinal service Onward Referral Criteria Emergency: - Suspected fracture, dislocation WAD IV → ED - Suspected CAD/vertebral artery dissection → ED + vascular/neurosurgery - Acute spinal cord injury signs → ED Urgent: - WAD III with progressive neurological deficit → spine surgery - Suspected PTSD → psychology within 4 weeks Routine: - Failure of 12 weeks conservative management → consider Pain Clinic - Persistent WAD III → spine surgery opinion - High psychological distress not responding to PiP → formal psychology/CBT referral --- Key References 1. Spitzer WO, Skovron ML, Salmi LR, et al. Scientific monograph of the Québec Task Force on Whiplash-Associated Disorders. Spine . 1995;20 8 Suppl :1S–73S. 2. Stiell IG, Wells GA, Vandemheen K, et al. The Canadian C-Spine Rule for radiography in alert and stable trauma patients. JAMA . 2001;286 15 :1841–1848. 3. Barnsley L, Lord S, Wallis B, Bogduk N. The prevalence of chronic cervical zygapophyseal joint pain after whiplash. Spine . 1995;20 1 :20–25. 4. Sterling M, Jull G, Vicenzino B, Kenardy J. Sensory hypersensitivity occurs soon after whiplash injury and is associated with poor recovery. Pain . 2003;104 3 :509–517. 5. Sterling M. A proposed new classification system for whiplash associated disorders — implications for assessment and management. Man Ther . 2004;9 2 :60–70. 6. Rosenfeld M, Gunnarsson R, Borenstein P. Risk factors for persistent problems following whiplash injury: results of a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther . 2009;39 5 :334–350. 8. Elliott JM, Jull GA, Noteboom JT, Darnell R, Galloway G, Gibbon WW. Pain . 2007;129 1–2 :28–34. 11. NICE. Neck pain – whiplash injury. Clinical Knowledge Summary. 2023. Available at: cks.nice.org.uk/topics/neck-pain-whiplash-injury/ 12. title: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome (Ulnar Neuropathy at the Elbow)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Cubital tunnel syndrome CuTS is the second most common peripheral nerve entrapment syndrome after carpal tunnel syndrome , accounting for approximately 20% of peripheral nerve compressions. Prevalence estimates range from 25–38 per 100,000 person-years; higher in manual wo
headings: Elbow Extension Splinting at Night Grade A
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Cubital tunnel syndrome CuTS is the second most common peripheral nerve entrapment syndrome after carpal tunnel syndrome , accounting for approximately 20% of peripheral nerve compressions. Prevalence estimates range from 25–38 per 100,000 person-years; higher in manual workers, musicians, and those with habitual elbow flexion. Anatomy of the Cubital Tunnel: The cubital tunnel is a fibroosseous tunnel at the medial elbow through which the ulnar nerve passes. Key anatomical structures: - Floor: Medial collateral ligament ulnar head and posterior capsule - Roof: Osborne's fascia arcuate ligament — the most common site of compression - Walls: Medial epicondyle medial , olecranon lateral - Contents: Ulnar nerve + accompanying vessels Other sites of ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow: 1. Medial intermuscular septum proximal compression 2. Arcade of Struthers fascial band, 8 cm proximal to medial epicondyle 3. Cubital tunnel Osborne's fascia — most common 4. Between heads of flexor carpi ulnaris distal to cubital tunnel Pathophysiology of compression: - During elbow flexion, the cubital tunnel narrows by 55% MacNicol 1979 , increasing intraneural pressure - Normal nerve: 7–8 mmHg at rest; cubital tunnel pressure rises to 100–200 mmHg at 90° flexion - Sustained compression → intraneural oedema → myelin loss → axonal degeneration in severe/chronic cases - Nerve subluxation snapping over medial epicondyle in 20% of population → repetitive traction injury Risk factors: - Habitual elbow flexion sleeping, driving, phone use - Prolonged leaning on medial elbow - Repetitive elbow flexion-extension overhead athletes, musicians - Medial epicondyle fracture/deformity - Cubitus valgus deformity - Medial elbow osteoarthritis, loose bodies - Diabetes mellitus peripheral neuropathy — double crush - Obesity, smoking --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Elbow Flexion Test 0.75 0.99 75.0 0.25 High Tinel's Sign at Cubital Tunnel 0.70 0.66 2.06 0.45 Moderate Elbow Flexion + Wrist Extension Novak's combined 0.98 0.95 19.6 0.02 High Scratch Collapse Test 0.69 0.99 69.0 0.31 Moderate-High Froment's Sign intrinsic weakness — adductor pollicis 0.82 0.87 6.31 0.21 Moderate-High Wartenberg's Sign abducted little finger 0.76 0.68 2.38 0.35 Moderate First Dorsal Interosseous Wasting 0.68 0.91 7.56 0.35 Moderate 2-Point Discrimination ulnar territory 0.62 0.84 3.88 0.45 Moderate Grip Strength Deficit 0.71 0.61 1.82 0.48 Low-Moderate Pinch Strength Deficit lateral pinch 0.78 0.64 2.17 0.34 Moderate Elbow Flexion Test Wadsworth 1987 : Patient maximally flexes elbow with wrist extended, held for 60 seconds. Positive = tingling/numbness in ring and little finger. Best single test for CuTS. Novak's Combined Provocation Test: Elbow flexion + wrist extension + pressure over cubital tunnel × 60 seconds. Near-perfect sensitivity; highest diagnostic value. Scratch Collapse Test Cheng et al. 2008 : Examiner scratches skin over suspected compression site; patient momentarily loses shoulder resistance. Highly specific for nerve compression location. Froment's Sign: Patient holds paper between thumb and index finger; examiner pulls paper away. Positive = thumb IP joint flexes compensating for adductor pollicis weakness with FPL — indicates ulnar nerve motor involvement. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Urgent assessment and escalation required. - Rapidly progressive motor deficit: Significant intrinsic muscle wasting or clawing developing over days-weeks → urgent surgical referral nerve decompression within weeks to prevent permanent deficit - Complete sensory loss in ulnar distribution with marked motor weakness → severe/advanced compression; surgical review as priority - Post-traumatic ulnar neuropathy following elbow fracture medial epicondyle, supracondylar, distal humerus : late-onset ulnar palsy may be progressive → orthopaedic + neurophysiology - Cubitus valgus with ulnar neuropathy tardy ulnar palsy : may be post-traumatic childhood fracture ; progressive without intervention → surgical decompression/transposition - Rapidly expanding medial elbow mass: Suspect ganglion, lipoma, tumour compressing nerve → urgent imaging + referral - Pancoast tumour/Thoracic outlet: Pain radiating from shoulder/neck into ulnar distribution; Horner's syndrome; weight loss → urgent chest X-ray + CT - Double crush syndrome: Concurrent cervical radiculopathy C8/T1 + cubital tunnel compression; both sites need treatment --- Clinical Frameworks McGowan Classification of CuTS Severity Grade Symptoms Sensory Motor Management ------- ---------- --------- ------- ------------ I Mild Intermittent paraesthesia; minimal Normal or intermittent loss Normal intrinsics Conservative splinting, activity modification II Moderate Persistent paraesthesia; aching Constant sensory deficit Moderate weakness Conservative trial 3–6 months; consider surgery III Severe Constant symptoms Marked sensory deficit Significant wasting; clawing Surgical decompression; conservative unlikely to succeed Dellon Classification - Mild: Intermittent paraesthesia; positive elbow flexion test; no muscle weakness - Moderate: Intermittent paraesthesia; positive provocative tests; weak interossei - Severe: Persistent paraesthesia; clawing; intrinsic muscle atrophy Neurodynamic Assessment Upper Limb Neurodynamic Test 3 ULNT3 — ulnar bias : - Position: Shoulder depression, wrist/finger extension, elbow flexion, shoulder abduction, cervical lateral flexion away - Sensitising: Cervical lateral flexion toward; wrist extension/flexion - Positive: Reproduction of concordant symptoms; asymmetrical response vs contralateral - Use for: Screening, differentiating peripheral vs central sensitisation, guiding neural mobilisation --- Outcome Measures Patient-Reported Measures DASH / QuickDASH: - Most widely used for upper limb nerve compression - MCID: DASH 10.2 points; QuickDASH 16 points - Work module available for occupational contexts Boston/Levine CTS Questionnaire: Not validated for CuTS; use DASH instead. Patient-Rated Ulnar Nerve Evaluation PRUNE : Validated specifically for ulnar neuropathy; 17 items; symptom and function subscales. Less widely available but more condition-specific. Objective Measures Grip Strength Jamar : - Compare dominant vs non-dominant; affected vs unaffected - MCID: 6.5 kg; ICC 0.97–0.98 - Serial measurement tracks motor recovery post-decompression Pinch Strength lateral and tip pinch : - Tip pinch directly measures intrinsic function - Lateral pinch tests adductor pollicis ulnar nerve + FPL median nerve Sensory Testing: - Semmes-Weinstein monofilament testing: quantifies sensory threshold in ring/little finger - 2-point discrimination static and moving : >6 mm static 2PD = abnormal; tracks recovery - Vibration threshold 128 Hz tuning fork : reduced in ulnar distribution in moderate/severe CuTS Functional Dexterity: - Purdue Pegboard test manual dexterity; sensitive to intrinsic muscle weakness - Nine-hole peg test: functional fine motor speed assessment --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical diagnosis based on symptom pattern + provocative tests is appropriate for initial management. NCS confirmation required before surgical intervention. Nerve Conduction Studies NCS — Gold Standard: - Ulnar motor conduction velocity across elbow: 10 m/s slowing compared to forearm segment is diagnostic - Compound Motor Action Potential CMAP amplitude: reduced in axonal degeneration - Sensory nerve action potential SNAP : reduced or absent in sensory fibre involvement - Inching technique: localises compression to specific 2 cm segment - Referral pathway HSC NI : Via GP or outpatient consultant; Neurophysiology departments in Belfast Trust, Southern Trust, Western Trust; typical wait 6–16 weeks EMG: - Detects denervation in FDI, ADM, FCU - Chronic denervation: fibrillations, positive sharp waves, reduced recruitment - Useful for severity stratification and surgical planning Ultrasound: - Cross-sectional area of ulnar nerve at cubital tunnel: >10 mm² associated with compression sensitivity 70–80% - Dynamic assessment: nerve subluxation over medial epicondyle - Increasingly used as first-line imaging; lower cost than MRI MRI: - Nerve signal change, perineural fibrosis, intraneural oedema - Identifies compressive lesions ganglion, accessory muscle, post-traumatic fibrosis - Reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or surgical planning --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features Key Investigation ----------- ------------------------ ------------------- Cervical radiculopathy C8 Neck pain; Spurling's positive; triceps weakness; absent triceps reflex Cervical MRI; NCS shows normal forearm ulnar velocity Thoracic outlet syndrome Positional; overhead provocation; vascular signs; Adson's/ROOS positive Cervical X-ray; vascular duplex; NCS Medial epicondylalgia Tendinopathy signs; no sensory deficit; no intrinsic weakness Clinical; NCS normal Guyon's canal syndrome ulnar at wrist Spares FCU wrist flexion intact ; NCS shows distal compression; dorsal ulnar sensory SNAP normal NCS/EMG; wrist ultrasound Double crush syndrome Combined cervical + cubital compression NCS both regions; MRI spine Pancoast tumour Shoulder girdle pain; Horner's; weight loss; smoking history Chest X-ray; CT chest Peripheral neuropathy diabetic, alcoholic Bilateral; length-dependent; other nerves involved NCS bilateral; bloods Ulnar nerve tumour Firm, fixed mass on nerve; Tinel's at mass MRI; ultrasound --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Community Physiotherapy: - Mild-moderate CuTS McGowan Grade I–II : initial management in community - Activity modification, splinting, neural mobilisation, ergonomic advice - Monitor neurological status; refer urgently if motor deficit progresses Neurophysiology: - NCS via GP referral or consultant referral in secondary care - Belfast Trust Royal Victoria Hospital, Musgrave Park , Southern Trust Daisy Hill , Western Trust Altnagelvin - Wait times: 6–16 weeks typically; urgent pathway via consultant if rapid neurological decline Orthopaedics / Hand Surgery Secondary Care : - Referral via GP elective or direct from neurophysiology if severe NCS findings - McGowan Grade II–III with failed conservative management → surgical assessment - Pre-surgical NCS/EMG mandatory in most units Private / Expedited Pathway: - Private neurophysiology available in Belfast, Derry, Newry for faster access - Private hand surgery available at Ulster Independent Clinic, Kingsbridge Private Hospital --- Conservative Management Activity Modification Grade B - Avoid sustained elbow flexion >90° : phone use speaker/headset , sleeping position - Avoid repetitive elbow flexion-extension under load - Avoid medial elbow pressure : padding on work surfaces, armrests - Workplace ergonomic assessment HSE NI guidance Elbow Extension Splinting at Night Grade A - Evidence: RCT Dellon 1989; Seror 1993 — night splinting equivalent to surgical decompression in mild-moderate CuTS at 12 months - Splint: elbow at 30–45° flexion extension ; wrist neutral or slight extension - Fabricated thermoplastic splint hand therapy or prefabricated elbow extension orthosis - Duration: minimum 3 months; worn during sleep and prolonged elbow-flexion activities - Compliance is the limiting factor Nerve Gliding Exercises Grade B Upper Limb Neurodynamic Mobilisation ULNT3 — Ulnar Bias : - Position: shoulder abduction, external rotation; elbow flexion; wrist/finger extension - Sliding technique neural flossing : Alternating neck lateral flexion away with elbow extension; 10 × 3 reps/day - Tensioner technique: For more chronic presentations; hold position at neural tissue tension - Pain should not exceed 4/10 during exercise; no lasting post-exercise symptoms Education - Sleep position modification pillow under arm to prevent elbow flexion >90° - Phone/device use modification - Workplace assessment: seated ergonomics, tool use, forearm support --- Pharmacological Oral NSAIDs Grade C — limited evidence for nerve entrapment : - Short course for acute inflammatory flare or concurrent medial epicondylalgia - No direct evidence in CuTS; reduce perineural inflammation theoretically - NICE: lowest effective dose; gastroprotection if >7 days; avoid in renal impairment Corticosteroid Injection: - Limited evidence for CuTS vs carpal tunnel where CSI has good evidence - Risk: ulnar nerve injury with perilesional injection → ultrasound guidance mandatory - Not standard practice; occasionally used for severe inflammatory/rheumatoid cases - Discuss risk/benefit with patient; document informed consent Gabapentinoids neuropathic pain : - Pregabalin 25–150 mg BD or gabapentin 300 mg TDS for neuropathic pain component - NICE guidance: consider if neuropathic pain component prominent - Caution: sedation, dependence potential Schedule 3 CD in UK since 2019 Vitamin B6/B12: - No robust evidence for CuTS; sometimes used empirically in peripheral neuropathy - Not routinely recommended in NICE guidance --- Onward Referral Criteria Refer to Orthopaedics/Hand Surgery elective if: - McGowan Grade II–III moderate-severe - Failed ≥3–6 months conservative management splinting + activity modification - NCS confirmed significant conduction slowing ulnar CV <50 m/s across elbow or axonal loss - Occupation at risk musician, manual worker with persistent symptoms URGENT referral if: - Progressive motor deficit intrinsic wasting, clawing over weeks - Severe NCS: CMAP amplitude <50% of normal; fibrillations on EMG - Anatomical cause identified post-traumatic, ganglion, accessory muscle Surgical Options Consultant Decision : Procedure Indication Evidence ----------- ----------- ---------- In-situ decompression Mild-moderate; no nerve subluxation; no anatomical cause Good; 70–85% success Anterior transposition subcutaneous Nerve subluxation; anatomical compression Equivalent to in-situ in most; 75–90% success Anterior transposition submuscular Severe compression; revision; valgus deformity More complex; longest recovery Medial epicondylectomy Selected cases; less common Equivalent outcomes but nerve risk Post-operative physiotherapy: scar management, oedema, ROM, progressive strengthening; hand therapy involvement essential. --- Key References 1. content: Elbow Osteoarthritis Overview Elbow osteoarthritis OA is a degenerative joint disease characterised by progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral bone changes, osteophyte formation, and synovial inflammation within the elbow joint complex humeroulnar, humeroradial, and proximal radioulnar joints . It is relatively uncommon compared to hip and knee OA, accounting for approximately 2% of all OA presentations , but causes significant functional impairment given the elbow's role in positioning the hand in space. Epidemiology - Prevalence: ~2% of the general population; higher in heavy manual workers and throwing athletes - Peak onset: 5th–6th decade; male:female ratio approximately 4:1 in primary OA - Primary idiopathic OA accounts for ~50% of elbow OA; often bilateral - Secondary OA follows prior trauma post-traumatic , inflammatory arthropathy, osteochondral defects, or repetitive occupational loading Pathoanatomy Elbow OA characteristically produces: - Osteophyte formation at the coronoid fossa, olecranon fossa, and radial head - Loose body formation — a cardinal feature; fragments from osteophytes or osteochondral surfaces cause mechanical symptoms - Progressive loss of terminal flexion and extension terminal arc most affected first - Relative preservation of the mid-arc 60°–120° until advanced disease - Capsular contracture contributing to stiffness Typical Clinical Presentation Feature Detail --- --- Pain End-range aching; may be sharp with loose body impingement Stiffness Loss of terminal extension > terminal flexion initially Functional arc Typically 30°–130° preserved in mild–moderate disease Locking/catching Suggests loose body; episodic, position-dependent Crepitus Coarse, palpable; reproducible with passive ROM Swelling Effusion palpable in posterolateral triangle Occupation/sport history Heavy manual work, throwing athletes, combat sports > Normal elbow ROM for reference: Flexion 0°–145°; Pronation 75°; Supination 85°. Functional arc: 30°–130° flexion-extension; 50° pronation–50° supination Morrey et al., 1981 . --- Red Flags Red flags require urgent or urgent-plus escalation — do not manage as routine OA. Red Flag Possible Pathology Action --- --- --- Significant trauma + inability to extend Radial head fracture; distal humerus fracture Same-day imaging; ED/orthopaedics Hot, swollen, erythematous joint + fever / systemically unwell Septic arthritis Emergency — same-day ED referral Progressive neurological deficit hand weakness, wasting Cubital tunnel syndrome; cervical myelopathy; Pancoast tumour Urgent neurology / orthopaedics Night pain unresponsive to analgesia; unexplained weight loss Primary bone tumour; metastatic disease Urgent 2-week-wait referral suspected cancer pathway Bilateral symmetrical joint involvement + systemic features Rheumatoid arthritis; psoriatic arthritis Urgent rheumatology referral Elbow pain + ipsilateral shoulder/neck pain + C-spine symptoms Cervical radiculopathy C6/C7 ; referred pain Full cervical spine screen; consider nerve conduction Haemarthrosis without adequate trauma Haemophilia; pigmented villonodular synovitis PVNS Haematology / rheumatology Skin changes over olecranon erythema, tracking Olecranon bursitis with cellulitis Antibiotic review; may require aspiration --- Special Tests > Sensitivity Sn and specificity Sp data are derived from published validation studies. Most elbow OA-specific test accuracy data are limited; values reflect best available evidence and are presented with appropriate caution. Range of Motion Examination Essential Active and passive ROM measurement with a standard goniometer is the cornerstone of elbow OA assessment. Loss of terminal extension is the earliest and most consistent finding. Provocative & Diagnostic Tests Test Technique Positive Finding Sensitivity Specificity Clinical Use in Elbow OA --- --- --- --- --- --- Terminal arc pain Outerbridge–Kashiwagi sign Passive flexion–extension through full range; note where pain is provoked Pain at end-range extension 120° ~85% expert consensus Moderate Confirms terminal arc impingement — hallmark of elbow OA Loose body provocation test Examiner passively moves elbow through arc while applying axial compression Reproducible locking, catching, or sharp pain Not formally validated — Suggests intra-articular loose body; consider imaging Posterolateral rotatory instability PLRI test lateral pivot shift Supine; shoulder abducted 90°, forearm supinated; apply valgus + supination + axial compression through elbow flexion Apprehension or subluxation of radial head Sn 38%–100% wide range; highly examiner-dependent Sp ~96% O'Driscoll et al., 1991 Rules in ligamentous instability contributing to OA pattern Valgus stress test UCL integrity Elbow at 15°–30° flexion; apply valgus force; compare medial joint opening Pain ± gapping medially Sn 65% Safran & Ahmad, 2005 Sp 60% UCL insufficiency secondary to valgus overload; relevant in throwing athletes Milking manoeuvre UCL Traction on thumb with elbow >90° flexion and shoulder ER; valgus stress applied Medial elbow pain Sn 82% O'Driscoll et al., 2005 Sp 91% UCL integrity; differentiates medial pain source Tinel's sign at cubital tunnel Percussion over ulnar nerve in cubital tunnel medial epicondyle groove Paraesthesia in ring/little finger distribution Sn 54–70% Sp 77–98% Novak et al., 1994 Detects cubital tunnel syndrome — common OA co-pathology Elbow flexion test Maximal elbow flexion + wrist extension sustained 60 seconds Paraesthesia ulnar nerve distribution Sn 75% Sp 99% Novak et al., 1994 Sensitive screen for cubital tunnel syndrome Radiocapitellar compression test Elbow slightly flexed; passive forearm rotation pronation/supination with axial compression Lateral elbow pain Not formally validated for OA — Screens radiocapitellar joint involvement; also used in radial head pathology Extension impingement test Rapid passive extension of elbow Posterior elbow pain at end-range Not formally validated — Posterior osteophyte / olecranon impingement Crepitus assessment Palpation during passive ROM Coarse crepitus throughout arc or at terminal range Moderate examiner agreement — Consistent feature of cartilage degeneration > Note: Elbow OA diagnosis is primarily clinical + radiological . No single provocative test is pathognomonic. Imaging plain radiograph is required for confirmation and surgical planning. --- Clinical Frameworks Outerbridge–Kashiwagi OK Classification Radiological/Intraoperative Widely used for surgical planning but informs clinical staging: Grade Description --- --- I Osteophytes at coronoid/olecranon tip; joint space preserved II Moderate osteophytes; mild joint space narrowing; loose bodies may be present III Severe osteophytes; significant joint space narrowing; multiple loose bodies IV End-stage: complete joint space loss; gross deformity Broberg & Morrey Functional Rating System Used in outcome assessment for elbow OA interventions: - Score 0–100 based on pain 45 pts , motion 25 pts , stability 10 pts , function 20 pts - Excellent: 96–100 Good: 80–95 Fair: 60–79 Poor: 1hr; systemic features; warm joint; raised CRP/ESR; RF+/anti-CCP+ Bloods: CRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP; hand/wrist X-ray Psoriatic arthritis Psoriasis history/family history; DIP involvement; enthesitis; dactylitis Dermatology review; HLA-B27; imaging Gout / pseudogout Acute episodic flares; olecranon tophi gout ; hot swollen joint; hyperuricaemia Serum urate; synovial fluid for crystals; X-ray Septic arthritis Fever; raised WBC/CRP; very hot/swollen joint; systemically unwell; rapid onset Emergency : joint aspiration; blood cultures; WBC Cubital tunnel syndrome Medial elbow pain + ulnar paraesthesia ring/little finger ; intrinsic wasting NCS/EMG; Tinel's; elbow flexion test Lateral epicondylalgia Lateral pain on resisted wrist extension/gripping; point-tender lateral epicondyle; no ROM loss initially Clinical diagnosis; USS if uncertain; exclude radial nerve entrapment Medial epicondylalgia Medial pain on resisted wrist flexion/pronation; no joint line tenderness Clinical diagnosis Osteochondritis dissecans OCD Younger patient Physiotherapists should be aware of the NICE NG226 pharmacological pathway for co-ordinated MDT management. Prescribing remains with the GP/prescribing clinician. Step Agent NICE NG226 Recommendation Notes --- --- --- --- Step 1 Topical NSAIDs e.g., diclofenac 1% gel First-line analgesia for peripheral joint OA Apply 3–4x/day; lower systemic risk; trial for 4–6 weeks; limited evidence specifically for elbow OA Step 2 Oral NSAIDs e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen, celecoxib Consider if topical insufficient Use lowest effective dose, shortest duration; gastroprotection PPI if indicated; caution in CKD, CVD, GI risk Step 3 Paracetamol NG226 2022 update : no longer recommended as routine first-line for OA evidence insufficient for meaningful pain relief at recommended doses May still be used for individual patient preference alongside other analgesia Step 3 Intra-articular corticosteroid injection Consider for short-term flare management when other treatments inadequate Benefit typically 4–12 weeks; ultrasound guidance improves accuracy; no more than 3 injections/year; evidence modest for elbow specifically Avoid Opioids NG226: Do not offer opioids for OA management Harms outweigh benefits in OA; significant addiction risk Avoid Glucosamine / chondroitin NG226: Do not offer No clinically meaningful benefit demonstrated Avoid Intra-articular hyaluronic acid Not recommended by NICE NG226 Insufficient evidence of benefit in peripheral joint OA > NICE NG226 core principle : Pharmacological management should always be adjunctive to core treatments education + exercise . Do not use pharmacology as a substitute for exercise-based management. --- Onward Referral Criteria Orthopaedic Referral Elective Refer when the following criteria are met: - Conservative physiotherapy management for ≥12 weeks has failed to achieve adequate pain control or functional improvement - Significant functional limitation confirmed by PROMs DASH ≥40; OES ≤30/100 - Radiological evidence of moderate-severe OA Grade II–IV - Loose bodies causing recurrent locking episodes — arthroscopic removal indicated - Flexion contracture >30° with significant functional impact unresponsive to conservative management - Patient is willing and medically fit to consider surgical intervention Surgical Options for Orthopaedic Awareness Procedure Indication Evidence --- --- --- Arthroscopic debridement Outerbridge–Kashiwagi procedure Loose body removal; osteophyte resection; capsular release; mild–moderate OA Good short-term outcomes; 70–90% satisfaction at 2 years Antuna et al., 2002; Krishnan et al., 2007 Open debridement Moderate–severe OA where arthroscopic access limited; posterior osteophytes Historical gold standard; superseded by arthroscopy in many centres Total Elbow Arthroplasty TEA End-stage OA; RA; failed previous surgery 10-year survival ~85–90% Cheung et al., 2010 ; activity restrictions post-TEA : lifting limit 2.3kg 5lbs long-term Radial head arthroplasty Isolated radiocapitellar OA; failed radial head excision Limited elbow OA-specific data Interposition arthroplasty Young active patients unsuitable for TEA Alternative to TEA; preserves bone stock Urgent/Expedited Orthopaedic Referral - Acute locking with inability to extend — possible displaced loose body - Rapid neurological deterioration cubital tunnel compression by osteophyte - Suspected septic arthritis same-day ED - Suspected malignancy 2-week-wait pathway Rheumatology Referral - Suspected inflammatory arthropathy RA, PsA, gout refractory to GP management - Unusual presentation; young age; polyarthritis Occupational Therapy Referral - Patients with significant ADL or work-related functional impairment - Manual workers requiring workstation/tool adaptation - Post-surgical rehabilitation TEA --- Key References > Evidence base for elbow OA is predominantly Level III–IV case series, expert consensus, extrapolation from other joints . content: Overview & Pathophysiology Lateral epicondylalgia LE — commonly termed "tennis elbow" — is the most prevalent elbow disorder in primary care, with a population prevalence of 1–3% and peak incidence in the 35–54 age group. It accounts for approximately 5% of all shoulder and arm complaints presenting to GPs, with an estimated annual incidence of 4–7 per 1000 patients. Pathophysiology: Contemporary understanding has shifted decisively away from an inflammatory model. Histological studies Nirschl & Pettrone 1979; Khan et al. 2002 consistently demonstrate angiofibroblastic hyperplasia rather than inflammatory infiltrate — absence of inflammatory cells, disordered collagen Type III predominance , neurovascular in-growth, and failed healing response. The condition is therefore better classified as a tendinopathy rather than tendinitis. Primary structure involved: Extensor carpi radialis brevis ECRB origin at the lateral epicondyle — specifically the anterior and superior aspect. ECRB is most vulnerable due to: - Mechanical impingement against the capitellum during elbow extension and forearm pronation - High tensile load during wrist extension under load - Relatively avascular region at the origin contributing to failed healing Contributing structures: Extensor digitorum communis, extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi ulnaris. Risk factors: Manual occupations, repetitive gripping >2 kg, keyboard/mouse use, racquet sports backhand technique errors , age 40–50, smoking, obesity, previous episode. Natural history: Spontaneous resolution expected in 80–90% within 12–18 months without treatment. However, recurrence rates are high up to 72% at 5 years in some cohorts . --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Cozen's Test resisted wrist extension 0.84 0.75 3.36 0.21 Moderate Mill's Test passive wrist flexion, elbow extended 0.68 0.69 2.19 0.46 Moderate Maudsley's Test resisted middle finger extension 0.88 0.58 2.10 0.21 Low-Moderate Lateral epicondyle palpation tenderness 0.91 0.45 1.65 0.20 Moderate Resisted wrist extension with elbow extended loaded 0.79 0.83 4.65 0.25 Moderate Grip strength deficit affected vs unaffected 0.73 0.68 2.28 0.40 Low Chair pick-up test patient version Cozen's 0.72 0.74 2.77 0.38 Low Cozen's Test Protocol: Stabilise the elbow; patient makes fist with wrist in neutral. Examiner resists wrist extension. Positive = pain at lateral epicondyle. Mill's Test Protocol: Elbow extended, forearm pronated. Examiner passively flexes wrist fully. Positive = pain at lateral epicondyle. Maudsley's Test Protocol: Patient resists examiner pressing down on middle finger with elbow extended. Positive = lateral epicondyle pain. Clinical note: No single test is diagnostic in isolation. A cluster of positive tests ≥2 of: lateral epicondyle tenderness, positive Cozen's, positive Mill's increases diagnostic confidence. Exclude radial nerve compression radial tunnel syndrome as concurrent or alternative diagnosis. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ The following presentations require urgent assessment and should not be attributed to simple tendinopathy. - Bony tenderness directly over lateral epicondyle with trauma history → suspect lateral epicondyle avulsion/fracture; request X-ray - Elbow effusion, erythema, warmth, systemic fever → suspect septic arthritis or crystal arthropathy; urgent bloods + aspiration - Progressive neurological deficit weakness, sensory loss in radial nerve territory → suspect posterior interosseous nerve entrapment or cervical radiculopathy; urgent imaging - Night pain, unexplained weight loss, age >50 with new-onset lateral elbow pain → consider malignancy; urgent X-ray + referral - Rapidly progressive elbow stiffness → consider aggressive articular pathology, tumour, or infection - Vascular compromise pulselessness, pallor, paraesthesia, pain, paralysis → emergency vascular referral --- Clinical Frameworks Tendinopathy Continuum Model Cook & Purdam 2009; updated Cook et al. 2016 The continuum model provides a framework for staging tendinopathy and guiding management: Stage Pathology Clinical Features Management Approach ------- ----------- ------------------- --------------------- Reactive tendinopathy Short-term adaptive response; increased proteoglycan, water content Acute onset after sudden load increase; swelling possible; pain with all load Load reduction; relative rest; isometrics may reduce pain Tendon dysrepair Failed healing; early matrix disruption; neurovascular in-growth Sub-acute; pain with higher loads; some thickening on US Moderate load modification; graduated isotonic loading Degenerative tendinopathy Cell death, matrix disruption, failed collagen; angiofibroblastic changes Chronic; pain with daily activities; may have pain-free window mid-activity Graded loading; accept some pain during exercise NRS 0–4 ; longer rehab timeline Pain Monitoring Model - 0–4/10 NRS during loading — acceptable; continue programme - 5–7/10 NRS — monitor closely; modify load - >7/10 NRS or pain lingering >24 hours post-exercise — reduce load; reassess stage Biopsychosocial Considerations Central sensitisation is prevalent in chronic LE >3 months . Assess: - Pain catastrophising PCS >30 → elevated risk of poor outcome - Fear-avoidance FABQ - Work-related psychosocial factors job demands, control, support - Sleep quality --- Outcome Measures Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation PRTEE - Format: 15 items; 0–100 scale 10 pain items + 5 function specific + 10 usual activities - Score interpretation: 0 = no pain/disability; 100 = worst possible - MCID: 11 points Stratford et al. 2001 - MDC: 17 points - Time to complete: 5 minutes DASH / QuickDASH - DASH: 30 items; 0–100 0 = no disability - QuickDASH: 11 items; 0–100 - MCID for LE: DASH 10.2 points; QuickDASH 16 points - Limitation: Less condition-specific; useful for cross-condition comparison Grip Strength Jamar Dynamometer - Protocol: Elbow at 90°, neutral forearm; 3 trials; mean recorded - Normative comparison: Compare to contralateral limb expect 5–10% dominant hand advantage - Pain-free grip strength often more clinically useful than maximum grip - MCID: Approximately 6.5 kg for meaningful change - Reliability: ICC 0.97–0.98 for Jamar at standardised handle position Global Rating of Change GRC - 15-point scale −7 to +7 ; clinically meaningful change = ±3 points --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical diagnosis is appropriate in typical presentations. Imaging is not routinely required for initial diagnosis. Ultrasound US : - Sensitivity 64–82%; specificity 64–100% for tendinopathic changes hypoechogenicity, thickening, neovascularity - Useful to confirm diagnosis in atypical cases, guide injection, rule out partial/full-thickness tear - Power Doppler demonstrates neovascularisation but correlation with symptoms is inconsistent - Indication: Persistent symptoms >6 months despite conservative management, prior to injection, surgical planning MRI: - Higher soft tissue resolution than US; gold standard for detecting intra-tendinous tears - T2 signal increase at ECRB origin diagnostic of tendinopathy - Reserve for surgical planning or diagnostic uncertainty - Not routinely indicated in primary/community physiotherapy X-ray: - Not required for diagnosis; may show calcification 25–30% of chronic cases or reveal alternative pathology - Indicated with trauma history or red flags NCS/EMG: - Not indicated for lateral epicondylalgia - Consider if radial tunnel syndrome or posterior interosseous nerve palsy suspected Clinical Prediction Rule: No validated CPR exists for LE. Diagnosis is clinical based on: 1. Lateral epicondyle pain 2. Reproduced by resisted wrist extension and/or passive wrist flexion 3. Tenderness on palpation of the lateral epicondyle --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features Key Test ----------- ------------------------ ---------- Radial tunnel syndrome Pain 3–5 cm distal to lateral epicondyle; deep ache; nocturnal pain; weakness; positive resisted supination Resisted supination at 0°; Frohse arcade tenderness Posterior interosseous nerve palsy Finger/wrist drop; weakness of finger extensors; may be painless Neurological examination; NCS/EMG Cervical radiculopathy C6/C7 Neck pain; dermatomal sensory loss; reduced reflexes; Spurling's positive Spurling's test; cervical spine examination Lateral elbow instability PLRI Clicking, locking, giving way; trauma history; positive lateral pivot shift Lateral pivot shift test; MRI Synovial plica irritation Intermittent snapping sensation; pain with full extension Clinical; MRI Elbow OA Age >50; stiffness; crepitus; full ROM loss; X-ray changes X-ray Osteochondral loose body Locking, catching, extension block X-ray; MRI Referred pain from shoulder/neck Absence of local signs; pain not reproduced by local provocation Full UL neurodynamic screen Lateral epicondyle stress fracture Rare; athletes; local bony tenderness; positive imaging X-ray; MRI --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Community Physiotherapy: - First-line management; majority should be managed in community MSK services - GP referral to community physiotherapy or self-referral where available Trust-dependent - Occupational health physiotherapy for work-related cases - Hand therapy services: referral via GP or hospital consultant; appropriate for complex/chronic cases Secondary Care: - Consultant referral Orthopaedics or Rheumatology if: - Failed 6 months conservative management - Diagnostic uncertainty - Consideration of injection therapy PRP, autologous blood, corticosteroid - Surgical assessment - Nerve conduction studies: available via Neurophysiology Belfast Trust, Southern Trust ; referral via GP or consultant; waitlist variable Regional variation: Check individual Trust physiotherapy department protocols; self-referral available in some Trusts Western, Southern . BHSCT community MSK direct access available. --- Conservative Management Load Management Grade A evidence - Acute phase: Relative rest from provocative activities; avoid sustained gripping >2 kg; modify keyboard/mouse ergonomics - Wrist splinting: Cockup wrist splint 20–30° wrist extension reduces ECRB load; evidence for symptom reduction in acute phase moderate ; not recommended long-term - Counterforce brace epicondyle strap : Moderate evidence for short-term pain reduction with activity; mechanism = force dampening at muscle belly Exercise Therapy Grade A evidence — strongest recommendation Eccentric Exercise Programme Svernlöv & Adolfsson 2001; Tyler et al. 2010 : - Wrist extension eccentrics with forearm pronated over table edge - 3 × 15 repetitions; 2× daily; 12-week programme - Progress via increase in load dumbbell/putty/theraband - Pain up to 5/10 acceptable Isometric Exercise Stasinopoulos et al. 2017; Rio et al. 2015 : - Wrist extension isometric holds: 5 × 45-second holds at 70% MVC - Analgesic effect demonstrated; useful in reactive/irritable tendinopathy - Can precede isotonic loading programme Heavy Slow Resistance HSR Protocol Beyer et al. 2015 — adapted for LE : - Wrist extension with load: 3 sets; 15 reps → 8 reps → 6 reps over 12 weeks - Load progressed to near-maximum effort - Shown superior to eccentric-only in Achilles; extrapolated to upper limb Elbow Manipulation + Exercise Bisset et al. 2006 — landmark RCT : - Mulligan's Mobilisation with Movement MWM : lateral glide of elbow combined with gripping - Combined with exercise showed superior outcomes to corticosteroid injection at 12 months - 8 sessions over 8 weeks; pain-free grip force primary outcome Ergonomic Advice Grade B - Keyboard positioning; mouse size; tool grip modification - Avoiding repetitive wrist extension under load - Occupational therapy assessment if work-related --- Pharmacological Topical NSAIDs Grade A : - Topical diclofenac gel — NICE recommended first-line; good local effect; avoids systemic side effects - Apply 2–4× daily to lateral epicondyle region; 4–6 week trial Oral NSAIDs Grade B : - Short-term 1–2 weeks for acute flares - NICE: lowest effective dose; consider GI protection if >7 days - Evidence limited for chronic tendinopathy Corticosteroid Injection CSI : - Short-term pain relief 6–8 weeks — Grade A - Long-term outcomes inferior to physiotherapy and wait-and-see at 12 months Bisset et al. 2006 — high quality RCT - Risk of recurrence and tendon weakening with repeat injections - Consider: single injection for severe acute presentation to enable rehabilitation engagement - NICE CKS guidance: Advise patients of short-term benefit but inferior long-term outcome vs exercise Platelet-Rich Plasma PRP : - Emerging evidence; some RCTs show benefit over placebo/corticosteroid at 6–12 months - Not currently commissioned within HSC NI patient-funded in private sector - Systematic review Arirachakaran et al. 2016 shows possible superiority over CSI at 6+ months - Insufficient evidence to recommend routinely Autologous Blood Injection: - Similar rationale to PRP; limited high-quality RCT evidence - Not routinely commissioned Nitric Oxide Patches GTN : - Topical glyceryl trinitrate patches 1.25 mg/24h over lateral epicondyle - Paoloni et al. 2003 RCT showed significant improvement vs placebo - Poor palatability headache side effect ; limited uptake in clinical practice --- Onward Referral Criteria Refer to Orthopaedics/Hand Surgery if: - Symptoms persisting >12 months despite optimal conservative management minimum 6 months of structured physiotherapy - Significant functional impairment affecting work or daily activities - Evidence of structural tear on imaging requiring surgical consideration - Consideration for PRP, autologous blood injection, or dry needling under image guidance Surgical options consultant-led decision : - Open ECRB debridement Nirschl technique — Gold standard; 85–90% good/excellent outcomes - Arthroscopic debridement — Equivalent outcomes to open; shorter recovery - Percutaneous tenotomy — Less invasive option - Ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle tenotomy TENEX/Tenex Health TX — emerging Criteria for surgical consideration NICE / BOA guidance : - Failed ≥6 months conservative management including physiotherapy - Documented tendinopathic changes on US or MRI - Significant functional limitation --- Key References 1. title: Medial Epicondylalgia (Golfer's Elbow)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Medial epicondylalgia ME — historically termed "golfer's elbow" or medial epicondylitis — is a common cause of medial elbow pain, accounting for approximately 10–20% of elbow tendinopathies presenting in clinical practice. True incidence is lower than lateral epicondylalgi
headings: Valgus Extension Overload Assessment throwing athletes
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Medial epicondylalgia ME — historically termed "golfer's elbow" or medial epicondylitis — is a common cause of medial elbow pain, accounting for approximately 10–20% of elbow tendinopathies presenting in clinical practice. True incidence is lower than lateral epicondylalgia; estimated at 0.4% of the general population per year, with peak onset in the 4th–5th decade. Pathophysiology: As with lateral epicondylalgia, histological evidence confirms angiofibroblastic tendinosis rather than true inflammation. Nirschl 1992 described the same pathological changes: disorganised collagen, fibroblast proliferation, neovascularisation, absence of inflammatory cells. The condition represents failed tendon healing at the common flexor-pronator origin. Primary structures involved: - Pronator teres — most commonly affected originates from medial epicondyle - Flexor carpi radialis — frequently co-involved - Flexor carpi ulnaris, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis — less commonly The origin is on the anterior aspect of the medial epicondyle; valgus stress during acceleration phases of throwing or golfing creates repetitive tensile overload. Mechanism of injury: - Repetitive wrist flexion and forearm pronation under load - Valgus loading of medial elbow throwing, golf, racquet sports - Occupational exposure: carpentry, plumbing, manual handling Important association — Ulnar collateral ligament UCL : - UCL insufficiency co-exists in up to 60% of throwing athletes with ME - Distinguish clinically as management differs UCL reconstruction vs tendinopathy rehabilitation Concurrent cubital tunnel syndrome: - Ulnar nerve involvement in 20–60% of ME cases - Critical to assess for ulnar neuropathy at every consultation - Failure to identify ulnar nerve involvement leads to suboptimal outcomes --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Medial epicondyle palpation tenderness 0.89 0.42 1.53 0.26 Moderate Resisted wrist flexion Cozen's medial equivalent 0.74 0.65 2.11 0.40 Low-Moderate Resisted forearm pronation 0.68 0.69 2.19 0.46 Low Passive wrist extension stretch medial Mill's 0.62 0.72 2.21 0.53 Low Golfer's elbow test combined wrist flexion + forearm pronation under resistance 0.71 0.66 2.09 0.44 Low Valgus stress test UCL assessment 0.65 0.48 1.25 0.73 Low Moving valgus stress test O'Driscoll 0.100 0.75 4.00 0.00 Moderate throwing athletes Tinel's at cubital tunnel 0.70 0.66 2.06 0.45 Moderate Elbow flexion test ulnar nerve provocation 0.75 0.99 75.0 0.25 Moderate-High Resisted Wrist Flexion Protocol: Elbow extended, forearm supinated. Examiner resists wrist flexion. Positive = medial epicondyle pain reproduction. Moving Valgus Stress Test O'Driscoll et al. 2004 : Shoulder abducted 90°, elbow taken from 120° flexion to 70° extension while maintaining constant valgus stress. Positive = medial elbow pain between 120–70° shear angle . High sensitivity/specificity for UCL injury in throwing athletes. Elbow Flexion Test: Maximum elbow flexion with wrist neutral maintained for 60 seconds. Positive = tingling/numbness in ring/little finger distribution. Best test for cubital tunnel syndrome. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Urgent or time-sensitive pathology requiring escalation. - Medial epicondyle fracture particularly in children/adolescents — "Little Leaguer's elbow" : acute trauma, point tenderness, avulsion on X-ray → urgent X-ray + orthopaedic assessment - Medial epicondyle apophysitis in skeletally immature athletes: growth plate disruption → X-ray; activity restriction - UCL rupture with acute valgus trauma: significant instability, immediate swelling, inability to continue sport → MRI arthrogram + orthopaedic referral - Ulnar artery thrombosis hypothenar hammer syndrome : medial forearm pain, Raynaud-like symptoms, pulsatility changes → urgent vascular assessment - Septic olecranon bursitis or septic arthritis : fever, systemic signs, erythema, warmth → emergency aspiration + bloods - Cubital tunnel syndrome with rapid neurological deterioration : progressive weakness of intrinsic hand muscles, clawing → urgent neurophysiology + surgical review - Medial elbow malignancy : rare; pain at rest, night pain, unexplained constitutional symptoms, age extremes → X-ray + referral --- Clinical Frameworks Tendinopathy Continuum Model Cook & Purdam 2009 Apply same staging as lateral epicondylalgia: - Reactive: Acute load spike; manage with relative rest, isometrics, provocative load avoidance - Dysrepair: Subacute; graduated isotonic loading; monitor 24-hour pain response - Degenerative: Chronic; accept working pain NRS 0–4 ; long-term loading programme; psychosocial screen Ulnar Nerve Assessment Framework In all ME cases, systematically assess: 1. Subjective: Paraesthesia/numbness in ring/little finger; nocturnal symptoms elbow flexion in sleep ; pain radiating down medial forearm 2. Objective: Froment's sign intrinsic weakness ; first dorsal interosseous wasting; clawing ring/little finger ; sensory testing light touch, 2-point discrimination in ulnar nerve territory 3. Special tests: Elbow flexion test, Tinel's at cubital tunnel 4. Severity classification: - Mild: Intermittent paraesthesia; no motor deficit - Moderate: Persistent paraesthesia; early motor weakness - Severe: Constant symptoms; significant weakness/wasting; consider urgent surgical referral Valgus Extension Overload Assessment throwing athletes - Screen for UCL insufficiency moving valgus stress test - Screen for posterior impingement valgus extension overload test - Screen for radiocapitellar pathology --- Outcome Measures Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation PRTEE - Although named for tennis elbow, validated for use in medial epicondylalgia - Score: 0–100; 0 = no pain/disability - MCID: 11 points DASH / QuickDASH - DASH MCID: 10.2 points LE/ME combined upper limb - QuickDASH MCID: 16 points - Useful for occupational/functional tracking Grip Strength Jamar Dynamometer - Protocol: Elbow at 90°; 3 trials; dominant vs non-dominant comparison - Pain-free grip is more clinically relevant than maximum grip in ME - Expect deficit on affected side; monitor improvement over 6–8 weeks Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS - MCID: 2 points 0–10 scale for musculoskeletal pain - Assess: worst pain last 7 days , average pain, pain during resisted testing --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on: 1. Medial elbow pain ± radiation into proximal forearm 2. Reproduction with resisted wrist flexion and/or forearm pronation 3. Medial epicondyle tenderness on palpation Ultrasound: - Sensitivity 72–90%; shows hypoechoic changes, tendon thickening, neovascularity at common flexor-pronator origin - Power Doppler: neovascularisation correlates with symptom severity - Indicated for diagnostic uncertainty, injection guidance, pre-surgical planning - Can also assess UCL integrity dynamic valgus stress view MRI: - Gold standard for full characterisation: tendinopathy, partial tear, UCL injury, ulnar nerve oedema - Indicated if UCL injury suspected, pre-surgical planning, diagnostic uncertainty - MRI arthrogram superior for UCL assessment in throwing athletes NCS/EMG: - Indicated if ulnar neuropathy suspected Elbow flexion test positive, Tinel's positive, motor deficit - Neurophysiology referral via GP or consultant HSC NI: Belfast Trust, Southern Trust, Western Trust - NCS findings: reduced ulnar nerve conduction velocity across elbow 90° at night — particularly important if ulnar neuropathy - Elbow extension orthosis for sleep if cubital tunnel concurrent diagnosis --- Pharmacological Topical NSAIDs Grade A : - Topical diclofenac gel — NICE CKS first-line recommendation - 2–4× daily application; 4–6 week trial Oral NSAIDs Grade B : - Short course 7–14 days for acute presentations - NICE: use lowest effective dose; prescribe gastroprotection if >7 days; avoid if renal impairment Corticosteroid Injection Grade B — short-term : - Methylprednisolone 40 mg / triamcinolone 40 mg at common flexor-pronator origin - Short-term pain relief 6–8 weeks but no evidence of long-term benefit over physiotherapy - Risk: ulnar nerve injury if poor technique landmark or US-guided preferred - Important: Landmark injection at medial elbow carries risk of ulnar nerve damage; ultrasound guidance recommended - Maximum 2 injections; minimum 6-week interval Nitric Oxide Patches: - Limited evidence for ME; extrapolated from Achilles/lateral elbow data - GTN 1.25 mg/24h patch applied over medial epicondyle --- Onward Referral Criteria Refer to Orthopaedics/Hand Surgery if: - Failure of ≥6 months conservative management structured physiotherapy - UCL insufficiency confirmed on MRI requiring reconstruction particularly throwing athletes - Progressive ulnar neuropathy not responding to conservative management - Medial epicondyle fracture or avulsion Surgical options consultant-led : - Medial epicondyle debridement open or arthroscopic - UCL reconstruction Tommy John procedure — throwing athletes - Cubital tunnel decompression concurrent ulnar neuropathy - Outcomes: 85–90% good/excellent at 2-year follow-up with surgical debridement --- Key References 1. The "moving valgus stress test" for medial collateral ligament tears of the elbow. American Journal of Sports Medicine , 32 4 , 888–892. 3. Descatha A, Leclerc A, Chastang JF, Roquelaure Y. 2003 . Medial epicondylitis in occupational settings: prevalence, incidence and associated risk factors. Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine , 45 9 , 993–1001. 4. Ciccotti MC, Schwartz MA, Ciccotti MG. 2004 . Diagnosis and treatment of medial epicondylitis of the elbow. Clinics in Sports Medicine , 23 4 , 693–705. 5. Park GY, Lee SM, Lee MY. 2008 . Diagnostic value of ultrasonography for clinical medial epicondylitis. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation , 89 4 , 738–742. 6. Calfee RP, Patel A, DaSilva MF, Akelman E. 2008 . Management of lateral epicondylitis: current concepts. Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons , 16 1 , 19–29. 7. Cook JL, Purdam CR. 2009 . Is tendon pathology a continuum? British Journal of Sports Medicine , 43 6 , 409–416. 8. Vangsness CT Jr, Jobe FW. 1991 . Surgical treatment of medial epicondylitis. Results in 35 elbows. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery , 73 3 , 409–411. 9. NICE CKS. 2022 . Elbow pain — Clinical Knowledge Summary . Available at: https://cks.nice.org.uk/ 10. title: Olecranon Bursitis
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Olecranon bursitis is inflammation of the olecranon bursa — a superficial synovial-lined sac located between the olecranon process of the ulna and the overlying skin. It is the most common bursitis of the elbow and one of the most frequently encountered superficial bursiti
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Olecranon bursitis is inflammation of the olecranon bursa — a superficial synovial-lined sac located between the olecranon process of the ulna and the overlying skin. It is the most common bursitis of the elbow and one of the most frequently encountered superficial bursitides in clinical practice. Anatomy: The olecranon bursa sits subcutaneously over the posterior olecranon. It does not normally communicate with the elbow joint. Normal bursa contains negligible fluid; in pathological states may enlarge significantly 2–3 cm or greater . Prevalence: Exact epidemiology uncertain; more common in males and in manual occupations involving prolonged elbow contact surfaces. Gout, pseudogout, and rheumatoid arthritis are systemic risk factors. Classification by aetiology: Type Mechanism Features ------ ----------- ---------- Traumatic Direct blow acute or repetitive pressure chronic Most common; clear history Septic Bacterial infection usually Staph. aureus 80% Erythema, warmth, fever, elevated WBC Crystal-induced Gout uric acid or pseudogout CPPD Aspirate shows crystals; may be recurrent Inflammatory Rheumatoid arthritis, other spondyloarthropathies Bilateral; systemic features; rheumatoid nodules Idiopathic No identifiable cause Diagnosis of exclusion Occupational associations: "Student's elbow," "miner's elbow," "plumber's elbow" — prolonged pressure on elbows during work, studying, or sports wrestling, hockey goalies . Pathophysiology: Trauma or sustained pressure causes microhaemorrhage within the bursal walls → inflammatory response → synovial hypertrophy → increased fluid production → bursal enlargement. In septic bursitis, bacteria enter via skin abrasion, puncture wound, or haematogenous spread. Gout deposits urate crystals which trigger intense inflammatory response. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Bursal fluctuance on palpation fluid wave 0.85 0.72 3.04 0.21 Moderate Bursal erythema extending beyond bursa 0.72 0.82 4.00 0.34 Moderate for septic Skin abrasion/puncture wound at olecranon 0.68 0.90 6.80 0.36 Moderate for septic Fever >38°C 0.40 0.97 13.3 0.62 Moderate for septic Tenderness of bursal wall not just fluid 0.78 0.65 2.23 0.34 Low-Moderate Elbow ROM preserved distinguishes from joint pathology 0.88 0.70 2.93 0.17 Moderate Key Distinction — Septic vs Non-Septic: No clinical sign reliably discriminates septic from non-septic olecranon bursitis. The gold standard is bursal fluid aspiration and analysis . Aspiration findings: Parameter Non-Septic Septic ----------- ----------- -------- WBC/mm³ 2,000 often >50,000 % Neutrophils 75% Glucose Normal Decreased Gram stain Negative Positive in 50–70% Culture Negative Positive in 80–90% Crystals Absent unless crystal-induced Absent unless concurrent Elbow ROM: Should be full and pain-free in isolated olecranon bursitis. Restricted ROM suggests intra-articular pathology. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Septic olecranon bursitis is a medical emergency requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment. - Signs of septic bursitis ANY combination : fever, overlying cellulitis, rapid enlargement, warmth significantly greater than contralateral, skin breakdown/wound, haematogenous source e.g., IVDU, recent dental procedure, skin infection → urgent aspiration + bloods; admit if systemically unwell - MRSA risk factors: Healthcare workers, previous MRSA, institutional care, IVDU → adjust antibiotic choice accordingly - Rapid elbow joint involvement: Loss of ROM, joint line tenderness, joint effusion → suspect septic arthritis medical emergency; mortality if untreated → emergency joint aspiration - Immunocompromised patients HIV, diabetes, steroid use, immunosuppressants : higher risk of septic bursitis; lower threshold for aspiration and admission - Diabetic patients: More aggressive clinical course; higher risk of complications; lower threshold for IV antibiotics - Bursal sinus formation: Chronically infected bursa may spontaneously drain; requires surgical excision - Systemic features of gout flare: Consider concurrent gout arthropathy; serum urate; joint aspiration --- Clinical Frameworks Diagnostic Algorithm for Olecranon Bursitis Septic Bursitis Management Framework - Mild/moderate no systemic sepsis, immunocompetent, outpatient : oral flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS × 10–14 days; repeat aspiration at 3–5 days - Severe systemically unwell, rapid progression, immunocompromised, failed oral antibiotics : IV antibiotics + surgical drainage or excision - MRSA confirmed/suspected: Vancomycin IV or oral clindamycin; infectious disease advice --- Outcome Measures Primary Clinical Measures - Bursal size: Measure maximum diameter with tape measure or ultrasound at baseline and follow-up - NPRS Numeric Pain Rating Scale : 0–10; MCID = 2 points; assess posterior elbow pain - Elbow ROM: Flexion/extension/pronation/supination goniometry ; should remain full in isolated bursitis DASH / QuickDASH - Useful for functional impact assessment - MCID for upper limb: DASH 10.2; QuickDASH 16 points - Less specific to olecranon bursitis but useful in occupational contexts Patient Satisfaction - Global Rating of Change GRC scale at 4, 8, and 12 weeks post-intervention - Return to work/sport as functional endpoint --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical diagnosis is reliable in typical traumatic cases with characteristic swelling over the olecranon and preserved elbow ROM. Aspiration: - Recommended if: septic bursitis suspected, diagnostic uncertainty, crystal arthropathy queried, large painful bursa limiting function - Ultrasound-guided aspiration preferred for complete drainage; reduces recurrence vs landmark aspiration - Send aspirate for: MC&S septic , crystal analysis gout/pseudogout , WBC + differential Ultrasound: - Confirms bursal fluid, size, wall thickening, septation - Doppler: hyperaemia in septic/inflammatory bursitis - Guides aspiration and injection - Identifies concurrent triceps tendon pathology X-ray: - Not required for diagnosis; may show: - Olecranon spur associated with chronic bursitis - Gout tophi soft tissue calcification - Fracture traumatic - Indicated with trauma or concern for bony pathology MRI: - Reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, surgical planning - Distinguishes bursitis from triceps tendon pathology, tumour - Not routine in straightforward cases Bloods if septic bursitis suspected : - FBC, CRP, ESR, urea/electrolytes - Blood cultures if febrile - Serum urate gout screen — note: may be normal during acute flare - Rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP if inflammatory arthropathy suspected --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features Key Investigation ----------- ------------------------ ------------------- Septic arthritis of elbow ROM restricted/painful; fever; systemically unwell; joint effusion Joint aspiration; bloods Gout/crystal arthropathy Very painful; acute onset; hyperuricaemia; crystals on aspiration Serum urate; aspiration Rheumatoid arthritis Bilateral; rheumatoid nodules; systemic features; joint involvement Rheumatoid factor; anti-CCP; X-ray Psoriatic arthritis Psoriasis; dactylitis; enthesopathy; asymmetric joint involvement Clinical; X-ray Triceps tendon tear Posterior elbow pain with resisted extension weakness; palpable defect MRI; ultrasound Posterior elbow impingement Pain at end-range extension; bone spur; athletes X-ray; MRI Lipoma Soft, non-tender, no ROM loss, chronic Ultrasound; MRI Ganglion cyst Tense, translucent, may transilluminate Ultrasound Tumour synovial sarcoma Rare; firm; progressive; systemic features MRI; biopsy --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Community Physiotherapy / GP: - Traumatic/chronic non-septic bursitis: managed in community - GP: aspiration, oral antibiotics septic , referral decision - Physiotherapy: activity modification, compression, ergonomic advice Emergency Department / Acute Medical: - Systemically unwell septic bursitis → A&E assessment - IV antibiotics + surgical opinion if not responding to oral treatment within 48–72 hours Secondary Care — Orthopaedics/Hand Surgery: - Recurrent bursitis ≥2 episodes requiring aspiration → consider surgical bursectomy - Chronically infected bursa with sinus formation → surgical excision - Confirmed septic bursitis not responding to antibiotics → surgical washout/excision - Referral via GP or Emergency Department Rheumatology: - Crystal-induced bursitis — consider referral for urate-lowering therapy gout or systemic disease management - Inflammatory arthropathy causing bursitis --- Conservative Management Non-Septic Traumatic/Mechanical Bursitis Grade B Load Modification: - Avoid direct pressure on olecranon; protective elbow padding neoprene sleeve, foam pad - Avoid prolonged elbow weight-bearing - Avoid contact sports until resolved Compression: - Compression bandage or tubigrip reduces re-accumulation of fluid - Evidence: moderate; reduces swelling recurrence vs no compression - Elbow compression sleeve sport-specific for return to activity Ice Therapy: - 15–20 minutes, 3–4× daily; reduces acute inflammatory swelling - No high-quality RCT evidence but widely recommended and safe Aspiration GP/Secondary Care : - If large, painful, or limiting function: aspiration provides symptom relief - Recurrence common 50–70% without compression ; aspiration + compression dressing reduces recurrence - Ultrasound-guided aspiration superior for complete drainage Corticosteroid Injection into bursa — non-septic only : - Reduces recurrence vs aspiration alone in non-septic bursitis Weinstein et al. 1984 - Methylprednisolone 40 mg or triamcinolone 40 mg - Risk: skin atrophy, depigmentation, bursal sinus, infection → exclude septic bursitis before injecting - Maximum 2 injections --- Pharmacological NSAIDs oral or topical — non-septic : - Short course oral NSAIDs for acute traumatic bursitis - Indomethacin particularly effective for crystal-induced flares - Topical NSAIDs diclofenac gel for localised pain control Antibiotics septic bursitis — NICE/BNF aligned : - First-line non-MRSA : Flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS orally × 10–14 days - Penicillin allergy: Clarithromycin 500 mg BD or clindamycin 300–450 mg QDS - MRSA confirmed: Vancomycin IV weight-adjusted ; seek microbiologist/infectious disease advice - IV therapy if: systemically unwell, failed oral therapy, immunocompromised, deep infection, MRSA Gout Management: - Acute flare: colchicine 500 mcg BD–TDS NICE preferred for olecranon gout or oral NSAIDs; short-course prednisolone if contraindicated - Long-term urate-lowering therapy allopurinol : if ≥2 gout episodes per year; commence after acute flare resolves - Rheumatology referral for complex/refractory gout --- Onward Referral Criteria Refer to Orthopaedics/Hand Surgery if: - Recurrent non-septic bursitis ≥3 episodes - Failed conservative management including aspiration × 2 - Chronic infected bursa / sinus formation - Diagnostic uncertainty solid lesion, tumour, extensive inflammation - Septic bursitis not responding to 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics Surgical options: - Bursectomy: Excision of bursa ± skin graft if skin contracted; 85–90% resolution; wound healing complications in 10–20% - Arthroscopic bursectomy: Less common; smaller wounds; suitable for recurrent non-septic - Surgical drainage/debridement: For infected bursa with sinus Post-surgical: Physiotherapy for wound management, ROM restoration, scar management, compression to prevent recurrence. Typically 6–8 weeks before return to manual work. --- Key References 1. Baumbach SF, Lobo CM, Badyine I, Mutschler W, Kanz KG. 2014 .
