title: Radial Tunnel Syndrome
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Radial tunnel syndrome RTS is a chronic pain condition resulting from compression or irritation of the radial nerve specifically the posterior interosseous nerve — PIN within the radial tunnel. It is arguably the most diagnostically challenging and controversial condition
headings: Differential Framework: RTS vs Lateral Epicondylalgia
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Radial tunnel syndrome RTS is a chronic pain condition resulting from compression or irritation of the radial nerve specifically the posterior interosseous nerve — PIN within the radial tunnel. It is arguably the most diagnostically challenging and controversial condition in elbow pathology, with debate persisting in the literature regarding its existence as a distinct clinical entity separate from lateral epicondylalgia. Prevalence: Poorly defined due to diagnostic difficulty. Often under-diagnosed. Estimated to account for 5% of cases initially presenting as lateral epicondylalgia. More common in manual workers. Anatomy of the Radial Tunnel: The radial tunnel extends from the radiocapitellar joint to the proximal border of the supinator muscle — approximately 5 cm long. The posterior interosseous nerve deep branch of radial nerve traverses this tunnel. Sites of compression within the radial tunnel medial to lateral : 1. Fibrous bands anterior to radiocapitellar joint — most distal compression point 2. Radial recurrent vessels leash of Henry — vascular tether against nerve 3. Tendinous medial border of ECRB — sharp tendinous edge impinges nerve with pronation/wrist extension 4. Arcade of Frohse proximal edge of superficial head of supinator — most common compression site 75% of cases 5. Distal edge of supinator — less common Pathophysiology: Compression at any of the above sites produces: - Intraneural oedema → ischaemia → pain and in severe cases axonal compromise - In pure RTS: pain without significant motor deficit distinguishing from posterior interosseous nerve palsy — PINP - Mechanism: repetitive forearm rotation pronation/supination + elbow extension creates intermittent compression at Arcade of Frohse Important distinction: - Radial Tunnel Syndrome: Primarily painful; minimal or no motor deficit; often confused with lateral epicondylalgia - Posterior Interosseous Nerve Palsy PINP : Motor deficit prominent finger/wrist drop ; may be painless; different management Concurrent lateral epicondylalgia: Co-exists in up to 5% of cases; the two conditions can be concurrent but require independent assessment. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Radial tunnel tenderness 4–5 cm distal to lateral epicondyle 0.84 0.65 2.40 0.25 Low-Moderate Resisted supination elbow extended, forearm pronated 0.76 0.72 2.71 0.33 Low Resisted middle finger extension 0.72 0.58 1.71 0.48 Low Resisted elbow extension with forearm pronation PIN stretch 0.68 0.70 2.27 0.46 Low Passive forearm pronation PIN compression 0.63 0.68 1.97 0.54 Low Lateral epicondyle tenderness absent 0.62 0.85 4.13 0.45 Low-Moderate Radial tunnel Tinel's sign 0.58 0.71 2.00 0.59 Low Diagnostic nerve block radial tunnel ~0.90 ~0.85 ~6.0 ~0.12 Moderate as diagnostic tool Note on evidence quality: RTS diagnostic test evidence is of low quality. No high-quality systematic review of special tests exists. Values above represent best available data primarily from Lister et al. 1979, Portilla Molina et al. 1998, Sotereanos et al. 1999 . Radial Tunnel Palpation: Tenderness localised 3–5 cm distal and anterior to lateral epicondyle over radial tunnel , NOT over the lateral epicondyle itself. This is the key clinical differentiator from lateral epicondylalgia. Resisted Supination Test: Elbow extended, forearm fully pronated. Patient supinates against resistance. Positive = radial tunnel pain. Compresses PIN against Arcade of Frohse. Diagnostic Nerve Block: Infiltration of local anaesthetic e.g., 1% lidocaine 3–5 ml into the radial tunnel. Resolution of symptoms confirms diagnosis. More reliable than clinical tests alone in ambiguous cases. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Distinguishing RTS from posterior interosseous nerve palsy is critical — motor deficit requires urgent escalation. - Finger/wrist drop PINP : Inability to extend fingers/wrist at MCP level; wrist extensors may be partially preserved ECRL preserved — exits proximal to tunnel ; requires urgent assessment → MRI ± NCS/EMG ± surgical decompression - Rapidly progressive weakness developing over days-weeks → urgent MRI + orthopaedic/neurosurgical referral - Swelling or mass at lateral elbow/radial tunnel: Lipoma, ganglion, rheumatoid synovitis, tumour — common and treatable causes of compressive PINP → MRI + referral - Post-traumatic radial nerve palsy radial head fracture, proximal radius, elbow dislocation : PINP is a known complication → urgent orthopaedic assessment - Radial nerve palsy at spiral groove Saturday night palsy, humeral fracture : affects wrist extension + supinator; different level from RTS — distinguish on NCS - Systemic inflammatory disease RA, sarcoidosis : can cause nerve compression via synovial proliferation → systemic assessment --- Clinical Frameworks Differential Framework: RTS vs Lateral Epicondylalgia Feature Lateral Epicondylalgia Radial Tunnel Syndrome --------- ---------------------- ---------------------- Pain location Over lateral epicondyle 3–5 cm distal/anterior to LE radial tunnel Resisted wrist extension Painful Cozen's positive Usually negative Resisted supination Usually negative Positive Palpation tenderness At lateral epicondyle At radial tunnel over extensor muscle bulk Night pain Uncommon More common forearm ache US/MRI changes Tendon changes at epicondyle Normal tendons; may show nerve changes NCS/EMG Normal Normal or mildly abnormal in severe Diagnostic nerve block response Partial local anaesthetic Complete resolution in true RTS Severity Framework Lister Classification - Type I: Diffuse ache in dorsal forearm; no neurological deficit; tender at Arcade of Frohse - Type II: More localised pain; early motor fatigue; slight grip weakness - Type III PINP : Motor deficit prominent; wrist/finger extension weakness; surgical priority --- Outcome Measures Patient-Reported Outcomes DASH / QuickDASH: - Most commonly used in RTS research and clinical practice - MCID: DASH 10.2; QuickDASH 16 points - Captures functional disability from forearm pain and any motor deficit PRTEE Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation : - Often used in RTS studies due to clinical overlap with LE - 15 items; 0–100; MCID 11 points - Useful for monitoring symptom response to intervention Numeric Pain Rating Scale: - Forearm pain 0–10 ; assess at rest, with resisted supination, with sustained grip - MCID: 2 points Objective Measures Grip Strength: - Reduced in RTS due to pain inhibition and intrinsic weakness - Baseline measurement important; Jamar at 90° elbow flexion - MCID: 6.5 kg Pinch Strength: - Less affected in RTS vs PINP intrinsics partially spared - Baseline assessment useful Forearm Rotation ROM: - Supination may be restricted/painful in active radial tunnel compression - Goniometry at baseline and review --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis RTS remains a clinical diagnosis with no definitive objective test. The evidence base for diagnostic criteria is weak. Approach: Step 1 — Clinical Assessment: - History: occupational repetitive supination, lateral forearm ache often nocturnal , no sensory deficit, no motor weakness - Examination: tenderness at radial tunnel NOT lateral epicondyle ; positive resisted supination; negative Cozen's Step 2 — Exclude Lateral Epicondylalgia: - If Cozen's positive AND radial tunnel tenderness AND lateral epicondyle tenderness → concurrent LE and RTS possible - NCS normal in both conditions; does not differentiate Step 3 — Diagnostic Nerve Block: - If clinical diagnosis unclear: infiltrate 2–3 ml 1% lidocaine into radial tunnel - Complete relief: confirms RTS; partial relief: concurrent LE likely; no relief: alternative diagnosis Nerve Conduction Studies: - Usually NORMAL in RTS motor nerve conduction across tunnel may be mildly reduced: 3 mm² suggests compression limited data MRI: - Detects mass lesions, PINP, post-inflammatory changes - Not routine for RTS; indicated for surgical planning or atypical cases - Can show denervation oedema in extensor muscles in PINP --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features Key Investigation ----------- ------------------------ ------------------- Lateral epicondylalgia Lateral epicondyle tenderness; positive Cozen's; US tendinopathy Clinical; US Posterior interosseous nerve palsy Finger/wrist drop; no sensory deficit; motor deficit on EMG NCS/EMG; MRI Cervical radiculopathy C6/C7 Neck pain; Spurling's positive; dermatomal sensory change; reflex changes Cervical MRI Radial nerve compression at spiral groove Wrist drop; impaired brachioradialis; after prolonged arm compression NCS/EMG Elbow OA Stiffness; crepitus; X-ray changes; older patient X-ray Synovitis of radiocapitellar joint Joint line tenderness; effusion; ROM loss US; MRI Lateral elbow instability PLRI Clicking; apprehension; trauma history Pivot shift test; MRI Radial head fracture Acute trauma; bony tenderness; X-ray fracture X-ray Tendinopathy of ECRB isolated Mid-muscle belly tenderness; not at tunnel US --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Community Physiotherapy / GP: - Initial management of mild-moderate RTS - Education, activity modification, ergonomic advice, trial of conservative treatment - GP review if no improvement at 6–8 weeks Secondary Care Referral: - Orthopaedics/Hand Surgery if: - Diagnostic uncertainty requiring nerve block or MRI - PINP motor deficit — urgent pathway - Failed 6 months conservative management - Neurophysiology for NCS/EMG: via GP or consultant; confirms diagnosis/excludes PINP --- Conservative Management Activity Modification Grade C : - Avoid repetitive forearm pronation-supination - Reduce sustained elbow extension with forearm pronated - Ergonomic review: tool use, keyboard, assembly line tasks Rest and Splinting Grade C : - Cock-up wrist splint + forearm in neutral position during symptomatic phases - Reduces traction on PIN; no RCT evidence but theoretically sound - Avoid prolonged immobilisation >2–3 weeks — may worsen stiffness Exercise Therapy Grade C — extrapolated from LE evidence : - Supinator stretching: forearm pronation + wrist ulnar deviation gently holds 30 seconds × 5 - Progressive supinator and wrist extensor strengthening - No specific validated exercise protocol for RTS; adapt LE programme Neural Mobilisation Grade C : - Radial nerve neurodynamic technique: - Position: shoulder depression + internal rotation; elbow extension; forearm pronation; wrist/finger flexion; thumb flexion - Gentle sliding technique oscillate neck lateral flexion toward/away - 3 × 10 repetitions; 0–4/10 pain acceptable - Useful for concurrent neural tension component Manual Therapy Grade C : - Radiohumeral joint mobilisation lateral distraction, posterior glide - Limited evidence but may improve symptoms in concurrent LE/RTS presentations --- Pharmacological Oral NSAIDs Grade C : - Short course for acute inflammatory flares - Limited evidence specific to RTS; extrapolated from LE - NICE standard: lowest effective dose; gastroprotection if >7 days Corticosteroid Injection Grade B for diagnostic/therapeutic : - Combined diagnostic nerve block + corticosteroid: methylprednisolone 40 mg + 1–2 ml local anaesthetic - Provides diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic effect - Up to 70% respond to injection with sustained relief Roles & Maudsley 1972 - Ultrasound guidance recommended for accurate radial tunnel placement - Risk: PIN injury if intra-neural injection low with experienced operator + US guidance - Repeat injection: consider if initial response was good; maximum 2–3 injections Neuropathic agents: - If neuropathic component prominent burning, allodynia : pregabalin or gabapentin NICE neuropathic pain guidelines --- Onward Referral Criteria Refer to Orthopaedics/Hand Surgery if: - PINP with motor deficit → urgent referral within 2–4 weeks for surgical decompression - Mass lesion compressing PIN → semi-urgent referral - Failed 6 months conservative management with confirmed RTS - Diagnostic uncertainty after nerve block trial Surgical Options: - Open decompression: Release of all potential compression sites Arcade of Frohse, ECRB medial edge, leash of Henry, fibrous bands - Approach: Anterior Henry , posterior Thompson , or lateral approaches used - Outcomes: Variable; 67–92% improvement reported Roles & Maudsley 1972; Lister et al. 1979 - Recovery: 3–6 months for full return to manual work; physiotherapy for ROM and strengthening post-op Caution: Surgical outcomes for RTS inferior to surgical outcomes for PINP or lateral epicondylalgia. Patient selection critical — ensure diagnosis confirmed with nerve block prior to surgery. --- Key References 1. Roles NC, Maudsley RH. 1972 . Radial tunnel syndrome: resistant tennis elbow as a nerve entrapment. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery , 54 3 , 499–508. 2. Lister GD, Belsole RB, Kleinert HE. 1979 . The radial tunnel syndrome. Journal of Hand Surgery , 4 1 , 52–59. 3. Portilla Molina AE, Bour C, Oberlin C, Nzeusseu A, Vanwijck R. 1998 . The posterior interosseous nerve and the radial tunnel syndrome: an anatomical study. International Orthopaedics , 22 2 , 102–106. 4. Sotereanos DG, Varitimidis SE, Giannakopoulos PN, Westphal RA. 1999 . Results of surgical treatment for radial tunnel syndrome. Journal of Hand Surgery , 24 3 , 566–570. 5. Naam NH, Nemani S. 2012 . Radial tunnel syndrome. Orthopedic Clinics of North America , 43 4 , 529–536. 6. Sarhadi NS, Korday SN, Bainbridge LC. 1998 . Radial tunnel syndrome: diagnosis and management. Journal of Hand Surgery , 23 5 , 617–619. 7. van den Berg PJ, Pompe SM, Beekman R, Visser LH. 2011 . Sonographic incidence of ulnar nerve sub luxation and its associated clinical and electrodiagnostic characteristics. Muscle & Nerve , 43 3 , 347–351. 8. Henry M. 2008 . Radial tunnel syndrome. Journal of the American Society for Surgery of the Hand , 6 2 , 72–78. 9. Dang AC, Rodner CM. 2009 . Unusual compression neuropathies of the forearm, part II: median nerve. Journal of Hand Surgery , 34 10 , 1915–1920. 10. Huisstede BM, Miedema HS, van Opstal T, de Ronde MT, Verhaar JA, Koes BW. 2008 . Interventions for treating the radial tunnel syndrome: a systematic review of observational studies. Journal of Hand Surgery , 33 1 , 72–78.

title: Acromioclavicular Joint Disorders
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology The acromioclavicular joint ACJ is a diarthrodial joint between the distal clavicle and the acromion, stabilised by the acromioclavicular AC and coracoclavicular CC ligaments trapezoid and conoid . It transmits forces between the upper limb and axial skeleton and allows ap
content: Overview & Pathophysiology The acromioclavicular joint ACJ is a diarthrodial joint between the distal clavicle and the acromion, stabilised by the acromioclavicular AC and coracoclavicular CC ligaments trapezoid and conoid . It transmits forces between the upper limb and axial skeleton and allows approximately 20° of rotation during shoulder elevation. Conditions Covered ACJ Sprain / Separation Traumatic disruption of AC and/or CC ligaments, typically from a direct fall onto the point of the shoulder or onto an outstretched hand FOOSH . The distal clavicle rides superiorly relative to the acromion proportional to ligamentous damage. Most common in males aged 20–40 and in contact sports rugby, GAA, cycling . ACJ Osteoarthritis Degenerative joint disease of the ACJ, often presenting in middle-aged to older adults. Associated with repetitive overhead loading, prior trauma, and distal clavicle osteolysis. Cartilaginous narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation reduce the subacromial space and may contribute to secondary impingement. Distal Clavicle Osteolysis Stress-related resorption of the distal clavicle, classically in weight-lifters and overhead athletes. Histology shows microfractures, vascular proliferation, and osteoclastic resorption without infection. X-ray shows tapering and irregular resorption of the distal 2–3 cm of clavicle. --- Rockwood Classification ACJ Separation Grade Structures Damaged Clavicle Displacement Management ------- ------------------- ---------------------- ------------ I AC ligament sprain only None Conservative II AC ligament torn, CC sprain Clinical Note: Grades I–II = conservative. Grade III = individualise most evidence supports non-operative . Grades IV–VI = refer for orthopaedic assessment. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR −LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ----- ----- --------------- ------- O'Brien's Active Compression Test 0.16–0.41 0.79–0.99 1.6–41 0.60–0.85 Moderate Hegedus et al. 2012 High specificity for ACJ when pain localised to top of shoulder; lower sens for SLAP Cross-Body Adduction Test 0.77 0.79 3.7 0.29 Moderate Mazzocca et al. 2004 Arm adducted across chest in 90° flexion; reproduces ACJ pain Paxinos Test 0.79 0.50 1.58 0.42 Low–Moderate Walton et al. 2004 Examiner's thumb pushes clavicle anteroinferiorly; reproduces ACJ symptoms Horizontal Adduction Stress Test 0.82 0.28 1.14 0.64 Low Chronopoulos et al. 2004 High sensitivity but poor specificity ACJ Palpation 0.96 0.10 1.07 0.40 Low Chronopoulos et al. 2004 Useful for confirming location; poor for ruling in/out pathology > Diagnostic Tip: O'Brien's is most useful when pain is reproduced at the top of the shoulder AND relieved with palm-up position. Pain deep in the shoulder suggests SLAP lesion rather than ACJ pathology. Diagnostic Injection Gold Standard Lidocaine injection into ACJ with ≥50% pain relief is considered the clinical reference standard for ACJ pathology sensitivity 0.96, specificity 0.84 — Walton et al. 2004 . Request via GP or MSK consultant if diagnosis uncertain. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Refer urgently if any of the following are present: - Neurovascular compromise — paraesthesia, weakness, or absent pulses following trauma - Open ACJ dislocation or skin tenting/threat of skin breakdown Grade V/VI - Pathological fracture — no trauma history, known malignancy, unexplained weight loss, night pain out of proportion - Suspected septic arthritis — fever, systemic illness, rapid joint swelling, raised CRP/WBC - Cervical myelopathy — bilateral symptoms, gait disturbance, bladder/bowel dysfunction - Polyarthropathy — multiple joint involvement, morning stiffness >30 min consider inflammatory arthropathy → rheumatology - Distal clavicle osteolysis with systemic symptoms — consider PVNS or metabolic bone disease --- Clinical Frameworks Diagnostic Algorithm ICF Framework Domain Example -------- --------- Body structure/function ACJ instability, pain, reduced ROM, crepitus Activity limitation Difficulty dressing, reaching overhead, carrying Participation restriction Unable to return to sport, work overhead tasks Contextual factors Sport demands, occupation, psychosocial, activity goals --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID MDC Population Notes --------- ------ ----- ----------- ------- DASH Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder & Hand 10–15 points 12.7 General upper limb 30 items; 0=no disability, 100=most disabled QuickDASH 8–16 points 15.9 General upper limb 11-item version; good for clinical use SPADI Shoulder Pain & Disability Index 8–18 points 18 Shoulder conditions Pain + disability subscales 0–100 Oxford Shoulder Score OSS 5 points — Shoulder surgery/OA 12 items; 0=worst, 48=best; validated for shoulder OA Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS 2 points 1.74 All 0–10; use at every assessment --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Guidelines Modality Indication Findings ---------- ----------- --------- X-ray AP + Zanca 10° cephalic tilt First-line; trauma/OA CC distance normal 11–13 mm , joint space narrowing, osteolysis, stress views for instability Ultrasound Dynamic assessment, guided injection Joint effusion, capsular thickening, distal clavicle changes MRI Soft tissue assessment, planned surgery CC ligament integrity, labral pathology, bone oedema osteolysis CT Complex/comminuted fractures, pre-surgical Clavicle fracture pattern, posterior displacement Grade IV > Zanca View: 10–15° cephalic tilt reduces overlap with spine; reduces beam by 50% for better joint detail. Preferred over standard AP for ACJ assessment. Bilateral Stress Views Weight-bearing X-rays with 10 lb weights hung from wrists: identifies Grade III vs IV by measuring CC distance bilaterally. Now used selectively not routinely . --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Differentiating Features Investigation ----------- ------------------------------ -------------- Subacromial impingement Painful arc 60–120°, positive Neer/Hawkins USS, MRI Rotator cuff tear Weakness on resisted rotation, positive drop arm USS/MRI SLAP lesion O'Brien's positive with deep shoulder pain, biceps involvement MRI arthrogram Sternoclavicular joint pathology Pain medial to ACJ, SCJ tenderness, swelling X-ray, CT Cervical radiculopathy C4–C5 Dermatomal distribution, neck movement reproduces symptoms Cervical assessment, MRI Inflammatory arthropathy Bilateral, morning stiffness, systemic features Blood CRP, RF, anti-CCP , rheumatology Thoracic outlet syndrome Vascular/neurogenic symptoms with provocation EAST test, vascular studies Clavicle stress fracture Localised clavicle tenderness, overhead athletes X-ray, MRI bone oedema --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway > Physiotherapy First Access: > In HSC NI, patients with ACJ disorders can self-refer or be referred via GP to MSK Physiotherapy First Contact Practitioners at some sites . Onward referral to MSK Consultant / Orthopaedics follows failure of conservative management typically 6–12 weeks or specific indications Grade IV–VI, suspected septic arthritis . Pathway: 1. GP / Self-referral / FCP → MSK Physiotherapy assessment 2. Conservative management 6–12 weeks 3. No improvement → MSK Consultant / Orthopaedic review → Consider diagnostic injection / imaging 4. Surgical indications → Orthopaedic referral via MSK Consultant Conservative Management Grades I–III Acute Phase Week 0–3 : - Sling for comfort Grade II–III : typically 1–2 weeks maximum; avoid prolonged immobilisation - Ice 10–15 min, 3–4× daily , activity modification - Analgesia see pharmacological - Patient education: expected recovery timeline, activity modification, return-to-sport guidance Rehabilitation Phase Week 2–12 : - Range of motion : pendular exercises → active-assisted → full active ROM - Rotator cuff strengthening : isometric → isotonic bands → free weights - Periscapular strengthening : lower trapezius, serratus anterior — critical for ACJ load reduction - Proprioception / neuromuscular training : closed-chain progression - Sport-specific rehabilitation : graded return to impact/contact Evidence Base: - Mouhsine et al. 2003 : Grade I–III — 90% satisfaction with conservative management at 2 years - Mazzocca et al. 2011 : No significant difference in outcomes between surgical and conservative Grade III at 5 years ACJ OA / Distal Clavicle Osteolysis - Load modification : reduce overhead pressing, heavy bench press modify grip width — wider grip reduces ACJ stress - Periscapular strengthening as above - Manual therapy : ACJ mobilisation Grade III–IV Maitland ; may reduce pain limited RCT evidence - Distal clavicle osteolysis : relative rest from causative activity for 3–6 months; most resolve Pharmacological Management Drug Dose Duration Notes ------ ------ --------- ------- Paracetamol 1 g QDS PRN First-line; safest option NSAIDs e.g. Naproxen 500 mg BD, Ibuprofen 400 mg TDS Standard ≤4 weeks With food; contraindicated in renal impairment, GI history, anticoagulation Topical NSAIDs Diclofenac gel Apply 3–4× daily ≤4 weeks NICE preferred for local pain; reduced systemic effects Intra-articular corticosteroid injection e.g. Triamcinolone 20 mg + lidocaine 1–3 per joint/year Via GP, MSK consultant, or radiology; ≥50% pain relief expected if ACJ is source > NICE Guidance MSK conditions : Offer exercise-based therapy first. Corticosteroid injection for short-term relief while commencing rehabilitation. Avoid >3 injections/year to same joint. Onward Referral Criteria Situation Referral Destination Urgency ----------- --------------------- --------- Grade IV–VI ACJ separation Orthopaedics Urgent within days if neurovascular compromise Grade III — failed 3–6 months conservative; high-demand athlete MSK Consultant / Orthopaedics Routine ACJ OA — failed 6–12 weeks conservative + failed injection MSK Consultant / Orthopaedics Routine Distal clavicle osteolysis — failed 6 months conservative MSK Consultant Routine Suspected inflammatory arthropathy Rheumatology 2-week wait if systemically unwell Red flags septic arthritis, tumour A&E / Orthopaedics Same day Surgical Options for reference - Grade III : ACCR acromioclavicular coracoclavicular reconstruction or Weaver-Dunn procedure - ACJ OA / Osteolysis : Distal clavicle excision Mumford procedure — arthroscopic or open; high satisfaction rates 85–92% --- Key References 1. content: Overview & Pathophysiology Adhesive capsulitis frozen shoulder is a painful, progressive condition characterised by diffuse fibrosis and contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule, resulting in significant restriction of active and passive range of motion in a capsular pattern. It is a distinct clinical entity from other shoulder conditions and follows a broadly predictable natural history. Prevalence: - Lifetime prevalence: 2–5% of the general population - Peak incidence: 40–60 years rare 70 - Female preponderance: approximately 60–70% female - Second shoulder affected in 20–30% of patients usually contralateral; simultaneous bilateral uncommon Associated Conditions: Condition Relative Risk / Prevalence ----------- --------------------------- Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 3–5× increased risk; prevalence 10–20% in frozen shoulder Thyroid disease hypo- and hyperthyroid 2–3× increased risk Dupuytren's contracture Associated fibrotic diathesis Parkinson's disease Increased risk; may be early feature Cardiac disease / post-cardiac surgery Prolonged immobility Post-stroke ipsilateral shoulder Hemiplegia + immobility Cervical disc disease Neurogenic inflammation proposed Post-operative immobilisation Rotator cuff repair; mastectomy Hyperlipidaemia Emerging association Pathophysiology The pathological process involves: 1. Inflammatory phase: Synovial inflammation with fibroblast proliferation; increased vascularity; cytokine release IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6 2. Fibrotic phase: Dense fibrocollagenous tissue formation; capsule thickening normal 2–4 mm → up to 7–10 mm in contracted phase 3. Key site: Rotator cuff interval between supraspinatus and subscapularis — contracture here produces external rotation restriction first 4. Axillary recess obliteration: Normal joint volume 28–30 mL reduced to abduction > IR restriction proportional loss ; distinguishes from other shoulder conditions External Rotation abduction > IR - Exclusion of glenohumeral arthritis X-ray , rotator cuff tear USS , and other causes --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Onset 6 months no improvement ; excellent outcomes reported >90% satisfaction - Systematic review Omari & Bunker, 2001 : superior to MUA for recovery speed - Available at NI orthopaedic centres --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Differentiating Features Differentiating Assessment ----------- ------------------------------ --------------------------- Glenohumeral osteoarthritis Older age; crepitus; X-ray changes; gradual onset X-ray — joint space loss, osteophytes Rotator cuff tear with secondary stiffness Lag signs; weakness; USS/MRI confirms tear USS — full-thickness tear Subacromial pain syndrome Painful arc; strength variable; NOT globally restricted ROM testing — not capsular pattern Calcific tendinitis Acute severe pain; X-ray calcification; moves through X-ray — calcification Glenohumeral inflammatory arthritis RA/crystal Bilateral; systemic features; inflammatory bloods Bloods RF, anti-CCP, urate ; X-ray Shoulder impingement + secondary guarding Painful arc; resisted tests positive; ROM pain-limited not structurally restricted Passive ROM under distraction/supine Avascular necrosis AVN History steroids, alcohol, haemoglobinopathy; deep aching MRI — AVN signal Posterior shoulder dislocation missed Trauma; fixed IR; limited ER; BEWARE X-ray axillary view essential ; CT Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Vasomotor; trophic changes; allodynia; disproportionate Specialist assessment Cervical radiculopathy Neck symptoms; referred pain; neurological signs Cervical exam; ULTT; Spurling's --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care: - GP: clinical diagnosis; X-ray exclude OA/calcific ; blood glucose/HbA1c exclude/diagnose diabetes - Intra-articular corticosteroid injection landmark or USS-guided : available via GP or GPwSI - Referral to community physiotherapy for Stage 1 education, pain management or Stage 2/3 ROM exercises, mobilisation MSK Interface HSC NI : - USS-guided injection intra-articular methylprednisolone/triamcinolone + lidocaine - Hydrodilatation: available in some trusts via radiology or MSK service under fluoroscopy/USS guidance - Belfast Trust: orthopaedic MSK interface; South Eastern Trust: community injection service - Waiting times: community physio 6–20 weeks; MSK interface 8–16 weeks; orthopaedic 12–26+ months Orthopaedic pathway: - Refractory cases >6 months no meaningful progression - MUA + post-operative physiotherapy - Arthroscopic capsular release Musgrave Park Hospital; Altnagelvin; Antrim Conservative Management Stage 1 Painful/Freezing — Priority: pain management: - Education: condition, stages, natural history, prognosis - Sleep position advice pillow under arm; avoid lying on affected side - Avoid aggressive stretching — counterproductive in Stage 1 - Gentle pendulum exercises; active-assisted ROM in pain-free range - Pain-free active exercises isometric, low-load - Early injection referral for pain management Stage 2 Frozen/Stiffening — Priority: ROM restoration: Technique Evidence Dosage ----------- ---------- -------- Passive ROM exercises Moderate 3×10 reps, 3×/day within pain tolerance Hold-relax contract-relax stretching Moderate 5 sec contract; 10 sec passive stretch; 3× each direction Glenohumeral joint mobilisation Grade III–IV Moderate Posterior capsule; inferior glide Physiotherapy-supervised stretching programme High 2–3× per week supervised + home programme Codman's pendulum exercises Low-moderate Daily Stage 3 Thawing/Resolution — Priority: function and strength: - Progressive strengthening: rotator cuff; scapular stabilisers - Return to overhead activities: graded exposure - Occupational/work activities — graded return - Prognosis counselling — complete resolution may take 2+ years Pharmacological NICE NG194 alignment: - NSAIDs: Topical first-line; oral NSAIDs for acute severe pain — minimum dose/duration; PPI cover - Simple analgesia: Paracetamol for mild-moderate pain - Corticosteroid injection intra-articular : - Most effective intervention for Stage 1 freezing - Carette et al. 2003 NEJM: intra-articular triamcinolone 40 mg superior to physiotherapy alone at 6 weeks - Repeat injection at 6 weeks if partial response — up to 3 per year - USS-guided preferred for accuracy - Hydrodilatation: Combine with corticosteroid for enhanced benefit Buchbinder et al. 2004 - Avoid: Opioids; headings: Interventional: ESWT Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Calcific tendinitis CT of the shoulder is characterised by the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals within the rotator cuff tendons, most commonly the supraspinatus 80–90% of cases , followed by infraspinatus ~10% and subscapularis ~5% . It affects 2.7–8% of the adult population, with peak incidence in the 4th–5th decades, and a female predominance F:M ≈ 2:1 . Pathophysiology: Uhthoff Model The most widely accepted pathophysiological model is Uhthoff & Loehr's 1997 cell-mediated theory — a fibrocartilaginous transformation of tendon tissue not a degenerative process , distinct from dystrophic calcification seen in chronic tendinopathy. Uhthoff Stages of Calcific Tendinitis: Stage Phase Histology Clinical Features Duration ------- ------- ----------- ------------------- ---------- Pre-calcific Fibrocartilaginous transformation Chondrocytic metaplasia of tendon fibrocytes; no calcium yet Often asymptomatic; possible mild aching Months Calcific — Formative Crystal deposition Calcium crystals deposited in matrix vesicles; chalk-like, soft consistency Mild–moderate pain; often episodic Weeks–months Calcific — Resting Quiescent Calcium consolidates; vascular ingrowth begins Variable — may be asymptomatic Variable Calcific — Resorptive ⚠️ Most painful Phagocytic resorption; toothpaste-like consistency; highly vascular; intense local inflammation Severe acute pain ; often the presenting crisis Days–weeks Post-calcific Remodelling Fibroblast invasion; collagen remodelling; calcium resolves Pain subsides; function recovers Weeks–months > Key clinical implication: The resorptive phase is the most acutely painful often presenting as apparent 'pseudo-acute' shoulder . Paradoxically, this phase has the best prognosis as calcium is being actively resorbed. Intervention aspiration/barbotage is most effective and technically easiest in this phase fluid/toothpaste consistency . Gärtner Radiographic Classification: Type Appearance Phase Correlation Clinical Note ------ ----------- ------------------- --------------- Type I Dense, homogeneous, well-defined border Formative/resting Harder; less likely to resolve spontaneously Type II Dense/translucent, heterogeneous or poorly defined Transitional Variable behaviour Type III Translucent, heterogeneous, poorly defined 'fluffy' Resorptive Soft; most amenable to barbotage; more likely to resolve spontaneously Why calcium deposits in the critical zone: The supraspinatus is most affected in its "critical zone" — 1 cm proximal to the insertion — an area of relative avascularity and high mechanical stress Rathbun & Macnab, 1970 . Hypoxic conditions may trigger fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and initiate the calcification cascade. Spontaneous resolution rate: 27–50% of deposits resolve within 3 years without intervention. Natural history is generally favourable, but 20–30% of patients develop chronic, recalcitrant symptoms. --- Special Tests > Clinical Note: No shoulder special test is specific for calcific tendinitis. Tests below detect subacromial impingement and rotator cuff pathology — calcific tendinitis should be confirmed by imaging. A positive impingement cluster with acute-onset severe pain warrants X-ray. Impingement & Rotator Cuff Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Painful Arc 0.53–0.74 0.81 3.7 0.57 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ Pain 60–120° abduction; non-specific — impingement, CT, RC tear Neer Impingement Sign 0.72 0.66 2.1 0.43 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ Passive forward flexion with IR; pain = positive Neer Impingement Test 0.83 0.54 1.80 0.31 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ ≥50% pain relief after subacromial lidocaine injection = positive Hawkins-Kennedy 0.72–0.79 0.56–0.66 1.84–2.32 0.34–0.50 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ Forward flexion 90°, forced IR; pain = positive Empty Can Jobe 0.69–0.86 0.66–0.74 2.8 0.28 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ Supraspinatus strength; weakness suggests RC involvement Full Can 0.66 0.64 1.83 0.53 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ Less discomfort than Empty Can; equivalent sensitivity Drop Arm 0.21–0.35 0.88–0.92 2.9 0.86 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ High specificity for full-thickness RC tear; low sensitivity External Rotation Lag Sign 0.56–0.77 0.98 28–38 0.28–0.45 High ⭐⭐⭐⭐ High specificity for posterosuperior RC tear Cross-body Adduction 0.82 0.28 1.14 0.64 Low ⭐⭐ AC joint pain; poor discrimination Impingement Test Cluster Hegedus et al., 2012 : Neer + Hawkins-Kennedy + Painful Arc: ≥2 positive tests → sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.74 for subacromial pathology > Calcific tendinitis-specific clinical pattern: Sudden onset of exquisite shoulder pain often overnight or following minor activity , severe movement restriction, marked tenderness over supraspinatus insertion, presentation mimicking septic arthritis. X-ray confirms diagnosis. --- Red Flags Red Flag Action ---------- -------- Fever + erythema + septic-appearing joint exclude septic arthritis A&E same day — joint aspiration required Severe acute pain with inability to move arm + preceding dental/GI/UTI reactive arthritis Urgent GP/A&E — same day Unexplained weight loss + night pain + age >50 exclude malignancy 2-week wait cancer pathway Acute neurological deficit in upper limb Urgent neurology/A&E Failure to improve after 3 months conservative treatment MRI to exclude concurrent full-thickness RC tear; consider escalation Progressive weakness not explained by pain inhibition Urgent referral — full-thickness tear or neurological cause Bilateral shoulder involvement + systemic symptoms RA, pseudogout, metabolic disorder Rheumatology referral Calcium deposit associated with cortical bone erosion on X-ray Orthopaedic referral — rare aggressive variant --- Clinical Frameworks Diagnostic Framework Treatment Decision Tree HSC NI --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID MDC Score Range Best For Validated? --------- ------ ----- ------------- ---------- ------------ SPADI Shoulder Pain & Disability Index 8–13 points 18 points 0–100 0=best Recommended first-line for CT; pain-heavy presentations; highly responsive to change ✅ Yes DASH Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder, Hand 10.8 points 12.7 points 0–100 0=best General UE function; good for tracking functional recovery across treatment phases ✅ Yes QuickDASH 14.9–15.9 points — 0–100 0=best Efficient screening at each contact; 11-item version ✅ Yes OSS Oxford Shoulder Score 5 points — 0–48 48=best Pre/post-op comparison; NHS standard for surgical referrals ✅ Yes ASES American Shoulder & Elbow Surgeons 6.4–17 points — 0–100 100=best Research; surgical outcomes ✅ Yes NRS Pain 0–10 1.5–2 points — 0–10 0=no pain Rapid pain monitoring; supplement to functional measure ✅ Yes > HSC NI Practice Recommendation: Use SPADI as primary outcome measure for calcific tendinitis pain-dominant condition; more responsive than DASH in acute presentations . Supplement with NRS pain at each contact. Re-measure SPADI at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, and post-intervention. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Comparison Modality Sensitivity Specificity Cost First-Line? Notes ---------- ------------- ------------- ------ ------------- ------- Plain X-ray AP + outlet 66–93% ~99% Low ✅ Yes Mandatory first-line; identifies deposit, size, morphology Gärtner classification Ultrasound USS 79–98% 88–99% Low-Moderate ✅ Yes adjunct Dynamic assessment; guides intervention barbotage ; detects concurrent RC tear; operator-dependent MRI 70–82% 98% High No second-line Best for soft tissue; concurrent pathology RC tear, AC joint ; calcium may appear as signal void CT ~100% ~100% High/Radiation No Rarely needed; useful pre-op planning for large/complex deposits Preferred imaging approach HSC NI : 1. Plain X-ray — confirm diagnosis, classify deposit Gärtner I/II/III , measure size 2. USS — if intervention planned, or if concurrent RC pathology suspected complementary to X-ray 3. MRI — if X-ray/USS inconclusive, suspected full-thickness RC tear, or pre-surgical assessment Deposit characteristics associated with spontaneous resolution: - Gärtner Type III 'fluffy', poorly defined - Smaller deposits 2 cm - Long symptom duration >12 months - Bursal-side deposits --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Differentiating Features Key Tests Imaging ----------- -------------------------- ----------- --------- Subacromial Impingement without calcification Painful arc; similar impingement signs; no sudden onset crisis; gradual onset Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy, Empty Can USS/MRI; X-ray normal or minor degenerative changes Rotator Cuff Tear full-thickness Weakness > pain full thickness ; Drop Arm positive; ER lag sign; older age Drop Arm, ER Lag Sign, Belly Press USS/MRI confirms; X-ray shows superior migration if massive Adhesive Capsulitis Global passive restriction all planes ; ER most restricted; capsular pattern Capsular pattern ROM testing MRI capsular thickening, reduced joint volume ; X-ray normal Septic Arthritis Fever, elevated CRP/ESR/WBC; erythema; systemically unwell; rapid onset FBC/CRP/ESR, joint aspiration USS shows effusion; X-ray may be normal early Acromioclavicular Joint Pathology Pain at AC joint; cross-body adduction positive; no calcium in supraspinatus Cross-body adduction, AC palpation, O'Brien's top pain X-ray AC views; USS Pseudogout CPPD Often older patient; knee/wrist also affected; synovial fluid analysis confirms Joint aspiration — positive birefringent crystals X-ray — chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage Cervical Radiculopathy C5 Dermatomal radiation; neck movement provokes; reduced biceps reflex Spurling's, ULTT, neurological exam Cervical MRI Glenohumeral Osteoarthritis Older patient; global ROM loss; crepitus; stiffness > pain; end-stage Passive ROM, crepitus X-ray joint space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis Reactive Arthritis Preceding infection; other joints affected; systemic features HLA-B27, ESR/CRP, urine culture X-ray; MRI Os Acromiale unfused secondary ossification centre Young adult; anterior acromial tenderness; acromion mobile; X-ray diagnostic X-ray axillary view critical CT for surgical planning --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Pathway > Aligned with NICE guideline NG233 Shoulder Pain, 2023 , BESS consensus statements , and SIGN guidelines. All patients should be offered structured physiotherapy before escalation. Entry Point: Community Physiotherapy / PCMSK MSK service Step 1 — Assessment & Imaging - Full MSK assessment; red flag screen - Plain X-ray if not already done — confirm diagnosis and Gärtner classification - Baseline outcome measures: SPADI + QuickDASH + NRS pain - Determine clinical phase resorptive vs. formative/resting Step 2 — Conservative Management Weeks 0–12 - All patients offered conservative physiotherapy + analgesia - Review at 6 weeks with repeat outcome measures Step 3 — Injection/Intervention if inadequate response at 6–12 weeks - Subacromial corticosteroid injection acute/resorptive phase — pain control - USS-guided barbotage/aspiration resorptive phase, Gärtner III - ESWT referral formative/resting phase, Gärtner I/II — conservative failure Step 4 — Orthopaedic Referral - Failure of ≥3 months conservative treatment including ESWT/barbotage - Significant quality of life impairment - Concurrent full-thickness RC tear requiring surgical management Conservative Management Physiotherapy Principles: Phase Timeframe Goals Interventions ------- ----------- ------- --------------- Acute Resorptive Weeks 0–4 Pain control; maintain ROM; patient education Pendulum exercises; cryotherapy; gentle passive ROM; avoid provocative overhead loading Subacute Weeks 4–8 Progressive ROM; begin RC strengthening Active ROM; scapular stabilisation; isometric RC; posterior capsule stretching Functional Weeks 8–12+ Full strength; return to function/work Progressive resistance; proprioception; functional tasks; sport-specific if applicable Manual Therapy: - Joint mobilisation GH and thoracic has low-level evidence as adjunct to exercise in subacromial pain — included in multimodal approach - Not recommended as primary or standalone treatment Exercise: - Supervised exercise superior to home exercise alone for subacromial conditions - Scapular stabilisation and rotator cuff strengthening are cornerstones - Avoid provocative overhead loading in acute/resorptive phase Pharmacological Agent Indication Evidence Dosing / Notes ------- ------------ ---------- ---------------- Oral NSAIDs e.g., naproxen 500mg BD, ibuprofen 400mg TDS Acute/subacute pain control Moderate 7–14 day course; gastroprotection PPI if risk factors; contraindicated in renal/cardiac disease Paracetamol 1g QDS Background analgesia, adjunct Low-Moderate Safe; useful for patients unable to tolerate NSAIDs Subacromial Corticosteroid Injection e.g., methylprednisolone 40mg + local anaesthetic Acute pain resorptive phase ; short-term pain control Moderate Effective short-term up to 6 weeks ; not disease-modifying; max 2–3 injections/shoulder/year; 48-hr post-injection flare possible Codeine / Tramadol Acute severe pain resorptive crisis ; short-term only Expert consensus Maximum 5–7 days; constipation counselling; tramadol — interactions, serotonin syndrome risk Colchicine Acute crystal-induced inflammatory crisis Limited evidence Off-label use; some case series support; specialist/GP discretion Interventional: ESWT Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy Mechanism: Acoustic pressure waves → mechanical disruption of calcium deposits → stimulate phagocytic resorption + neovascularisation Evidence Summary: Parameter Data ----------- ------ Efficacy vs placebo Significant pain reduction and deposit resorption vs sham at 3–12 months Level 1 evidence — multiple RCTs Responders Gärtner Type I/II deposits respond better to ESWT than Type III which is already resorbing Protocol High-energy ESWT 0.28 mJ/mm² : 1–3 sessions, 1500–3000 impulses per session Deposit resorption Complete resorption in 30–66% at 12 months; partial resorption additional 25–30% SPADI improvement Mean SPADI improvement ~25–35 points vs ~5–10 points placebo NNT NNT for significant improvement ≈ 3–5 Key RCT Gerdesmeyer et al. 2003 : High-energy ESWT vs sham; 85% success rate at 2 years Systematic review Louwerens et al. 2014 : ESWT superior to placebo for symptom reduction and deposit resorption HSC NI access Via orthopaedic physiotherapy or orthopaedic department; not universally available in primary care ESWT contraindications: Coagulation disorders/anticoagulants, local infection, malignancy, pregnancy, pacemaker, bony deposits overlying neurovascular structures Interventional: USS-Guided Barbotage / Needling & Lavage Mechanism: Direct mechanical disruption of calcium deposit via needle; lavage removes calcium debris; induces local inflammatory response to accelerate resorption. Evidence Summary: Parameter Data ----------- ------ Efficacy Significant pain reduction; superior to corticosteroid injection alone de Witte et al., 2012 Best phase Resorptive Gärtner III — calcium has toothpaste-like consistency; easier aspiration Technique USS guidance essential; 18G needle; 2-needle technique preferred in/out ; lavage with 0.9% NaCl; attempt aspiration of calcium Combined with corticosteroid Corticosteroid injection after barbotage standard practice for post-procedure flare management Key RCT Randomised trial de Witte et al., 2012 : barbotage + corticosteroid vs corticosteroid alone — ASES score superior in barbotage arm at 12 months Success rate 60–80% significant improvement at 12 months; deposit clearance in 30–70% HSC NI access Musculoskeletal radiologist or orthopaedic consultant; USS required; routine orthopaedic outpatient pathway Surgical Management Arthroscopic Removal Indication: Failure of ≥3–6 months conservative treatment including ESWT and/or barbotage ; significant ongoing disability. Procedure: Arthroscopic debridement and removal of calcium deposit ± subacromial decompression acromioplasty if hook acromion/subacromial narrowing Evidence: - Success rate 85–90% at 2 years - Acromioplasty added in ~70% of cases Ark et al., 1992 - Rarely required: 50 at 3 months Rheumatology Suspected systemic cause bilateral CT, CPPD, RA, metabolic disorder --- Key References 1. title: Shoulder Labral Tears (SLAP & Bankart Lesions)
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the periphery of the glenoid fossa, deepening the socket by approximately 50% and contributing significantly to glenohumeral stability. Labral tears fall into two main clinical categories encountered in MSK physiot
headings: SLAP Lesions Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior
Onward Referral Criteria HSC NI MSK Pathway
content: Overview & Pathophysiology The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the periphery of the glenoid fossa, deepening the socket by approximately 50% and contributing significantly to glenohumeral stability. Labral tears fall into two main clinical categories encountered in MSK physiotherapy practice: SLAP Lesions Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior SLAP lesions involve the superior labrum at the biceps anchor long head of biceps tendon inserts at the supraglenoid tubercle and superior labrum . They are common in overhead athletes, throwing sports, and following traction/compression injuries. Snyder Classification 1990 : Type Description Prevalence Management Implication ------ ------------- ----------- ------------------------ Type I Superior labral fraying/degeneration; biceps anchor intact ~11% Conservative Type II Detachment of superior labrum and biceps anchor from glenoid most common ~41% Often surgical if conservative fails Type III Bucket-handle tear of superior labrum; biceps anchor intact ~33% Surgical resection Type IV Bucket-handle tear extending into biceps tendon ~15% Surgical repair/tenotomy Type V–X Extended classifications Morgan/Maffet including combined lesions Variable Specialist-led Pathomechanics: - Repetitive overhead loading : Peel-back mechanism during late cocking phase — posterior biceps vector peels the labrum off the glenoid - GIRD Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit : Posterior capsule tightness shifts humeral head posterosuperiorly, increasing shear on superior labrum - Traction injury : Sudden inferior distraction force e.g., catching a heavy object - Compression : FOOSH fall on outstretched hand with superior shear force Bankart Lesions Anterior Labral Tears Bankart lesions involve detachment of the anteroinferior labrum typically 3–6 o'clock position from the glenoid rim. They are the primary pathological lesion in traumatic anterior glenohumeral instability, present in >85% of first-time anterior dislocations . Subtypes: - Classic Bankart : Labrum and periosteum stripped from glenoid rim - Bony Bankart : Associated anterior glenoid bone loss >15–20% glenoid width indicates critical bone loss and alters surgical planning - ALPSA Anterior Labroligamentous Periosteal Sleeve Avulsion : Periosteum intact; labrum medially displaced — poorer proprioceptive outcome if untreated - HAGL Humeral Avulsion of Glenohumeral Ligament : Less common; IGHL avulses from humeral attachment Associated lesions: Hill-Sachs defect posterolateral humeral head impression fracture in 47–90% of dislocations; engaging Hill-Sachs lesions complicate surgical planning. --- Special Tests > Clinical Note: No single special test confirms labral pathology with sufficient diagnostic certainty. A cluster approach combining ≥3 positive tests improves accuracy. MR arthrography remains the gold standard for SLAP sensitivity 82–92%, specificity 85–98% . SLAP-Specific Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- O'Brien's Active Compression 0.47–0.67 0.11–0.98 1.1–3.0 0.50–0.68 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ High false-positive rate; AC joint pathology also positive Crank Test 0.46 0.56 1.05 0.97 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ Supine: 90° abduction, axial load + IR/ER rotation; pain/clunk = positive Biceps Load II 0.90 0.97 29.9 0.10 High ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Best individual SLAP test; 90° abduction, 90° ER, resisted elbow flexion from supination Anterior Slide Test 0.78 0.92 9.75 0.24 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ Anterior directed force on elbow with hand on hip; pain/click at anterosuperior joint Kim Test SLAP variant 0.80 0.94 13.3 0.21 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ 90° abduction; axial load + 45° diagonal elevation + posterior-inferior force Speed's Test 0.32–0.69 0.55–0.67 1.27 0.90 Low ⭐⭐ Primarily biceps tendinopathy; poor SLAP discrimination Yergason's Test 0.43 0.79 2.05 0.72 Low ⭐⭐ Bicipital groove tenderness more informative Compression Rotation 0.24 0.76 1.00 1.00 Low ⭐⭐ Poor LRs; not recommended in isolation SLAP Test Cluster Meserve et al. : O'Brien's + Crank + Anterior Slide — ≥2 positive tests: sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.85, +LR 5.0 Instability / Bankart Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Apprehension Test 0.50–0.72 0.96–0.99 17.6–20.0 0.32–0.53 High ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Apprehension not just pain is key finding Relocation Test Jobe 0.57–0.81 0.87–0.92 6.7–10.0 0.21–0.48 High ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Relief of apprehension with posterior pressure = positive Anterior Release Test 0.92 0.89 8.4 0.09 High ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Removal of posterior force causes return of apprehension Sulcus Sign 0.28 0.97 9.33 0.74 Moderate ⭐⭐⭐ Inferior instability / MDI component Load and Shift 0.50 0.66 1.47 0.76 Low ⭐⭐ Examiner-dependent; establishes direction of laxity > Diagnostic rule: Apprehension + Relocation + Anterior Release triad has been shown to have sensitivity of 0.68 and specificity of 0.99 for anterior instability Lo et al., 2004 . Apprehension alone is the single best test. --- Red Flags The following warrant urgent onward referral or emergency management — do not manage conservatively without senior review: Red Flag Action ---------- -------- Acute traumatic dislocation with neurovascular compromise axillary nerve deficit, absent radial pulse A&E same day Bony Bankart with >25% glenoid bone loss on imaging Urgent orthopaedic referral — high recurrence risk, Latarjet procedure indicated Associated proximal humerus fracture fracture-dislocation A&E same day Unreduced glenohumeral dislocation A&E same day Progressive neurological deficit brachial plexus neuropraxia not resolving at 6 weeks Urgent neurology/orthopaedic referral Recurrent instability with Hill-Sachs engaging on external rotation Orthopaedic referral — remplissage or Latarjet may be required First-time dislocation in patient 50 with insidious onset 2-week wait cancer pathway --- Clinical Frameworks SLAP Decision Framework Bankart / Instability Framework HSC NI GIRD Management SLAP prevention/rehab - Sleeper stretch : Side-lying on affected shoulder, horizontal adduction + IR — target ≥5° gain in IR compared to contralateral - Cross-body stretch : Horizontal adduction in standing — posterior capsule release - Goal : Achieve GIRD HSC NI Practice Recommendation: Use WOSI for instability/labral presentations and DASH or QuickDASH as a general upper extremity functional baseline. OSS if surgical referral likely standardises pre/post-op comparison . --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Hierarchy Modality SLAP Sensitivity SLAP Specificity Notes ---------- ----------------- ----------------- ------- MR Arthrography MRA 82–92% 85–98% Gold standard; intra-articular gadolinium required Plain MRI 3T 63–82% 79–94% Adequate for Bankart; misses 18–26% SLAP II Plain MRI 1.5T 44–68% 66–87% Inferior; request MRA if clinical suspicion high Ultrasound Poor for SLAP/Bankart — Not indicated for labral pathology CT Arthrography 78–91% 91% Alternative if MRI contraindicated; better for bone loss quantification Plain X-ray AP/Axillary/Scapular-Y N/A N/A Mandatory first-line to exclude fracture, bone loss, Hill-Sachs Diagnostic Accuracy Summary For SLAP lesions: Biceps Load II is the most accurate standalone test sens 0.90, spec 0.97 . A positive cluster ≥2 of 3: O'Brien's + Crank + Anterior Slide improves specificity to 0.85. If clinical cluster positive → MR arthrography. For Bankart/instability: History of dislocation is the most powerful diagnostic factor. Apprehension + Relocation + Anterior Release triad achieves specificity of 0.99. Plain X-ray to exclude fracture/bone loss is mandatory first-line. --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Differentiating Features Key Tests Imaging ----------- -------------------------- ----------- --------- Subacromial Impingement / RC Tear Pain arc 60–120°, painful resisted abduction/ER; older age group Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy, Empty Can, Lift-Off USS first-line; MRI if full-thickness tear suspected AC Joint Pathology Pain localised to AC joint; positive cross-body adduction; O'Brien's positive with pain at top not deep in shoulder Cross-body adduction, AC joint palpation X-ray AC views, USS Biceps Tendinopathy / Rupture Anterior groove tenderness; "Popeye" deformity rupture ; speed's positive Speed's, Yergason's, palpation USS bicipital groove Adhesive Capsulitis Global passive ROM restriction all planes ; insidious onset; ER most restricted Capsular pattern assessment X-ray to exclude OA; MRI shows capsular thickening SLAC Superior Labral Anterior-posterior Cyst Paralabral cyst on imaging; suprascapular nerve compression; spinati wasting EMG/NCS, suprascapular notch palpation MRI Multidirectional Instability MDI Bilateral laxity; atraumatic onset; sulcus sign; Beighton score Sulcus sign, load-and-shift all directions, Beighton score MRI; often normal Cervical Radiculopathy C5/C6 Dermatomal symptoms; neck movement provokes; reflexes affected Spurling's, Upper limb tension test Cervical MRI Glenohumeral OA Older age; end-stage reduced ROM; crepitus; loss of joint space Crepitus, passive ROM X-ray joint space narrowing, osteophytes --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Pathway > Aligned with NICE guidelines and BESS British Elbow & Shoulder Society consensus recommendations. Refer to local MSK pathway documentation for specific waiting time targets. Step 1: Initial Physiotherapy Assessment Community/PCMSK - Full subjective and objective assessment - Red flag screen see above - Baseline outcome measures WOSI + DASH - Imaging: Plain X-ray if not already done exclude fracture, bone loss - Onward imaging request: MRI or MR arthrography if labral pathology suspected and clinical cluster positive Step 2: Conservative Management Primary - Indicated for all patients initially except surgical red flags above - Duration: minimum 12–16 weeks structured physiotherapy Step 3: Onward Referral Triggers - Failure of 12–16 weeks structured physiotherapy - Recurrent instability ≥2 episodes despite rehab - Age 85% of maximum score - Negative apprehension/biceps provocation tests - Functional/sport-specific tasks completed without limitation Pharmacological Agent Indication Evidence Notes ------- ------------ ---------- ------- NSAIDs oral Acute pain, swelling post-dislocation Moderate 7–14 day course; gastroprotection if risk factors Paracetamol Background analgesia Moderate First-line adjunct; safe long-term Intra-articular corticosteroid Significant synovitis / concurrent impingement Low-Moderate Not recommended as primary treatment for labral tears; may mask symptoms Opioids Post-reduction acute pain only Expert consensus Short-term 72 hrs ; not for ongoing management > No pharmacological agent treats the labral tear itself. content: Overview & Pathophysiology Rotator cuff tears are among the most clinically significant shoulder conditions encountered in musculoskeletal physiotherapy. They represent a spectrum from partial-thickness tears through full-thickness complete tears to massive rotator cuff tears involving multiple tendons. The condition sits at the severe end of the tendinopathy continuum model. Prevalence: - Asymptomatic tears identified in 22% of adults overall; rises to 54% in those >60 years Yamamoto et al., 2010 - Symptomatic full-thickness tears: ~2–3% of the general population - Prevalence doubles each decade after age 50 - Bilateral tears in ~35% of those with symptomatic unilateral tear Classification: Classification Description --------------- ------------- Partial-thickness Bursal-sided, articular-sided PASTA lesion , or intratendinous Full-thickness small 5 cm or involving ≥2 tendons Irreparable massive With muscle atrophy, fatty infiltration Goutallier Grade 3–4 Pathophysiology Degenerative tears >90% of all RC tears : - Culmination of the continuum model — reactive → dysrepair → degenerative tendinopathy → tear - Critical zone of supraspinatus 1 cm from insertion : zone of relative avascularity - Fatty infiltration Goutallier classification correlates with chronicity and repair prognosis - Increasing tear size over time in 40–80% of untreated full-thickness tears Moosmayer et al., 2013 Traumatic tears: - Acute forced abduction/ER against resistance e.g., fall on outstretched arm - More common in younger patients with previously healthy tendons - More likely surgically repairable; better healing rates Relevant Anatomy - Rotator cuff interval: Between supraspinatus and subscapularis; contains biceps tendon and coracohumeral ligament; disruption affects inferior capsule stability - Subscapularis: Largest and strongest cuff muscle; anterior stabiliser; tears often missed clinically - Fatty infiltration Goutallier : Grade 0 normal → Grade 4 fat > muscle ; Grade ≥3 = poor surgical prognosis - Pseudoparalysis: Inability to actively elevate arm despite passive ROM due to massive cuff tear --- Special Tests Supraspinatus Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Empty Can Jobe's 69% 66% 2.03 0.47 High 90° abduction, 30° horizontal adduction, IR, resist downward force Full Can Test 74% 78% 3.36 0.33 Moderate ER throughout; less painful than empty can Drop Arm Test 27% 88% 2.25 0.83 Moderate Arm slowly lowered from 90° — drops = full-thickness tear Painful Arc 74% 81% 3.89 0.32 High Best single test for subacromial pathology Infraspinatus / Teres Minor Tests ER weakness Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ----- ----- ---------------- ------- External Rotation Lag Sign ERLS 70% 100% ∞ 0.30 High Arm at 20° ER, near-ER — inability to hold position = large/full-thickness IR/ER tear Hornblower's Sign 100% 93% 14.3 0.00 Moderate Abduct 90°, elbow 90°, resist ER — positive = teres minor tear External Rotation Strength 85% 55% 1.89 0.27 Moderate Grade 3 or less ER strength — associated with large tears Subscapularis Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Lift-Off Test Gerber 62% 100% ∞ 0.38 High Hand behind back, palm out — inability to lift from back = subscapularis tear Belly-Press Test 40% 98% 20.0 0.61 Moderate Press palm into abdomen — elbow drops back = positive Bear-Hug Test 60% 92% 7.50 0.43 Moderate Elbow forward, resist palm pull from shoulder; most sensitive for upper subscapularis Napoleon Test 55% 90% 5.5 0.50 Moderate Cannot press belly with flat wrist = positive Internal Rotation Lag Sign 97% 96% 24.3 0.03 Moderate Near-IR, maintain position — lag = subscapularis tear Full-Thickness Tear Cluster Murrell & Walton, 2001 If 3 of the following positive → Sensitivity 98%, Specificity 96%: - Age >60 - Positive supraspinatus weakness - Positive impingement sign - Night pain --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Acute onset weakness after trauma fall, FOOSH Full-thickness traumatic tear; fracture Urgent X-ray; orthopaedic review within 2 weeks Pseudoparalysis cannot initiate elevation Massive RC tear Urgent USS/MRI; orthopaedic referral Signs of axillary nerve injury post-dislocation Axillary nerve palsy deltoid paralysis Urgent neurology; EMG at 4–6 weeks Rapid wasting supraspinatus/infraspinatus fossa Suprascapular nerve entrapment; tumour MRI; neurology referral Systemic features — fever, constitutional symptoms Septic arthritis; tumour Emergency/urgent medical review Severe pain, marked ecchymosis, deformity Fracture or complete muscle rupture X-ray; Emergency Department Left arm pain with cardiac symptoms Cardiac event 999 — Emergency --- Clinical Frameworks Surgical Decision Framework Kuhn et al. The decision between conservative and surgical management for rotator cuff tears involves: 1. Tear characteristics: Size, location, fatty infiltration Goutallier , tendon retraction 2. Patient factors: Age, activity level, hand dominance, comorbidities 3. Response to conservative management: 3–6 months' trial first for most tears 4. Chronicity: Acute traumatic tears → earlier surgical review Prognosis for conservative management: - Small/medium tears: 75–80% satisfactory outcomes at 2 years with structured rehabilitation Moosmayer et al., 2010; RCT — surgery vs physio comparable at 2 years for small-medium tears - Massive tears: poorer conservative outcomes; augmentation strategies superior capsule reconstruction, tendon transfer emerging Lewis Framework Applied to RC Tears - Differentiate symptomatic from asymptomatic prevalence of asymptomatic tears is high - Functional deficit is the key clinical driver — not imaging findings alone - Imaging should not drive surgery unless functional deficit correlates --- Outcome Measures Measure Score Range MCID Best Utility --------- ------------- ------ -------------- WORC Western Ontario Rotator Cuff 0–2100 higher = better 275 pts Disease-specific — most responsive for RC pathology ASES American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons 0–100 100 = best 12–17 pts Surgical audit; combines pain VAS + function Constant-Murley Score 0–100 100 = best 10–16 pts Surgical outcomes; requires dynamometer OSS Oxford Shoulder Score 0–48 48 = best 5 pts Post-surgical; simple; patient-completed SPADI 0–100 0 = best 8–13 pts Pain + disability; responsive in conservative management QuickDASH 0–100 0 = best 11–16 pts Upper limb function; useful for work-related cases --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging for RC Tears Ultrasound USS — first-line: - Sensitivity full-thickness: 92%; Specificity: 97% de Jesus et al., 2009 — meta-analysis, n=2,144 - Sensitivity partial-thickness: 67%; Specificity: 94% - Advantages: dynamic assessment, bilateral comparison, real-time, no radiation, guided injection - Limitations: operator-dependent; cannot assess labrum; poor visualisation under acromion MRI — gold standard for surgical planning: - Sensitivity full-thickness: 94%; Specificity: 93% - Sensitivity partial-thickness: 64%; Specificity: 92% - Advantages: multiplanar; Goutallier grading; fatty infiltration; bone assessment; labrum - MR arthrogram: preferred for partial-thickness tears sensitivity increases to 86% X-ray: - Subacromial space 45 years; COX-2 selective if high GI risk - Corticosteroid injection: - Subacromial injection: short-term pain relief Level I — Cochrane ; useful to enable rehabilitation - Intra-tendinous injection contraindicated — associated with tendon weakening and rupture - USS-guided preferred; up to 3 per year per NICE/HSC guidance - Avoid: Opioids for chronic shoulder pain; hyaluronic acid insufficient evidence Onward Referral Criteria Urgent orthopaedic referral within 2–4 weeks : - Acute traumatic full-thickness tear with significant weakness, age <60 - Pseudoparalysis following acute trauma - Associated fracture or dislocation Routine orthopaedic referral standard pathway : - Failed 3–6 months structured conservative management documented - Large/massive tear with functional deficit impacting activities of daily living or work - Progressive weakness despite conservative management - Young, active patient <60 with symptomatic full-thickness tear - Patient preference for surgical discussion after fully informed Pre-referral requirements HSC NI standard : - USS or MRI confirming tear size and characteristics - Documented physiotherapy trial minimum 3 months - Outcome measure scores SPADI/WORC at baseline and discharge --- Key References 1. It represents one of the most prevalent musculoskeletal conditions in clinical
