Cluster Testing Approach Hegedus et al., 2012
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Rotator cuff tendinopathy is a broad term encompassing pain and dysfunction arising from the rotator cuff tendons — most commonly the supraspinatus, followed by infraspinatus and subscapularis. It represents one of the most prevalent musculoskeletal conditions in clinical practice, accounting for 44–65% of shoulder pain presentations in primary care. Prevalence: Point prevalence of shoulder pain is approximately 7–26% in the general population, with rotator cuff pathology implicated in 65–70% of cases. Prevalence increases sharply with age, particularly after 50 years. Continuum Model of Tendinopathy Cook & Purdam, 2009; revised 2016 The continuum model — now the dominant explanatory framework — describes tendinopathy as a spectrum rather than a discrete entity: 1. Reactive tendinopathy: Acute response to compressive or tensile overload. Non-inflammatory cell-mediated matrix changes. Clinically: sudden onset after unaccustomed loading. Potentially reversible. 2. Tendon dysrepair: Failed or incomplete healing response. Disorganised matrix, increased ground substance and vascularity. Clinically: subacute/chronic presentation. 3. Degenerative tendinopathy: Cell death, lipid infiltration, calcification, disorganised collagen. High risk of tear. Clinically: chronic, often in older patients. Key principle: Tendinopathy is a failed healing response, not classic inflammation. This drives management decisions — compressive loading and prolonged rest are counterproductive; progressive tensile loading is the evidence-based intervention. Relevant Anatomy - Supraspinatus: Arises from the supraspinous fossa, inserts on the greater tuberosity superior facet . Primary abductor and force-couple stabiliser. - Infraspinatus: External rotator; inserts on greater tuberosity middle facet . - Subscapularis: Internal rotator; inserts on lesser tuberosity. - Teres minor: External rotator; inserts on greater tuberosity inferior facet . - Critical zone: The avascular zone 1 cm from the supraspinatus insertion — primary site of degenerative change and tears. - Subacromial space: Normal space 7–14 mm; reduction causes impingement on the bursa and rotator cuff. Mechanism Multifactorial — intrinsic and extrinsic factors: - Intrinsic: Age-related tendon degeneration, vascularity compromise, genetic predisposition COL5A1 gene variants , tendon morphology. - Extrinsic: Repetitive overhead activity, heavy lifting, acromion morphology Bigliani Type II/III , scapular dyskinesis, altered glenohumeral kinematics, poor rotator cuff strength/endurance. - Compressive loading at the subacromial space is now recognised as a key perpetuating factor, particularly for supraspinatus tendinopathy. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Neer Impingement Sign 72% 95% CI 61–81% 60% 95% CI 52–68% 1.8 0.47 Moderate Passive flexion, IR, stabilise scapula. Positive = pain arc reproduced Hawkins-Kennedy Test 79% 95% CI 72–85% 59% 95% CI 52–66% 1.93 0.36 High Passive shoulder/elbow 90° flexion, IR. High sensitivity — useful to rule OUT Empty Can Jobe's 69% 95% CI 56–80% 66% 95% CI 55–75% 2.03 0.47 High Shoulder 90° abduction, 30° horizontal adduction, IR, resist downward force Full Can Test 74% 78% 3.36 0.33 Moderate As empty can but ER — less painful, better tolerated Painful Arc 74% 81% 3.89 0.32 High Pain 60–120° abduction arc — most useful single test for SIS/tendinopathy External Rotation Lag Sign ERLS 70% 100% ∞ 0.30 High For infraspinatus/teres minor full-thickness tear Drop Arm Test 27% 88% 2.25 0.83 Moderate Low sensitivity — useful only if positive Lift-Off Test Gerber 62% 100% ∞ 0.38 High Subscapularis; hand behind back, lift off. If unable = subscapularis tear Bear-Hug Test 60% 92% 7.50 0.43 Moderate Subscapularis; elbow forward, resist palm pull from shoulder Internal Rotation Resistance Test IRRT 88% 96% 22.0 0.13 Moderate Differentiates intra-articular from subacromial pathology Neer Impingement Test injection 88% 44% 1.57 0.27 Moderate Relief after lidocaine injection confirms subacromial source Speed's Test 56% 67% 1.7 0.66 Moderate For biceps tendinopathy/SLAP — limited utility for cuff Lateral Jobe 66% 64% 1.83 0.53 Low Clinical pearl — Cluster testing for rotator cuff tendinopathy: Hegedus et al. 2012 systematic review confirms no single test is diagnostic. Use clusters: - Hawkins-Kennedy + Painful Arc + Infraspinatus muscle test 3-positive cluster : +LR 10.56 for subacromial impingement syndrome Michener et al., 2009 - Sensitivity maximised by Hawkins-Kennedy; specificity maximised by Painful Arc and muscle testing --- Red Flags Red Flag Possible Diagnosis Action ---------- ------------------- -------- Night pain disproportionate to activity, unexplained weight loss, age >50 + new onset Malignancy primary or secondary — Pancoast tumour, bone metastasis Urgent referral; chest X-ray Fever, hot swollen joint, systemically unwell Septic arthritis Emergency assessment; joint aspiration History of significant trauma + severe weakness Full-thickness rotator cuff tear; fracture X-ray; urgent orthopaedic review Left shoulder/jaw pain, diaphoresis, dyspnoea Cardiac event referred pain Emergency — 999 Upper shoulder/neck pain after diaphragmatic irritation e.g., post-surgical, haemothorax Diaphragmatic referred pain C3/C4 Urgent medical review Rapidly progressive neurological deficit Brachial neuritis Parsonage-Turner syndrome Urgent neurology referral Progressive weakness without pain Cervical myelopathy; neurological cause Urgent neurology/spinal referral Axillary nerve deficit post-dislocation Axillary nerve injury EMG/NCS; monitor 3–6 months Wasting of supraspinatus/infraspinatus fossa Suprascapular nerve entrapment; space-occupying lesion MRI; neurology referral --- Clinical Frameworks Lewis Shoulder Framework 2009, updated 2015 Jeremy Lewis's clinical framework for shoulder assessment emphasises: 1. Symptom behaviour — directional preference, aggravating/relieving factors 2. Movement assessment — active ROM, painful arc, end-range pain 3. Load assessment — rotator cuff strength testing ER, IR, abduction, flexion 4. Differentiation testing — supine positioning to offload subacromial space 5. Treatment-based classification — responds better than diagnosis-based for directing exercise loading Cools Rehabilitation Framework 2016 Ann Cools's evidence-based rehabilitation model for shoulder: 1. Phase 1 — Pain management: Activity modification, posture correction, scapular control 2. Phase 2 — Motor control: Low-load rotator cuff activation, scapular stabilisers 3. Phase 3 — Strength: Progressive loading, ER/IR ratio restoration target ER:IR ≥ 0.66 4. Phase 4 — Function: Sport/work-specific loading, overhead mechanics Cluster Testing Approach Hegedus et al., 2012 - Never rely on a single test - Combine high-sensitivity tests rule out with high-specificity tests rule in - Assess response to load — does isometric contraction reproduce/resolve pain? - Musculoskeletal ultrasound is the recommended first-line imaging in most guidelines --- Outcome Measures Measure Structure Score Range MCID MDC Clinical Utility --------- ----------- ------------- ------ ----- ----------------- DASH Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder and Hand 30-item PRO; optional work and sport modules 0–100 0=best 10–15 points 12.7 Gold standard; comprehensive; time-consuming QuickDASH 11-item abbreviated DASH 0–100 0=best 11–16 points 15.9 Excellent for clinical use; highly correlated with DASH SPADI Shoulder Pain and Disability Index 13-item; pain 5 + disability 8 subscales 0–100 0=best 8–13 points 18 Simple; widely validated; best for shoulder-specific pain OSS Oxford Shoulder Score 12-item 0–48 48=best 5 points — Preferred by orthopaedic surgeons; post-surgical monitoring Constant-Murley Score 35-point subjective + 65-point objective 0–100 100=best 10–16 points — Requires dynamometer for abduction strength; gold standard for surgical outcomes WORC Western Ontario Rotator Cuff 21-item VAS-based 0–2100 2100=best 275 points — Disease-specific; most responsive for rotator cuff pathology PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 3–5 self-selected activities 0–10/activity 2 points — Excellent for individualised goal tracking; highly responsive Recommendation for routine practice: SPADI + QuickDASH at baseline and discharge. Add Constant-Murley if post-surgical or when objective comparison required. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Guidelines Ultrasound USS : - First-line imaging per BESS British Elbow and Shoulder Society and NICE guidelines - Sensitivity for full-thickness RC tear: 92% 95% CI 82–97% ; Specificity: 97% 95% CI 91–99% — de Jesus et al., 2009 - Sensitivity for partial-thickness tear: 67%; Specificity: 94% - Operator-dependent; limited assessment of labrum and glenohumeral joint MRI: - Preferred for labral pathology, bony assessment, surgical planning - Sensitivity full-thickness tear: 94%; Specificity: 93% — de Jesus et al., 2009 - MR arthrogram for suspected partial-thickness tear, labral tears, instability X-ray: - Limited for soft tissue; useful for: calcific deposits, acromioclavicular joint, glenohumeral arthritis, acromion morphology, greater tuberosity irregularity - AP + axillary views minimum Key Systematic Reviews - Hegedus et al. 2012 — BJSM: Most comprehensive meta-analysis of shoulder special tests. Conclusion: No single test has sufficient diagnostic accuracy; clusters recommended. - Lenza et al. 2013 — Cochrane: USS and MRI comparable for full-thickness tears; MRI superior for partial tears. - Diercks et al. 2014 — BESS: USS first-line before MRI for suspected RC pathology. --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Differentiating Features Special Test Imaging ----------- ------------------------------ -------------- --------- Subacromial pain syndrome Painful arc 60–120°; pain with overhead activities; negative lag signs Hawkins + Neer positive; muscle tests variable USS — bursal thickening ± RC changes Full-thickness RC tear Significant weakness; may have lag signs Positive lag signs; Drop Arm USS/MRI — confirms tear Adhesive capsulitis Global ROM restriction; capsular pattern ER > abduction > IR All movements restricted X-ray ± USS Glenohumeral arthritis Age; morning stiffness; crepitus; gradual onset Restricted capsular pattern X-ray — joint space loss Cervical radiculopathy Arm symptoms; neurological signs; neck movement reproduces arm pain Spurling's positive; ULTT positive Cervical MRI Acromioclavicular joint pathology Superior shoulder pain; direct AC joint tenderness O'Brien's; Cross-arm adduction X-ray; USS Biceps tendinopathy/tear Anterior shoulder pain; Speed's; Yergason's Speed's + Yergason's USS — biceps tendon Calcific tendinitis Severe acute pain; may mimic infection Often all tests painful X-ray — calcific deposits Shoulder instability Age <35; history of trauma or hyperlaxity; apprehension Apprehension + Relocation; load and shift MRI arthrogram Thoracic outlet syndrome Vascular/neurological symptoms; positional Roos; Adson's; Wright's Doppler USS; CXR; MRI Brachial neuritis Parsonage-Turner Acute severe pain followed by rapid weakness; post-viral/vaccination Wasting without impingement MRI neurography --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / GP: - Physiotherapy self-referral available across most HSC Trusts Belfast, South Eastern, Northern, Western, Southern - First 6 weeks: conservative management in primary care - Image-guided corticosteroid injection: referral to GP with special interest GPwSI in MSK or MSK interface clinic - MSK interface clinics e.g., Belfast Trust MSK First Contact Practitioner : triage, USS, injection, physiotherapy — avoiding unnecessary orthopaedic referral MSK Interface Services HSC NI : - First Contact Practitioners FCPs in GP practices expanding across all trusts 2023–2026 - Community MSK services: offer USS-guided injection, exercise prescription, structured rehabilitation - Waiting times indicative 2024–2025 : Community physio 6–20 weeks; MSK interface 8–16 weeks; orthopaedic outpatient 52+ weeks Red Flag / Urgent Pathway: - Suspected septic arthritis → Emergency Department - Suspected malignancy → 2-week wait urgent cancer referral - Significant trauma with weakness → ED/direct orthopaedic assessment Conservative Management Evidence-based exercise prescription: Phase Timeframe Exercise Focus Dosage Evidence ------- ----------- ---------------- -------- ---------- Acute reactive 0–4 weeks Pain-free isometrics; posture; scapular control 3×10–15 reps, daily Moderate RCT Sub-acute 4–8 weeks Isotonic ER/IR; scapular stabilisers; progressive load 3×12–15 reps, 3×/week High multiple RCTs Rehabilitation 8–16 weeks Functional strengthening; eccentric loading; overhead mechanics 3×8–12 reps progressive High Cochrane Return to activity 16–24 weeks Sport/work-specific; plyometric if relevant Graded exposure Moderate Key exercise principles: - Eccentric loading — most evidence base for patellar tendinopathy; emerging evidence for shoulder Level II - Heavy Slow Resistance HSR — Beyer et al. 2015 AJSM: HSR comparable to eccentric; better adherence - ER:IR strength ratio target ≥ 0.66 at 60°/s isokinetic testing - Scapular stabilisation: Serratus anterior activation; lower/middle trapezius; avoid upper trapezius dominance Manual therapy: - Thoracic manipulation: reduces shoulder pain and improves ROM — moderate evidence Haik et al., 2016 - Glenohumeral joint mobilisation posterior capsule : Grade III–IV for capsular restriction - Soft tissue release: limited high-quality evidence as standalone intervention Education: - Activity modification not rest ; load management principles; graded return - Posture correction; ergonomic advice particularly for occupational factors Pharmacological Per NICE guideline NG194 Shoulder Pain, 2021 : - NSAIDs: Topical first-line if tolerable; oral NSAIDs — minimum effective dose for shortest duration; gastroprotection with PPI if ≥45 years or risk factors - Corticosteroid injection: - Short-term benefit up to 6 weeks — Level I evidence Cochrane: Buchbinder et al., 2003 - No benefit over placebo at 12 months - Limit to 3 injections per shoulder per year HSC NI / NICE guidance - USS-guided preferred over landmark-guided Daniels et al., 2018 — superior accuracy - Subacute presentations respond better than chronic - Caution: repeated injections associated with tendon weakening Nichols, 2005 - Analgesics: Paracetamol — limited evidence for musculoskeletal pain; avoid opioids for non-cancer MSK pain NICE - Hyaluronic acid: Not recommended routinely — insufficient evidence NICE NG194 - Platelet-rich plasma PRP : Growing evidence base; not yet NICE-recommended for shoulder tendinopathy; commissioning decisions pending NICE review Onward Referral Criteria Orthopaedic referral indicated: - Failed 3–6 months of structured conservative management documented - Significant or progressive rotator cuff weakness suggesting large/massive tear - Age <40 with acute traumatic onset suggesting structural tear - Positive lag signs with functional deficit impacting work/quality of life - Persistent symptoms after 2 USS-guided injections - Suspected calcific tendinitis unresponsive to conservative care consider US-guided needling - Glenohumeral joint pathology requiring surgical assessment Imaging prior to referral HSC NI : - USS arranged by GP or MSK service prior to orthopaedic referral in most trusts - MRI where USS inconclusive or labral/instability pathology suspected --- Key References 1. content: Overview & Pathophysiology Shoulder instability refers to symptomatic excessive translation of the humeral head relative to the glenoid, ranging from subtle microinstability to recurrent dislocation. It is the most common joint dislocation, accounting for approximately 45% of all dislocations presenting to emergency departments. It represents a significant clinical challenge due to its heterogeneous aetiology, high recurrence rates, and impact on young, active populations. Prevalence / Incidence: - Annual incidence of primary glenohumeral dislocation: 11–27 per 100,000 - Peak incidence: males 20–30 years contact sport ; females 20–50 years atraumatic - Recurrence rate after first dislocation: 55–97% in those 40 years - Recurrence is the dominant clinical concern in young athletes Classification TUBS / AMBRI / AIOS TUBS Traumatic Unilateral Bankart Surgery : - Traumatic onset single event - Unilateral - Bankart lesion anteroinferior labral avulsion - Surgery often required for high recurrence risk AMBRI Atraumatic Multidirectional Bilateral Rehabilitation : - Atraumatic onset no single traumatic event - Multidirectional laxity inferior ± anterior ± posterior - Bilateral often - Rehabilitation primary treatment - Inferior capsular shift if surgery required AIOS Acquired Instability from Overuse in Sport : - Overhead throwing athletes - Acquired internal impingement; microinstability - Direction-specific; sport-related Stanmore Classification Rowe & Zarins / Revised Bayley et al. : Three-point triangle: - Type I: Structural traumatic — Bankart, Hill-Sachs - Type II: Atraumatic structural involuntary; dysplastic glenoid - Type III: Muscle patterning non-structural; habitual; voluntary Relevant Anatomy and Stabilisers Static stabilisers: - Glenoid labrum: Deepens glenoid cavity by ~50%; increases contact area; functions as chock-block for humeral head - Glenohumeral ligaments GHL : - Superior GHL: resists inferior translation in neutral and adduction - Middle GHL: resists anterior translation at 45° abduction - Inferior GHL IGHL : primary restraint at 90° abduction — most important ligament - IGHL anterior band: resists anterior translation with ER - IGHL posterior band: resists posterior translation with IR - Rotator cuff interval: Coracohumeral + superior GHL; resists inferior translation - Bony glenoid: Pear-shaped; inverted glenoid version >15° retroversion = risk for posterior instability Dynamic stabilisers: - Rotator cuff: Compression into glenoid; concavity-compression mechanism - Long head of biceps: Superior glenohumeral stability - Scapular rotators: Position glenoid face; scapular dyskinesis → decreased stability Common Structural Lesions: Lesion Description Direction Imaging -------- ------------- ----------- --------- Bankart lesion Anteroinferior labral avulsion from glenoid Anterior MR arthrogram Bony Bankart Bankart + glenoid bone loss >20–25% = critical Anterior CT glenoid morphology Hill-Sachs defect Posterolateral humeral head impaction fracture Anterior CT; MRI HAGL Humeral Avulsion GHL GHL avulsion from humerus not labrum Anterior MR arthrogram Reverse Bankart Posteroinferior labral tear Posterior MR arthrogram Reverse Hill-Sachs Anteromedial humeral head posterior dislocation Posterior CT; MRI SLAP tear Superior labrum anterior-posterior — MR arthrogram --- Special Tests Anterior Instability Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Apprehension Test 72% 96% 18.0 0.29 High Supine; 90° abduction + ER; apprehension not just pain = positive Relocation Test Jobe 81% 92% 10.1 0.21 High Posterior force on proximal humerus during apprehension = relief; Gold standard combination Anterior Release Surprise Test 92% 89% 8.36 0.09 High Remove posterior force — sudden return of apprehension; most sensitive of trio Apprehension + Relocation + Release Cluster 56% 99.7% 187 0.44 High Combined approach — highly specific for anterior instability Load and Shift Test Anterior 53% 85% 3.53 0.55 Moderate Assess anterior translation under compression; Grade I-III Anterior Drawer Test 53% 85% 3.53 0.55 Moderate Similar to load and shift; examiner moves humeral head anteriorly Anterior Instability Fulcrum 82% 86% 5.86 0.21 Moderate Edge of table as fulcrum; apprehension with posterior force in flexion + IR Jerk Test 73% 98% 36.5 0.28 Moderate Axial load + adduction from 90° abduction: clunk = positive; highly specific Kim Test 80% 94% 13.3 0.21 Moderate 90° abduction, 45° elevation, inferior + posterior force; good for posteroinferior lesions Posterior Load and Shift 44% 97% 14.7 0.58 Moderate Less sensitive but high specificity Posterior Stress Test 55% 79% 2.62 0.57 Low-moderate Supine; 90° elevation + IR; posterior force Multidirectional Instability / Laxity Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Sulcus Sign 72% 85% 4.80 0.33 Moderate Downward traction; >1 cm dimple at acromion = positive; indicates inferior laxity Sulcus Sign ER High specificity — — — Moderate Positive in ER = IGHL laxity more specific for MDI Gagey Hyperabduction 85% 85% 5.67 0.18 Moderate Passive abduction >105° = IGHL laxity Beighton Score — — — — Moderate Generalised ligamentous laxity; ≥4/9 = hypermobility; EDS consideration Combined/Other Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity Evidence Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ---------- ------- Clunk Test 44% 99% Moderate Full circumduction with axial load; clunk = labral tear O'Brien's Active Compression 47–67% 37–89% Moderate Combined SLAP/ACJ test; limited alone Crank Test 91% 93% Moderate Supine; axial load + rotation; for labral tears --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Acute dislocation with inability to reduce Locked dislocation; fracture Emergency Department; X-ray before reduction Post-reduction neurological deficit Axillary nerve injury most common ; brachial plexus Deltoid sensation/function; EMG at 4–6 weeks Anterior shoulder pulsatile mass Axillary artery injury Vascular surgery — Emergency Posterior shoulder with wrist drop post-trauma Radial nerve injury rare Urgent neurology Instability in older patient >40 with trauma Associated full-thickness RC tear 60% in >40 years post-dislocation USS/MRI post-reduction First dislocation >50 years Much higher RC tear association; lower recurrence USS/MRI; managed differently Voluntary habitual dislocation Type III Stanmore — muscle patterning Specialist shoulder unit; psychiatric assessment if needed Progressive instability without trauma Tumour; infection; Charcot arthropathy MRI; investigations --- Clinical Frameworks Instability Severity Index Score ISIS — Balg & Boileau, 2007 Pre-operative scoring tool for predicting recurrence after Latarjet vs Bankart repair: Factor Score -------- ------- Age ≤20 2 pts Competitive sport 2 pts Contact/overhead sport 1 pt Hyperlaxity anterior apprehension 2 cm 1 pt Hill-Sachs on AP X-ray 2 pts Loss of sclerotic inferior glenoid contour on AP X-ray 2 pts - Score ≤3: Low recurrence risk — arthroscopic Bankart suitable - Score ≥4: High recurrence risk — Latarjet procedure recommended - Score ≥6: Very high risk — Latarjet mandatory FEDS Classification Functional, Emotion, Direction, Severity Modern classification for MDI — integrates structural, neuromuscular, and psychological components. Rehabilitation Framework for Instability Wilk & Macrina, 2012 Phase 1 — Acute protection 0–4 weeks : - Sling immobilisation IR position — debate ongoing; ER immobilisation: reduced recurrence in young males - Pain management; rotator cuff isometrics; elbow/wrist AROM - Early scapular control: retraction; no provocative positions Phase 2 — Intermediate 4–8 weeks : - Progressive ER; RC strengthening; scapular stabilisers - Proprioception training joint position sense - Activity modification — avoid apprehension position 90°ABD/ER Phase 3 — Advanced strengthening 8–16 weeks : - Progressive loading; functional patterns; perturbation training - Sport-specific preparation Phase 4 — Return to sport 4–6 months : - Graduated sport return; sport-specific exercises - Bracing consideration for contact sports --- Outcome Measures Measure Score Range MCID Application --------- ------------- ------ ------------- WOSI Western Ontario Shoulder Instability Index 0–2100 2100 = best 220–320 pts Disease-specific; most responsive for instability ASES American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons 0–100 100 = best 12–17 pts Surgical audit Rowe Score 0–100 100 = best — Recurrence rate; function; ROM; composite Melbourne Instability Shoulder Score 0–100 — Instability-specific; used in Australia/UK DASH / QuickDASH 0–100 0 = best 11–16 pts Upper limb function; useful for occupational impact PSFS 0–10/activity 2 pts Sport/activity-specific; individualised --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging X-ray first-line — mandatory after acute dislocation : - AP: Hill-Sachs; glenoid erosion; fracture - Axillary lateral: confirms anterior/posterior direction; glenoid morphology - Stryker Notch view: Hill-Sachs optimised - West Point view: anterior glenoid rim Bankart bony lesion CT glenoid bone loss assessment : - Mandated when bony Bankart or significant glenoid loss suspected - Critical threshold: >20–25% glenoid bone loss = Latarjet preferred over Bankart - CT arthrogram: bone loss + labral assessment combined MRI arthrogram definitive soft tissue assessment : - Sensitivity for Bankart: 85–91%; Specificity: 91–99% Waldt et al., 2005 - Sensitivity HAGL: MR arthrogram >> standard MRI - Preferred over standard MRI for labral tears gadolinium distension - Identifies: Bankart; HAGL; SLAP; Hill-Sachs; rotator cuff; posterior lesions USS: - Limited for instability; cannot adequately assess labrum - Useful adjunct for associated RC pathology especially in >40 years post-dislocation Key Evidence - Itoi et al. 2007 JBJS: ER immobilisation after primary dislocation reduces recurrence in young males 26% vs 42% at 2 years — but difficult to sustain compliance - Balg & Boileau 2007 : ISIS score — validated prediction of recurrence and surgical decision-making - Burkhart & De Beer 2000 : Glenoid bone loss >25% = "engaging" Hill-Sachs; Bankart repair fails; Latarjet required - Bessière et al. 2014 : Latarjet superior recurrence rate vs arthroscopic Bankart in high-risk patients --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Features Differentiation ----------- ------------- ---------------- Rotator cuff tear post-dislocation Weakness; lag signs; >40 years USS/MRI post-reduction Acromioclavicular dislocation Direct impact; AC step deformity X-ray; AC palpation Multidirectional laxity without instability Asymptomatic hypermobility Beighton score; symptom correlation SLAP tear Overhead athlete; mechanical symptoms MR arthrogram; special tests SAPS/rotator cuff tendinopathy Painful arc; no apprehension Apprehension test negative Cervical radiculopathy Neck; neurological signs; referred Cervical exam; ULTT Brachial neuritis Post-viral; acute severe pain; wasting EMG; MRI Glenohumeral OA Older; crepitus; X-ray changes X-ray Posterior shoulder tightness GIRD Overhead athlete; IR deficit IR ROM measurement --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Emergency/Acute Dislocation: - ED presentation: X-ray confirmation; reduction Cunningham/Milch/Kocher techniques - Post-reduction X-ray mandatory - Neurovascular assessment axillary nerve — deltoid sensation and function - Sling 1–3 weeks; GP/physio follow-up arranged from ED - Bloods not required routinely; consider in elderly or atypical Primary Care: - Post-reduction follow-up: assess neurovascular; arrange physiotherapy - Young patient first dislocation: refer early to orthopaedic shoulder specialist especially 40 years post-dislocation high RC tear association - MSK self-referral or GP physio referral for rehabilitation Orthopaedic Pathway HSC NI : - Referral: first dislocation age 20–25%; failed Bankart - Posterior capsulorrhaphy/capsular plication: posterior/MDI - Remplissage: Hill-Sachs lesion engaging; combined with Bankart --- Key References 1. SAPS encompasses pathology of the subacromial bursa, the rotator cuff
headings: CSAW Trial Beard et al., 2018 — JAMA
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Subacromial Pain Syndrome SAPS is the currently preferred umbrella term for pain arising from the subacromial space, replacing the older — and now disputed — term "subacromial impingement syndrome" SIS . SAPS encompasses pathology of the subacromial bursa, the rotator cuff tendons particularly supraspinatus , and the coracoacromial arch, without implying a specific structural mechanism. The terminology shift reflects a fundamental change in understanding: the mechanical impingement model Neer, 1972 has been largely replaced by a biopsychosocial and load-based framework. SAPS accounts for 44–65% of all shoulder pain presentations. Historical Concepts vs Current Understanding Model Historical Neer, 1972 Current Lewis, 2009–2016 ------- ------------------------ --------------------------- Mechanism Mechanical pinching of supraspinatus under coracoacromial arch Multifactorial: load, motor control, biopsychosocial Treatment Acromioplasty Exercise; surgical benefit not supported Terminology Subacromial Impingement Syndrome Rotator Cuff Related Shoulder Pain / SAPS Key evidence Cadaveric studies RCT: Beard et al. 2018 CSAW trial CSAW Trial Beard et al., 2018 — JAMA : Landmark RCT demonstrating that arthroscopic acromioplasty + physiotherapy was NOT superior to physiotherapy alone or sham surgery. This fundamentally challenged the impingement model and shifted treatment toward exercise-based management. Pathophysiology Primary contributors: 1. Subacromial bursal inflammation/thickening: The bursa lying between rotator cuff and acromion is highly innervated — a key pain source 2. Rotator cuff tendinopathy: Most commonly supraspinatus — on the continuum from reactive to degenerative 3. Altered shoulder kinematics: Scapular dyskinesis; reduced upward rotation; increased internal rotation during elevation 4. Rotator cuff force couple imbalance: Weakness/fatigue of external rotators and lower trapezius; relative upper trapezius overactivation Extrinsic factors: - Acromion morphology Bigliani Type II — curved; Type III — hooked : associated but not causal - Acromioclavicular joint osteophytes - Coracoacromial ligament thickening - Occupational overhead loading; sport swimming, throwing, racquet sports Intrinsic factors: - Rotator cuff tendon degeneration age-related - Reduced vascularity in supraspinatus critical zone - Tendon morphology and genetic factors Prevalence - Most common shoulder diagnosis in primary care 44–65% - Annual incidence in UK general practice: ~14.7/1000 patients/year Linsell et al., 2006 - Peak incidence: 45–64 years; increasing with overhead occupational exposure --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------ ------------ ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Hawkins-Kennedy 79% 59% 1.93 0.36 High Best sensitivity — use to rule OUT SAPS; passive shoulder/elbow 90° flexion, IR Neer Impingement Sign 72% 60% 1.80 0.47 High Passive arm elevation with ER blocked; stabilise scapula; watch for pain arc Painful Arc 60–120° 74% 81% 3.89 0.32 High Best specificity in isolation; pain during arc of elevation Empty Can Jobe's 69% 66% 2.03 0.47 High Supraspinatus load test; 90° abduction, 30° horizontal adduction, IR Full Can 74% 78% 3.36 0.33 Moderate Better tolerated than empty can; ER maintained Neer Impingement Test 88% 44% 1.57 0.27 Moderate Relief within 5 min of subacromial lidocaine injection confirms subacromial source Internal Rotation Resistance Test IRRT 88% 96% 22.0 0.13 Moderate Differentiates intra-articular from subacromial — IR resisted; if MORE painful than ER resisted = intra-articular Infraspinatus Muscle Test 42% 90% 4.20 0.64 Moderate ER strength deficit in neutral — if positive with Hawkins/Painful Arc, improves cluster accuracy Horizontal Adduction Scarf Test 77% 79% 3.67 0.29 Moderate Primarily for ACJ but pain may indicate posterior subacromial origin Diagnostic Cluster — Michener et al. 2009 Subacromial Impingement Cluster 3 tests positive : - Hawkins-Kennedy + Painful Arc + Infraspinatus Muscle Test - +LR = 10.56 for SAPS highly useful rule-in - -LR = 0.17 useful rule-out when all 3 negative Hegedus et al. 2012 systematic review conclusions: - No single test is sufficiently accurate for isolated diagnosis - Cluster testing significantly improves diagnostic accuracy - The painful arc + full can cluster has best clinical utility for ruling in subacromial pathology --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Age >50, unexplained weight loss, night sweats Malignancy Pancoast tumour, bone metastasis Urgent referral; CXR Fever, hot joint, systemically unwell Septic arthritis Emergency — joint aspiration Acute trauma with immediate severe weakness RC tear; fracture; dislocation X-ray; urgent orthopaedic assessment Disproportionate night pain waking multiple times Inflammatory arthritis; malignancy; septic Inflammatory markers CRP, ESR, WCC Left shoulder + jaw + chest pain, dyspnoea Cardiac ischaemia 999 — Emergency Shoulder/neck pain after abdominal event Diaphragmatic irritation C3/C4 referred Urgent medical review Rapid muscle wasting supraspinatus/infraspinatus Suprascapular nerve entrapment; space-occupying lesion MRI; neurology Progressive neurological deficit Cervical myelopathy; brachial neuritis Urgent neurology/spinal referral Bony tenderness, bruising after trauma Fracture X-ray --- Clinical Frameworks Lewis Shoulder Framework 2009, 2016 Jeremy Lewis's pragmatic approach to shoulder assessment challenges the impingement model: 1. Assessment Philosophy: Pain provocation tests have poor diagnostic accuracy; use clusters not single tests 2. Treatment Prioritisation: Shoulder exercise regardless of specific diagnosis; acromioplasty not supported 3. Staging by behaviour: - Stage 1: Pain only at end range/high load — progressive exercise tolerated - Stage 2: Pain through range — modify loading; isometrics may reduce pain - Stage 3: Pain at rest — protect and manage; graded return to load 4. Key principle: The painful arc itself is not diagnostic — assess what provokes, what reduces, and response to load Cools Rehabilitation Model 2016 Scapular focus in SAPS rehabilitation: - Assess scapular kinematics: upward rotation deficit SARD strongly associated with SAPS - Target serratus anterior and lower trapezius activation - Correct upper trapezius dominance - Posterior shoulder stretching for posterior capsule tightness GIRD — Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit GIRD Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit : - IR deficit >25° compared to contralateral = significant - Posterior capsule tightness → anterior-superior humeral head migration → subacromial space reduction - Posterior capsule stretching sleeper stretch, cross-body stretch — evidence from throwing athletes Biopsychosocial Considerations - Central sensitisation contributes to chronic SAPS — screen with PainDETECT - Catastrophising, fear-avoidance, low self-efficacy are predictors of poor outcome - Address from first consultation; avoid overmedicalising with imaging-driven diagnoses --- Outcome Measures Measure Score Range MCID Clinical Application --------- ------------- ------ --------------------- SPADI 0–100 0 = best 8–13 pts Best validated for SAPS specifically; pain 5 items + disability 8 items QuickDASH 0–100 0 = best 11–16 pts Quick screen; upper limb function DASH 0–100 0 = best 10–15 pts Comprehensive; work and sport modules OSS 0–48 48 = best 5 pts 12-item; used in NI orthopaedic pathway Constant-Murley 0–100 100 = best 10–16 pts For pre/post-surgical comparison; requires dynamometer PSFS 0–10 per activity 2 pts Patient-specific; most clinically responsive for individual goals ASES 0–100 100 = best 12–17 pts American standard; pain + function composite NI HSC recommended practice: SPADI at baseline and discharge as minimum; add Constant-Murley for surgical pathway cases. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis CSAW Trial Beard et al., 2018 — JAMA - Multicentre RCT; n=313; 3 arms: 1 arthroscopic acromioplasty + physio; 2 arthroscopic lavage sham + physio; 3 physiotherapy alone - Primary outcome Oxford Shoulder Score at 6 months: No significant difference between groups - Conclusion: Acromioplasty does not add benefit beyond physiotherapy - Impact: Major shift in surgical practice; acromioplasty rates declining significantly in UK/Ireland Imaging Evidence USS Ultrasound : - Identifies bursal thickening, rotator cuff changes, calcific deposits - Dynamic assessment of subacromial space - First-line investigation BESS guidelines; NICE NG194 MRI: - Better for partial-thickness tears, labral pathology, bone marrow changes - MR arthrogram where structural tear or instability suspected X-ray findings in SAPS: - Acromion morphology AP + outlet view - Acromioclavicular joint changes - Calcific deposits - Greater tuberosity sclerosis/cyst Clinical Prediction Rules - No single validated CPR for SAPS diagnosis equivalent to those in lumbar spine - Michener cluster Hawkins + Painful Arc + Infraspinatus remains most validated +LR 10.56 - Response to injection can confirm subacromial source functional diagnostic injection --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Features Differentiating Test Imaging ----------- ------------- --------------------- --------- Rotator cuff tendinopathy Overlaps significantly with SAPS Load response; muscle tests USS Full-thickness RC tear Lag signs positive; significant weakness Drop arm; ERLS USS/MRI Adhesive capsulitis Global ROM restriction; capsular pattern All directions restricted USS; X-ray ACJ pathology Direct AC tenderness; cross-body pain O'Brien's; AC palpation; injection test X-ray AC views Calcific tendinitis Acute severe pain; may mimic infection X-ray — calcific deposits X-ray diagnostic Glenohumeral OA Age; crepitus; restricted; gradual X-ray: joint space loss X-ray Cervical radiculopathy Neck; arm symptoms; neurological signs Spurling's; ULTT Cervical MRI SLAP tear Young; overhead sport; catching/clunking O'Brien's; Biceps Load II MR arthrogram Shoulder instability Young; hyperlaxity; apprehension Apprehension; Relocation MR arthrogram Thoracic outlet syndrome Vascular/neurological; positional Roos; Adson's; ULTT Doppler USS; MRI Brachial neuritis Severe pain → rapid weakness; post-viral EMG; weakness pattern MRI neurography --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Self-referral: - Physio self-referral operational in Belfast, South Eastern, Northern, Western, Southern Trusts - Initial presentation: conservative management for minimum 6 weeks before imaging or injection in non-urgent cases - GP arranged USS if: failure to respond to conservative care at 6–12 weeks; suspicion of structural pathology MSK Interface Service HSC NI : - MSK First Contact Practitioners FCPs in GP practices for triage and direct management - Community MSK services: USS-guided injection subacromial , structured rehabilitation prescription, advice - Image-guided corticosteroid injection: GPwSI/MSK interface pathway; reduces unnecessary orthopaedic referrals - Orthopaedic waiting times NI 2024–2025: routine 12–26 months; urgent if SAPS — rare 4–12 weeks Red Flag Escalation: Emergency cardiac/septic ; urgent 2-week wait malignancy ; urgent orthopaedic acute traumatic tear with weakness Conservative Management Exercise Programme Evidence Grade A — multiple RCTs, Cochrane : Exercise Type Example Dosage Rationale --------------- --------- -------- ----------- Scapular stabilisation Prone Y/T/W; band retraction; push-up plus 3×15 reps, daily Lower trap/serratus activation; correct dyskinesis RC activation Side-lying ER; ER at 0°; band ER 3×12–15 reps, daily Restore ER:IR ratio; reduce superior migration Progressive loading Scaption; shoulder press; HSR 3×8–12 reps progressive Tendon adaptation; pain modulation Posterior stretching Sleeper stretch; cross-body stretch 3×30 sec, daily Correct GIRD; improve IR ROM Thoracic mobility Thoracic extension; rotation Daily Improve scapular platform Manual therapy Moderate evidence : - Thoracic spine manipulation: short-term improvement in pain and function Bang & Deyle, 2000; Haik et al., 2016 - Glenohumeral mobilisation posterior capsule : Grade III–IV for internal rotation deficit - NOT recommended as standalone; adjunct to exercise Education Essential : - Explain SAPS framework — avoid impingement/wear-and-tear language negative effects on prognosis - Activity modification: avoid provocative positions initially; graded return - Self-management: posture, sleep position, ergonomics - Prognosis: most SAPS resolves with structured exercise over 3–6 months 80% satisfactory outcome Pharmacological NICE NG194 2021 guidance: - Topical NSAIDs: First-line analgesic — equivalent to oral NSAIDs with less systemic risk Level A - Oral NSAIDs: Lowest effective dose; shortest duration; ibuprofen 400 mg TDS or naproxen 500 mg BD with food; add PPI if >45 years or other risk factors - Corticosteroid injection: - Subacromial space: triamcinolone 40 mg + lidocaine; USS-guided superior to landmark accuracy >95% vs 75% - Short-term benefit up to 6 weeks : Level I evidence Cochrane — Koester et al., 2007 - Not superior to exercise at 3–6 months - Clinical utility: provides pain window to engage with rehabilitation - Maximum 3 injections per shoulder per year NICE; HSC NI guidance - Consider 2-week wait after injection before commencing loading exercises - Avoid: Opioids no evidence; harm ; hyaluronic acid insufficient evidence — NICE NG194 Onward Referral Criteria Routine orthopaedic referral: - Failed 3–6 months structured conservative management with documented evidence - Suspected large/full-thickness rotator cuff tear with functional deficit USS first - Recurrent disabling pain despite 2 image-guided injections - Calcific tendinitis unresponsive to conservative care consider US-guided needling first Note on acromioplasty post-CSAW : - Acromioplasty should no longer be routinely offered for SAPS without full-thickness tear NHS England NHS Procedures of Limited Clinical Value, 2018 - Orthopaedic referral for SAPS alone not indicated unless surgical question exists e.g., associated tear, failed injection USS/imaging prior to referral: Required in most HSC NI trusts; arrange before orthopaedic letter --- Key References 1. title: Costochondritis
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Costochondritis is inflammation of the costochondral or costo-sternal junctions causing anterior chest wall pain. It is one of the most common causes of chest pain presenting to both primary care and emergency departments, accounting for approximately 13–36% of chest pain
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Costochondritis is inflammation of the costochondral or costo-sternal junctions causing anterior chest wall pain. It is one of the most common causes of chest pain presenting to both primary care and emergency departments, accounting for approximately 13–36% of chest pain presentations Proulx AM & Zryd TW, 2009 . Distinction from Tietze Syndrome - Costochondritis: Inflammation of the costochondral junctions — no visible or palpable swelling . Multiple levels often affected. More common. - Tietze Syndrome: Localised non-suppurative inflammation with visible/palpable swelling at the costochondral/costo-sternal junction, typically affecting the 2nd or 3rd rib. Rarer; often younger patients. Prevalence & Demographics - Accounts for 13–36% of musculoskeletal chest pain in primary care - Peak age: 20–40 years for Tietze; broader age range for costochondritis - Female:male ratio: approximately 3:1 - Often bilateral involvement; most commonly affects ribs 2–5 at costo-sternal junctions Relevant Anatomy - The costal cartilages connect the osseous ribs to the sternum at costo-sternal junctions - Ribs 1–7 connect directly to the sternum true ribs - Ribs 8–10 connect to costal cartilage of the rib above false ribs - Ribs 11–12 are floating no anterior attachment - The costo-sternal joint is a fibrous rib 1 or synovial ribs 2–7 joint — synovial joints may undergo inflammatory arthritis Mechanism & Aetiology - Often idiopathic ; proposed mechanisms include: - Repetitive microtrauma heavy lifting, coughing, exercise - Viral upper respiratory infection preceding cough - Direct chest trauma - Seronegative spondyloarthropathy e.g., ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis - Post-sternotomy cardiac surgery - Fibromyalgia costochondritis as component - Rarely: septic IV drug use, immunocompromised --- Special Tests > Key point: Costochondritis is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on reproduction of pain with palpation of costochondral junctions. Sensitivity and specificity data specific to costochondritis is limited. The most important role of clinical examination is ruling out serious cardiac, pulmonary, and GI pathology. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Costochondral Palpation reproduction of concordant chest pain ~0.70–0.80 ~0.90 ~7.0–8.0 ~0.22–0.33 Low–Moderate Key diagnostic manoeuvre; press firmly on costal cartilages 2–5 bilaterally Rib Spring Test lateral compression Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Lateral compression of thorax reproducing anterior chest pain; differentiates from rib fracture Sternal Compression Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Compression of sternum reproducing local pain Hooking Manoeuvre Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion For lower rib syndrome ribs 8–10 ; hooking fingers under lower rib margin and pulling anteriorly Key Diagnostic Manoeuvres Expert Consensus 1. Systematic palpation of all costochondral junctions — reproduce concordant pain at ≥1 junction 2. Arm movements: Pain reproduced or worsened with arm elevation, pectoral stretch 3. Deep inspiration/cough: Worsens costochondral pain — important history feature 4. Response to local pressure: Pain reproduced and correlates with patient's presenting complaint References: Proulx AM & Zryd TW 2009 . American Family Physician ; Disla E et al. 1994 . Archives of Internal Medicine . --- Red Flags > This condition requires thorough cardiac, pulmonary, and GI exclusion before confirming a musculoskeletal diagnosis. Chest pain in any patient requires systematic red flag screening. Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Crushing/pressure central chest pain radiating to jaw/left arm Acute coronary syndrome ACS 999 — Emergency Chest pain + diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting ACS / MI 999 — Emergency Pleuritic chest pain + dyspnoea + haemoptysis Pulmonary embolism 999 — Emergency Sudden onset severe chest pain radiating to back Aortic dissection 999 — Emergency Chest pain + fever + productive cough + reduced air entry Pneumonia / pleuritis Same-day GP; chest X-ray Chest pain + weight loss + haemoptysis in smoker Lung malignancy 2WW GP referral Swelling/redness over costochondral junction in IVDU or immunocompromised Septic costochondritis Urgent A&E / bloods Chest pain in patient with known malignancy Metastatic disease to ribs/sternum Urgent oncology review ECG changes ST elevation/depression, new LBBB ACS Emergency Chest pain + haemodynamic instability Tension pneumothorax/PE/dissection 999 Costochondral tenderness + sacroiliitis/uveitis/IBD Seronegative spondyloarthropathy Rheumatology referral --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Costochondritis does not directly fit Maitland's intervertebral movement assessment - However, thoracic spine hypomobility at the costovertebral joints T2–T7 may contribute to anterior chest wall pain - Assess PA central and unilateral pressures at mid-thoracic spine - Rib mobilisation PA on rib angle posteriorly may reduce anterior chest wall pain - Evaluate costo-sternal joint mobility directly cautious anterior pressure on costal cartilage McKenzie/MDT Framework - Thoracic kyphosis correction may reduce sternal/costo-sternal compression anteriorly - Extension exercises thoracic extension over foam roller, doorway pectoral stretches open the anterior chest - Useful when combined with poor posture forward head, protracted shoulder girdle as contributing factor - Patient education: postural correction, activity modification avoid provocative movements during acute phase Pattern Recognition - Mechanical costochondritis: Reproducible with palpation, positional, worse with specific movements/activities; better with rest; no cardiac risk factors - Inflammatory costochondritis spondyloarthropathy : Bilateral, insidious onset, morning stiffness, associated HLA-B27 features, elevated CRP/ESR - Post-infectious: Following viral URTI/cough; diffuse, bilateral, settles over 4–12 weeks - Post-traumatic: Direct blow or sternotomy; localised, appropriate history --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in Costochondritis --------- ------------- ------ ---------------------- NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Primary pain measure PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Activities limited by anterior chest wall pain Chest Pain Questionnaire Not widely validated for MSK chest pain — Consider GPE/GRC as functional measure Global Rating of Change GRC –7 to +7 Likert +2 to +3 Overall recovery SF-36 / EQ-5D-5L Quality of life EQ-5D MCID 0.037 If chronic/persistent >3 months --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic Criteria There are no validated formal diagnostic criteria for costochondritis. Diagnosis is clinical: 1. Chest pain that is reproducible with palpation of costochondral/costo-sternal junctions 2. No swelling swelling = Tietze syndrome 3. Exclusion of cardiac, pulmonary, and GI causes 4. Pain reproducible with trunk movements or deep inspiration Systematic Review Evidence - Disla E et al. 1994 : Prospective study of 122 patients presenting to ED with chest pain — 30% had reproducible chest wall tenderness; however, 6% of those also had concurrent MI → chest wall tenderness does NOT exclude ACS - Fruergaard P et al. 1996 : 204 patients with acute chest pain — 13% diagnosed with costochondritis/musculoskeletal cause after cardiac exclusion - Levy MJ 2021 : Systematic review of MSK chest pain — costochondritis most common MSK diagnosis; resolution in most cases within 12 months Imaging - Generally not indicated for straightforward presentation - CXR: Required if pulmonary cause not excluded; normal in costochondritis - ECG: Mandatory in any chest pain presentation — to exclude ACS - Cardiac troponin / D-dimer: If clinical presentation raises ACS/PE concern GP/ED decision - Ultrasound: May show costochondral joint hypoechogenicity in Tietze syndrome; limited for costochondritis - Bone scan / MRI: If malignancy or stress fracture suspected; increased uptake in Tietze on bone scan --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Acute Coronary Syndrome Central/crushing, diaphoresis, ECG changes, troponin rise; NOT position-dependent; not reproducible with palpation Pericarditis Pleuritic chest pain, worse lying flat, better leaning forward; pericardial rub; ECG changes saddle ST Pulmonary Embolism Pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, hypoxia, Wells score, D-dimer, CTPA Pneumonia / Pleuritis Fever, productive cough, reduced air entry; CXR consolidation Aortic Dissection Sudden severe tearing pain, BP differential, haemodynamic instability Rib Fracture History of trauma, bony tenderness, X-ray/CT confirmation Tietze Syndrome Visible/palpable swelling at costochondral junction; localised Herpes Zoster Shingles Dermatomal burning pain, vesicular rash may precede rash by 3–7 days Seronegative Spondyloarthropathy Bilateral chest wall pain, morning stiffness, sacroiliitis, enthesopathy, HLA-B27 Fibromyalgia Widespread pain, multiple tender points, fatigue, poor sleep Gastro-oesophageal reflux Burning, retrosternal, relation to meals, improved with antacids Oesophageal spasm Severe, episodic, can mimic cardiac; relieved by GTN problematic for diagnosis Intercostal neuralgia Band-like, dermatomal, often post-herpetic --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Community: - GP assessment mandatory to exclude cardiac/pulmonary causes ECG, CXR, clinical assessment - Once excluded → community physiotherapy referral self-referral or GP referral - Typically managed in community MSK physiotherapy across all HSC Trusts - If seronegative spondyloarthropathy suspected → rheumatology referral Secondary Care: - Rarely required for simple costochondritis - Rheumatology if inflammatory arthropathy suspected - Pain management referral if >3 months, severe, and not responding to conservative management - Orthopaedic/surgical referral not typically indicated Conservative Management Physiotherapy — Evidence Grade C limited RCTs; expert consensus : 1. Patient Education Grade A — expert consensus : - Benign, self-limiting condition; most resolve within 12 months - Activity modification during acute phase — avoid provocative heavy lifting, pushing, pulling - Avoid positions that stretch costochondral junctions e.g., reaching overhead during acute phase - Reassurance is a key therapeutic intervention — reduces anxiety-driven symptom amplification 2. Relative Rest then Graded Return to Activity: - Acute phase 0–2 weeks : Avoid provocative activities - Subacute phase 2–6 weeks : Gradual reintroduction of upper limb/thoracic activities - Return to sport/work: Progressive loading programme 3. Manual Therapy: - Thoracic joint mobilisation PA central/unilateral at mid-thoracic levels — may reduce referred anterior chest pain - Rib mobilisation posteroanterior on rib angles - Soft tissue therapy: pectoralis minor, intercostal muscles, sternalis 4. Exercise Therapy: - Thoracic extension exercises foam roller, doorway stretch - Pectoral stretching — cautious in acute phase - Deep breathing exercises diaphragmatic to maintain thoracic cage mobility - Gradual strengthening: scapular stabilisers, thoracic extensors 5. Physical Modalities: - TENS: May provide short-term pain relief Grade C - Ice/Heat: Patient preference; ice for acute inflammation, heat for chronic - Ultrasound: Limited evidence; may consider for Tietze syndrome 6. Acupuncture: Limited evidence; NICE supports acupuncture for chronic primary pain NICE NG193, 2021 Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - NSAIDs first-line : Ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD with PPI cover — 2–4 weeks NICE NG59 - Topical NSAIDs: Diclofenac gel 3x/day — NICE preferred for localised musculoskeletal pain NICE NG59 ; fewer systemic side effects - Paracetamol: Limited evidence for musculoskeletal pain NICE NG59 but useful adjunct - Corticosteroid injection: Local corticosteroid methylprednisolone 20–40mg + local anaesthetic injection at costo-sternal junction — under GP/pain clinic guidance; useful for refractory cases. Evidence from case series Waldman SD, 2009 - Avoid long-term opioids for costochondritis — not indicated per NICE NG59 Onward Referral Criteria Back to GP urgent : - Any new cardiac/pulmonary red flag identified during physiotherapy assessment - Features suggesting inflammatory arthropathy bilateral, morning stiffness, sacroiliitis - No improvement after 6–8 weeks conservative management — consider imaging and bloods Rheumatology: - Suspected seronegative spondyloarthropathy - Bilateral costochondritis + elevated inflammatory markers Pain Management: - Persistent costochondritis >3 months unresponsive to conservative management - For consideration of corticosteroid injection or pain management programme Surgical rare : - Septic costochondritis — surgical debridement infectious disease/orthopaedic/thoracic surgery --- Key References 1. The diagnoses of patients admitted with acute chest pain but without myocardial infarction. European Heart Journal , 17 7 , 1028–1034. 4. Waldman SD. 2009 . Costochondritis pain. In: Pain Review . Saunders Elsevier. pp. 222–224. 5. Levy MJ, Fayaz A, Freemantle N, Howes N, Langford RM. 2010 . Randomised controlled feasibility trial of acupuncture for chronic pain in the emergency department. Emergency Medicine Journal , 28 6 , 482–485. 6. NICE guideline NG59 2016, updated 2020 . Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s . Applied to MSK chest pain . NICE. 7. NICE guideline NG193 2021 . title: Scheuermann's Disease
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Scheuermann's disease Scheuermann's kyphosis; juvenile kyphosis is a structural developmental disorder characterised by anterior vertebral body wedging producing a rigid thoracic hyperkyphosis. It is the most common cause of structural kyphosis in adolescents. Diagnostic C
headings: Diagnostic Criteria Sorensen Criteria — 1964, widely accepted
Postural Kyphosis vs Scheuermann's: Key Differentiation
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Scheuermann's disease Scheuermann's kyphosis; juvenile kyphosis is a structural developmental disorder characterised by anterior vertebral body wedging producing a rigid thoracic hyperkyphosis. It is the most common cause of structural kyphosis in adolescents. Diagnostic Criteria Sorensen Criteria — 1964, widely accepted - ≥3 consecutive thoracic vertebrae with ≥5° of anterior wedging each - Associated with irregular vertebral endplates - Presence of Schmorl's nodes nuclear herniations through endplates - Kyphosis typically rigid does not correct fully with hyperextension Prevalence & Demographics - Prevalence: 1–8% of the general population Bradford DS, 1977; Lowe TG, 1990 - Onset: typically 10–15 years of age adolescent growth spurt - Male:female ratio: approximately 2:1 some studies suggest equal distribution - Peak deformity progression during adolescent growth spurt Risser stage 0–3 - Thoracic Scheuermann's most common T7–T9 most frequently involved apex - Lumbar Scheuermann's: Also described; causes low back pain; less common; wedging of lumbar vertebrae Relevant Anatomy - Ring apophysis of vertebral endplate is vulnerable during adolescent growth - During rapid growth, the apophysis is cartilaginous and susceptible to mechanical loading - Proposed mechanism: Disruption of endplate ring apophysis → irregular endplate → asymmetric loading → anterior growth retardation → vertebral wedging - Schmorl's nodes: Herniation of nucleus pulposus through weakened vertebral endplate → reactive sclerosis - Adjacent disc spaces often narrowed Aetiology Multifactorial — exact cause unknown - Genetic predisposition: Autosomal dominant inheritance suggested Halal F et al., 1978 - Mechanical loading: Repetitive flexion loading during growth agricultural work, physical labour — historical association - Collagen/endplate abnormality: Proposed defect in collagen matrix of endplate - Osteoporosis: Some evidence of reduced bone density in affected vertebrae - Tight hamstrings and hip flexors: Common associated finding; may contribute to compensatory thoracic kyphosis Natural History - Adolescents with 75° may cause cardiopulmonary compromise in severe cases - Curve progression after skeletal maturity is generally slow Note: Scheuermann's disease is primarily a clinical + radiological diagnosis . There are no specific orthopaedic special tests with published sensitivity/specificity data for this condition. The following assessments are used clinically. Clinical Assessment Findings Assessment Finding in Scheuermann's Clinical Significance ------------ -------------------------- ---------------------- Adam's Forward Bend Test Kyphosis does not correct rigid ; scoliosis screen simultaneously Differentiates structural from postural kyphosis; postural kyphosis corrects Prone Press-Up / Extension Test Kyphosis partially or fully corrects in postural kyphosis ; remains in Scheuermann's Key differentiating test from postural round back Wall Stand Test Cannot flatten thoracic spine against wall; persistent curve Quantifies rigidity of kyphosis Hamstring Length Assessment SLR Frequently tight 75° FVC/FEV1 if >80° kyphosis Postural Kyphosis vs Scheuermann's: Key Differentiation Feature Postural Kyphosis Scheuermann's Disease --------- ------------------- ---------------------- Corrects with extension Yes — fully No — partially or not at all Vertebral wedging X-ray No Yes ≥5° in ≥3 vertebrae Schmorl's nodes Absent Present Endplate irregularities Absent Present Pain Variable Typically thoracic/lumbar pain Age of onset Any Adolescence 10–15 years --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Rapidly progressive kyphosis in skeletally immature Aggressive structural deformity Urgent orthopaedic/spinal surgery referral Neurological symptoms weakness, paraesthesia, gait change Cord compression from severe kyphosis Urgent MRI + neurosurgical referral Bowel/bladder dysfunction Cord/conus compression Emergency neurosurgical referral Kyphosis with systemic features weight loss, fever Malignancy / infection / inflammatory disease Urgent investigation + specialist referral Kyphosis in a child 80° + exertional dyspnoea Cardiopulmonary compromise Respiratory assessment; refer cardiac/respiratory Kyphosis + skin changes café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas Neurofibromatosis Paediatric genetics/orthopaedic referral Kyphosis + restricted chest expansion + spinal inflammatory markers Ankylosing spondylitis Rheumatology referral Severe thoracic pain at site of kyphosis Acute Schmorl's node, fracture, disc herniation MRI thoracic spine --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Manual therapy has a role in Scheuermann's primarily for pain management and mobility not deformity correction in skeletal maturity - Assess PAIVMs at each thoracic level for localised stiffness and pain - Grade III–IV mobilisations at painful/restricted levels - Rib mobilisation at costovertebral joints often restricted secondary to kyphosis - Extension mobilisations: unilateral and central PA to promote extension - Manipulation Grade V : use with caution; deformity alters biomechanics McKenzie/MDT Framework - Primary approach in adolescent Scheuermann's: - Thoracic extension exercises as cornerstone of conservative management - Prone lying → prone on elbows → prone press-up progression - Seated extension over back of chair, foam roller extension - Active thoracic rotation in flexion/extension to maintain segmental mobility - Postural education and correction - Directional preference: extension consistently beneficial directional preference - McKenzie classification: mostly dysfunction syndrome fixed kyphotic deformity + postural syndrome overlay Bracing Framework Orthopaedic - Milwaukee brace cervico-thoraco-lumbar orthosis : traditional; poor compliance - Boston/TLSO brace : thoraco-lumbar-sacral orthosis; used for apex below T7 - Indication: Cobb angle 45–70° in skeletally immature patient Risser 0–3 - Duration: Full-time wear ~20–23 hours/day until skeletal maturity; then weaning - Evidence: Sachs B et al. 1987 — bracing effective in reducing progression; improvement of 40% in kyphotic angle achieved in some series - Physiotherapy role during bracing: maintain core strength, exercise in and out of brace --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in Scheuermann's --------- ------------- ------ ---------------------- Cobb Angle X-ray Radiographic kyphosis measurement 5° change clinically meaningful Primary structural outcome; monitoring progression NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Pain management PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Functional activity limitations SRS-22 Scoliosis Research Society 22-item; 5 domains pain, function, self-image, mental health, satisfaction Domain-specific Best validated for spinal deformity in adolescents/adults ODI Oswestry Disability Index 10% Adult Scheuermann's with chronic pain/disability Chest expansion measurement Tape measure at 4th ICS; normal >5cm >1cm Severe kyphosis; respiratory monitoring Sagittal vertical axis SVA Radiographic global balance assessment — Surgical planning; >5cm positive SVA = surgical concern --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Radiographic Diagnosis Standard lateral thoracic X-ray standing, if possible confirms diagnosis: - Cobb angle of thoracic kyphosis normal 20–40° - Vertebral wedging anterior height 5°/year - Neurological involvement - NI referral: Royal Belfast Hospital for Sick Children RBHSC paediatric orthopaedics Secondary Care — Adult Orthopaedics/Spinal Surgery: - Refer adult patients with: - Severe kyphosis ≥75° with pain/functional limitation - Neurological compromise - Cardiopulmonary compromise - Surgical teams: Royal Victoria Hospital Belfast spinal surgery Conservative Management Exercise Therapy — Evidence Grade B: 1. Thoracic Extension Exercises Primary intervention : - Prone press-up McKenzie extension - Foam roller thoracic extension - Doorway/corner stretch bilateral shoulder external rotation + extension - Cat-camel mobilisation - Seated extension over chair back - Frequency: daily; 10–15 repetitions, 3 sets 2. Flexibility: - Hamstring stretching: Critical — address tight hamstrings to improve pelvic mechanics. Standing, supine, and neural-flossing techniques. Hold 30–45 seconds, 3–5 times/day - Hip flexor stretching: Thomas position, runner's lunge stretch - Pectoral stretching: Doorway stretch, foam roller bilateral arm extension 3. Strengthening: - Thoracic extensor strengthening: Prone cobras, back extensions hyperextension bench , rows, pull-aparts - Scapular retractors: Rows cable, band, dumbbell , face pulls, reverse flyes - Core stabilisation: Plank, bird-dog, dead bug — avoid excessive thoracic flexion loading - Respiratory training: Incentive spirometry, deep breathing — especially if chest expansion limited 4. Bracing Orthopaedic Prescription — Adolescents Only : - Indicated for Cobb angle 45–70° in skeletally immature Risser 0–3 - Milwaukee or TLSO brace prescribed and monitored by orthopaedics - Physiotherapy to support exercise compliance during bracing 5. Postural Education: - Ergonomics: desk height, monitor position, chair back support - Sleep position: no prone sleeping; supine with thoracic support - Self-monitoring of sitting posture Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD + PPI for pain during acute flares NICE NG59 - Topical NSAIDs: Diclofenac gel for localised thoracic pain NICE NG59 preferred for localised MSK - Paracetamol: Adjunct analgesia; limited evidence but commonly used - Vitamin D + Calcium: If bone density concerns / adolescent with restricted diet NICE NG187 — vitamin D supplementation - Avoid: Long-term NSAIDs in adolescents without gastroprotection; opioids not indicated Onward Referral Criteria Urgent: - Neurological deficit → MRI + neurosurgical referral - Severe cardiopulmonary compromise → respiratory/cardiac referral Elective Orthopaedic/Spinal Surgery: - Cobb angle >75° with pain/functional disability unresponsive to conservative management - Neurological compromise at any angle - Cosmetic deformity with significant psychosocial impact after skeletal maturity - Surgical technique: posterior spinal fusion most common ; occasionally combined anterior-posterior approach for rigid severe curves - Success rate: >85% correction maintained at 10 years Hosman AJF et al., 2002 --- Key References 1.
