title: Thoracic Disc Herniation
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic disc herniation TDH is the displacement of disc material nucleus pulposus, annulus fibrosus, or both beyond the intervertebral space in the thoracic spine T1–T12 . While less common than cervical or lumbar disc herniation, TDH carries significant clinical importan
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic disc herniation TDH is the displacement of disc material nucleus pulposus, annulus fibrosus, or both beyond the intervertebral space in the thoracic spine T1–T12 . While less common than cervical or lumbar disc herniation, TDH carries significant clinical importance due to the proximity of the spinal cord and the risk of myelopathy. Prevalence - Symptomatic TDH accounts for approximately 0.25–0.75% of all symptomatic disc herniations Wood KB et al., 1997 - MRI studies report incidental TDH in 11–37% of asymptomatic individuals Wood KB et al., 1995 - Peak age: 40–60 years; slight male predominance - Most common levels: T8–T12 lower thoracic — 75% of symptomatic cases , particularly T11–T12 Mechanism & Pathophysiology - The thoracic spine is relatively immobile rib cage stabilisation , placing lower mechanical stress compared to cervical/lumbar regions - However, the thoracic spinal canal is narrow relative to cord diameter cord:canal ratio ~0.4–0.7 , meaning even small disc protrusions can cause significant myelopathy - Types: - Soft disc herniation: acute, traumatic — nucleus pulposus extrusion - Hard disc/calcified herniation: chronic degeneration, calcification — more common in thoracic region ~70% of symptomatic TDH - Direction: Central and centrolateral protrusions most clinically significant cord compression ; lateral protrusions cause radiculopathy Relevant Anatomy - Spinal cord occupies a larger proportion of the canal than in the lumbar spine - Blood supply: anterior spinal artery single vessel — risk of cord ischaemia with anterior compression - T1–T6: relatively fixed, rib articulations on both superior and inferior costovertebral joints - T10–T12: floating ribs, relatively more mobile, therefore more susceptible to degenerative disc disease --- Special Tests > Critical note: There are no validated specific orthopaedic tests for thoracic disc herniation comparable to lumbar provocative tests. Diagnosis is primarily clinical symptoms + neurological examination confirmed by MRI. The tests below assess for myelopathy or radiculopathy secondary to TDH. Tests for Thoracic Myelopathy Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Babinski Sign 0.50 0.98 25.0 0.51 Moderate Present if UMN lesion; highly specific for cord compression Hoffmann's Sign 0.58 0.98 29.0 0.43 Moderate Cervical/upper thoracic cord compression; flick middle finger DIP Clonus ankle/knee 0.13–0.31 0.97–0.99 4.0–10.3 0.70–0.89 Low–Moderate Sustained clonus >5 beats pathological; indicates UMN lesion Lhermitte's Sign 0.27 0.97 9.0 0.75 Low–Moderate Electric shock sensation down spine/limbs with neck flexion; not thoracic-specific Hyperreflexia lower limb 0.78 0.61 2.0 0.36 Low UMN pattern below level of lesion Loss of Proprioception lower limb Variable Variable — — Expert opinion Posterior column involvement; assess with Romberg's test Romberg's Test 0.75 0.90 7.5 0.28 Low Posterior column dysfunction; positive if sways more with eyes closed For radiculopathy component: Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Kemp's Test thoracic Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion only Thoracic Slump Test Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion; neural tension test for thoracic levels Rib Spring posteroanterior pressure Not validated Not validated — — Clinical utility; pain reproduction at affected level References for myelopathy tests: Cook CE & Hegedus EJ. 2013 . Orthopedic Physical Examination Tests: An Evidence-Based Approach . Pearson; Tong HC et al. 2002 . Spine . --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Bilateral lower limb weakness / paraparesis Cord compression / myelopathy Emergency MRI + neurosurgical referral Bowel or bladder dysfunction retention or incontinence Cord compression / cauda equina-equivalent Emergency neurosurgical referral same day Saddle anaesthesia Conus medullaris compression Emergency referral Progressive gait disturbance / ataxia Myelopathy Urgent MRI within 24–48 hours Night pain, constant pain, systemically unwell Malignancy / metastatic disease Urgent MRI + bloods PSA, CEA, ESR, CRP, calcium, alkaline phosphatase Age >50, history of malignancy Metastatic cord compression MSCC Same-day oncological assessment; refer to MSCC coordinator per NICE NG23 Fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression + back pain Discitis / epidural abscess Urgent MRI + bloods WCC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures ; admit Trauma + thoracic pain Fracture / instability X-ray ± CT; immobilise if instability suspected Thoracic pain + hypotension + pulsatile mass Aortic aneurysm/dissection 999 — Emergency vascular Unexplained weight loss + thoracic pain Malignancy 2-week-wait GP referral --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Passive accessory intervertebral movements PAIVMs at suspected level s : posteroanterior PA central and unilateral pressures - Passive physiological intervertebral movements PPIVMs : flexion, extension, rotation, lateral flexion - Note: with myelopathy, avoid forceful manipulations — Grade I–II mobilisations only pending MRI - Establish comparable sign symptom-reproducing movement then reassess after intervention - Maitland grades III–IV for pain-dominant non-myelopathic TDH McKenzie/MDT Framework - Postural assessment: thoracic kyphosis assessment, correction of slouched sitting - Directional preference: thoracic extension exercises may centralise or reduce symptoms in discogenic pain - Extension bias: thoracic extension in prone press-up , standing extension over foam roller - Contraindicated if extension worsens/peripheralises symptoms — reassess direction - Flexion bias less common in thoracic disc, but assess systematically - Relevant for lower thoracic levels T10–T12 with lumbar-type presentation Pattern Recognition Approach - Myelopathic pattern: UMN signs below lesion level spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski , bilateral involvement, gait disturbance — refer urgently - Radiculopathic pattern: Band-like chest/abdominal pain following dermatomal distribution, unilateral, neurological signs at level - Discogenic/mechanical pattern: Central thoracic pain, worse with flexion/loading, improved with extension — conservative management appropriate --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in TDH --------- ------------- ------ ------------ NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 Primary pain outcome Oswestry Disability Index ODI 10-item back-specific disability 10–12 points 10% Widely used for spinal conditions including thoracic PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Individualised functional limitation Modified JOA Score for myelopathy Japanese Orthopaedic Association score for myelopathy Variable Post-surgical outcome for myelopathy Nurick Classification Myelopathy severity grading 0–5 — Clinical grading for myelopathic presentation EQ-5D-5L Generic health-related quality of life 0.037 NICE/NHS recommended outcome for cost-effectiveness GRC Global Rating of Change –7 to +7 +2 to +3 Patient-perceived recovery --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Clinical Diagnosis - Diagnosis is made by clinical examination + MRI - Physical examination alone is insufficient; MRI is the investigation of choice - High incidence of asymptomatic MRI findings means clinical correlation is essential Imaging Guidelines - MRI thoracic spine: Gold standard — assess disc morphology, cord signal change T2 hyperintensity indicates myelopathy , degree of canal compromise - CT myelography: Alternative when MRI contraindicated; better for calcified disc - Plain X-ray: Limited utility; may show disc space narrowing, calcification, kyphosis — not diagnostic - CT without contrast: Useful for identifying calcified disc important for surgical planning — calcification changes surgical approach risk Key Evidence - Wood KB et al. 1995 demonstrated 37% prevalence of TDH on MRI in 90 asymptomatic volunteers — underscoring need for clinical correlation - Stillerman CB et al. 1998 : Retrospective review of 82 surgically treated TDH — 76% presented with myelopathy or mixed myeloradiculopathy; conservative management successful in mild cases - Bouthors C et al. 2018 : 10-year outcomes study — myelopathic TDH rarely improves without surgical decompression; 75% surgical success rate - No Level 1 RCT evidence exists for conservative vs surgical management of TDH --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Thoracic facet joint pain Localised paraspinal tenderness, no neurological signs, no imaging changes Intercostal neuralgia Band-like pain, dermatomal, often post-herpetic; no cord signs Scheuermann's disease Young patients, kyphotic deformity, wedge vertebrae on X-ray Costochondritis Anterior chest pain, point tenderness on rib/costal cartilage Cardiac ischaemia / angina Mid-sternal chest pain, exertional, ECG changes, troponin elevation Aortic dissection Sudden severe tearing pain, BP differential between arms, haemodynamic instability Oesophageal pathology Pain related to swallowing, GORD symptoms, relieved by antacids Metastatic spinal disease Known malignancy, constant night pain, bone destruction on imaging Multiple sclerosis Relapsing-remitting neurological symptoms, positive Lhermitte's, MRI plaques Spinal cord tumour ependymoma/astrocytoma Progressive myelopathy, MRI intrinsic cord lesion with enhancement Osteoporotic fracture Post-menopausal female, acute onset, deformity, DEXA scan osteoporosis --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Community Physiotherapy: - Suitable for non-myelopathic TDH with manageable pain - GP referral to community MSK physiotherapy or direct access where available - Red flag screen mandatory at first assessment - If any UMN signs, bowel/bladder involvement → same-day emergency neurosurgical referral Royal Victoria Hospital Belfast / Altnagelvin Secondary Care: - Orthopaedic/neurosurgical referral for surgical consideration in: - Myelopathy progressive or moderate-severe - Failure of ≥6 weeks conservative management with severe radiculopathy - Significant canal compromise on MRI >50% canal occlusion - Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression MSCC coordinator contact: per NICE NG23; NI MSCC pathway via Belfast City Hospital oncology Conservative Management Physiotherapy — Evidence Grade C limited high-quality RCTs : 1. Education: Natural history majority of non-myelopathic TDH improves with time , activity modification, load management 2. Posture & ergonomics: Thoracic extension exercises, postural correction to reduce disc loading — especially lower thoracic levels 3. Manual therapy: Grade I–II Maitland mobilisations for pain relief; avoid Grade V manipulation without myelopathy exclusion. Soft tissue techniques to thoracic paraspinals, erector spinae 4. Thoracic extension exercises: McKenzie extension exercises, foam roller thoracic extension, seated thoracic rotation — for non-myelopathic cases 5. Neural mobilisation: Thoracic Slump sliders for radiculopathic presentation 6. Core stability: Graduated programme targeting deep thoracic/lumbar stabilisers — avoid high-load flexion exercises 7. Hydrotherapy: Buoyancy-assisted exercise — lower thoracic/mild cases Duration: 6–12 weeks conservative management before surgical re-evaluation in non-myelopathic cases. Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - Analgesia Step 1 : Paracetamol 1g QDS limited evidence for back pain — NICE NG59 - NSAIDs Step 2 : Ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD with PPI NICE NG59 ; caution in renal impairment, cardiovascular disease, elderly - Neuropathic agents: Amitriptyline 10–75mg nocte or duloxetine 60–120mg daily for neuropathic/radicular pain NICE NG173 — note: pregabalin/gabapentin NOT first-line per NICE 2021 update without specialist advice - Opioids: Short-term weak opioids codeine ± paracetamol if NSAIDs insufficient — avoid long-term NICE NG59 - Oral corticosteroids: Short course dexamethasone 8mg daily reducing — may be used for acute myelopathic exacerbation pending neurosurgical review off-label; neurosurgery decision - Epidural steroid injection: Thoracic epidural under image guidance — specialist pain management referral; limited evidence Onward Referral Criteria Emergency same day : - Acute myelopathy with progressive paraparesis - Bowel/bladder dysfunction — neurosurgical emergency - Suspected MSCC NICE NG23 — refer within 24 hours to MSCC coordinator Urgent within 2 weeks : - Moderate myelopathy without emergency features - Failure of 4–6 weeks conservative management with significant disability Elective: - Persistent severe radiculopathy unresponsive to ≥12 weeks conservative management - Surgical options: thoracoscopic discectomy video-assisted , posterior laminectomy, transpedicular approach selected by neurosurgeon based on level and calcification --- Key References 1. Wood KB, Blair JM, Aepple DM, et al. 1995 . The natural history of asymptomatic thoracic disc herniations. Spine , 20 14 , 1631–1638. 2. Wood KB, Garvey TA, Gundry C, Heithoff KB. 1997 . Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine: evaluation of asymptomatic individuals. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery American , 77 11 , 1631–1638. 3. Stillerman CB, Chen TC, Couldwell WT, Zhang W, Weiss MH. 1998 . Experience in the surgical management of 82 symptomatic herniated thoracic discs and review of the literature. Journal of Neurosurgery , 88 4 , 623–633. 4. Bouthors C, Benzakour A, Court C. 2018 . Surgical treatment of thoracic disc herniation: a prospective study of clinical and functional outcomes at a mean follow-up of 10 years. European Spine Journal , 27 8 , 1835–1843. 5. Cook CE, Hegedus EJ. 2013 . Orthopedic Physical Examination Tests: An Evidence-Based Approach 2nd ed. . Pearson Education. 6. Tong HC, Haig AJ, Yamakawa K. 2002 . The Spurling test and cervical radiculopathy. Spine , 27 2 , 156–159. 7. NICE guideline NG59 2016, updated 2020 . Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s: assessment and management . NICE. Extrapolated to thoracic — no thoracic-specific NICE guideline 8. NICE guideline NG23 2008, updated 2023 . Metastatic spinal cord compression in adults . NICE. 9. NICE guideline NG173 2020 . Neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management in non-specialist settings . NICE. 10. Elhadi AM, Zehri AH, Acosta FL, et al. 2015 . Surgical efficacy of minimally invasive thoracic discectomy. Journal of Clinical Neuroscience , 22 12 , 1708–1713.

headings: Maitland Assessment Findings Consistent with Facet Pain
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic facet joint pain also termed thoracic zygapophyseal joint pain refers to pain arising from the synovial facet zygapophyseal joints of the thoracic spine. It is a recognised but frequently underdiagnosed cause of mid-back pain in the adult population. Prevalence - Estimated prevalence of thoracic facet joint pain in patients with thoracic back pain: 34–48% based on controlled diagnostic medial branch blocks Manchikanti L et al., 2007 - Cervical facet joint pain is better characterised; thoracic data extrapolated from cervical/lumbar literature - Can occur at any thoracic level; slightly more common at lower thoracic levels - Affects adults of all ages; increased prevalence with degenerative change in middle-older age Relevant Anatomy - Thoracic facet joints zygapophyseal joints are paired synovial joints between the superior and inferior articular processes of adjacent vertebrae - In the thoracic spine, the facet joints are oriented coronally frontal plane — approximately 60° from the horizontal — permitting rotation and lateral flexion, limiting flexion/extension - Each facet joint is innervated by the medial branch of the dorsal ramus from its own level and the level above dual innervation — basis for medial branch block diagnostic technique - Additionally, the thoracic spine has costovertebral joints articulations between rib head and vertebral body and costotransverse joints between rib tubercle and transverse process — these may also contribute to pain syndromes clinically overlapping with facet pain Mechanism & Aetiology - Degenerative: Articular cartilage loss, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis — most common in middle–older age - Postural: Prolonged thoracic flexion kyphotic postures, desk work loads posterior elements; increased facet joint compressive force in hyperkyphosis - Traumatic: Acute hyperextension or rotation injury whiplash-type mechanism , direct trauma - Inflammatory: Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis — facet joint synovitis - Acute locked facet meniscoid entrapment : Sudden onset acute thoracic pain following rotation — proposed entrapment of fibroadipose meniscoid structure within the joint --- Special Tests > Critical note: No single clinical test has been validated for thoracic facet joint pain with adequate sensitivity/specificity data. The gold standard for diagnosis is controlled comparative medial branch blocks two anaesthetics with different durations producing concordant relief . Clinical tests assist in identifying likely facet-mediated pain prior to diagnostic blocks. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Passive Accessory Intervertebral Movement PAIVM — PA Unilateral Not formally validated Not formally validated — — Expert consensus Unilateral PA on articular pillar reproducing concordant pain; primary clinical assessment tool Passive Physiological Intervertebral Movement PPIVM — Rotation Not formally validated Not formally validated — — Expert consensus Restricted painful rotation in direction of affected facet; compare bilaterally Kemp's Test Thoracic Extension-Rotation Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Extension combined with ipsilateral rotation loading facet joint; reproduces back ± referred pain Thoracic Extension Test Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Isolated extension reproducing posterior thoracic pain; suggests posterior element involvement Medial Branch Block diagnostic 0.92–0.96 for concordant ≥80% relief 0.72–0.82 controlled double block 3.3–5.3 0.05–0.10 High reference standard Diagnostic procedure; not a clinical test but the reference standard Maitland Assessment Findings Consistent with Facet Pain - Unilateral paraspinal tenderness at facet joint level - Restricted and painful thoracic rotation ipsilateral side - Positive PA unilateral accessory movement reproducing concordant pain - Often absent neurological signs References: Manchikanti L et al. 2007 . Pain Physician ; Bogduk N. 2011 . Practice Guidelines for Spinal Diagnostic and Treatment Procedures . --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Thoracic pain + fever + elevated inflammatory markers Septic arthritis of facet joint / discitis Urgent MRI + microbiology; admit Constant severe thoracic pain, worse lying Malignancy / metastatic disease Urgent MRI ± bone scan; bloods Age >50 + thoracic pain + history of malignancy Metastatic spinal disease Urgent oncology referral per NICE NG23 Thoracic pain + bilateral neurological signs Cord compression / myelopathy Emergency MRI Thoracic pain + bowel/bladder dysfunction Cord compression Emergency neurosurgical referral Sudden onset thoracic pain + haemodynamic compromise Aortic dissection / aneurysm 999 — Emergency Thoracic pain + weight loss + night sweats Malignancy / lymphoma Urgent GP referral / investigations Thoracic pain in patient with osteoporosis + acute onset Compression fracture X-ray / MRI Thoracic pain + morning stiffness >1 hour + bilateral Ankylosing spondylitis / axial SpA Rheumatology referral; HLAB27, MRI sacroiliac joints --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework Thoracic facet joint pain is highly amenable to the Maitland approach: Assessment: - PAIVMs: Central PA spinous process and unilateral PA articular pillar, 2–3cm lateral to spinous process — assess resistance, end-feel, and pain response. Grade I–IV on quality, resistance, and pain - PPIVMs: Rotation primary thoracic motion , lateral flexion — assess range, end-feel, symmetry - Comparable sign: Identify the movement/pressure that most closely reproduces the patient's concordant pain Treatment Grading: - Grade I–II: Pain dominant; oscillatory movements at start/middle of range acute/irritable presentation - Grade III–IV: Stiffness dominant; end-range mobilisation subacute/chronic presentation - Grade V manipulation : High-velocity low-amplitude thrust — for non-irritable stiff thoracic facet restriction; contraindications: osteoporosis, cord compression, instability, anticoagulation Reassessment: Always reassess comparable sign after each intervention. McKenzie/MDT Framework - Thoracic extension typically the directional preference in posterior element pain - Extension exercises: prone press-up, seated thoracic extension, foam roller extension - Correct flexion postures that load thoracic facets in extension gap - Education on postural modification — sustained flexion perpetuates facet joint stress - May classify as: dysfunction syndrome repeated extension exercises for restricted posterior elements or postural syndrome posture correction Bogduk's Approach Evidence-Based Diagnostic Framework - History-based clinical features alone have poor diagnostic accuracy for facet joint pain Bogduk N, 2011 - Controlled medial branch blocks remain the only validated diagnostic method - Clinical examination used to localise level s for diagnostic block - Identify: unilateral vs bilateral, acute vs chronic, suspected levels --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in Facet Joint Pain --------- ------------- ------ ------------------------ NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Primary pain outcome PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Individualised functional activities Oswestry Disability Index ODI Validated for spinal pain/disability 10–12 points 10% Widely used; validated for thoracic use Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire RMDQ 24-item back-specific 2.5 points Alternative to ODI; shorter FABQ Fear Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire Physical activity and work subscales 11 pts physical ; 8 pts work Identifies psychosocial barriers to recovery GRC Global Rating of Change +2 to +3 Recovery perception Thoracic range of motion goniometry/inclinometry Objective movement measure Variable Reassessment of mobility gains --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Prevalence Studies - Manchikanti L et al. 2007 : Using controlled double diagnostic medial branch blocks, found 34–48% prevalence of thoracic facet joint pain in patients presenting with chronic thoracic pain. Pain Physician , 10 4 , 521–532. - Atluri S et al. 2011 : Systematic review — thoracic medial branch blocks have good diagnostic accuracy when controlled double-block paradigm used Atluri S et al., Pain Physician , 14 5 , E241–E264 Clinical Prediction Rules - No validated clinical prediction rule exists specifically for thoracic facet joint pain - Cervical and lumbar facet prediction rules exist but have not been validated at thoracic levels - Schwarzer AC et al. 1994 demonstrated that clinical features cannot reliably identify lumbar facet pain — likely applicable to thoracic spine Diagnostic Imaging - Plain X-ray: May show degenerative facet changes, spondylosis, kyphosis — not diagnostic for pain source - CT scan: Better visualisation of facet joint morphology, osteophytes — cannot confirm pain source - MRI: Superior soft tissue assessment; may show facet joint synovitis joint effusion, synovial thickening on T2 — poor correlation with pain in isolation - Bone scan SPECT : Increased uptake at facet joints in active degeneration; moderate diagnostic value — sensitivity ~70%, specificity ~65% Pneumaticos SG et al., 2006 - Diagnostic medial branch blocks: Gold standard; controlled comparative blocks with short-acting lidocaine and long-acting bupivacaine anaesthetic; ≥80% pain relief with concordant duration = positive diagnosis --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Thoracic disc herniation Central or paracentral pain, may have neurological signs; MRI confirms Thoracic radiculopathy Dermatomal band-like pain, neurological deficit; MRI ± NCS Costochondritis Anterior chest pain, costo-sternal junction tenderness Costovertebral joint pain Very lateral paraspinal pain, reproduced by rib mobilisation rather than PA facet pressure Scheuermann's disease Kyphotic deformity, wedge vertebrae on X-ray; younger patients Osteoporotic compression fracture Acute onset, female >60, DEXA confirms osteoporosis; MRI shows fracture Metastatic spinal disease Constant pain, night pain, systemic symptoms, bone destruction on imaging Ankylosing spondylitis Bilateral, morning stiffness, sacroiliitis, elevated CRP/ESR, HLA-B27 Rheumatoid arthritis Symmetrical joint involvement, rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP, systemic features Intercostal neuralgia Band-like dermatomal pain; post-herpetic; no movement reproduction Cardiac/visceral referred pain Not reproducible with spinal palpation/movement; associated systemic symptoms --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Community Physiotherapy First-line : - GP referral or self-referral to community MSK physiotherapy - Appropriate for straightforward mechanical thoracic facet joint pain with no red flags - Adequate trial: 6–8 sessions over 8–12 weeks Secondary Care: - Pain management referral if no improvement after 8–12 weeks conservative management - Medial branch blocks / radiofrequency denervation — referred to pain clinic Belfast City Hospital Pain Management Centre; Causeway/Altnagelvin for western HSC Trusts - Rheumatology if inflammatory arthropathy suspected Occupational Health: Ergonomic assessment for work-related thoracic pain especially sedentary workers with prolonged thoracic flexion Conservative Management Physiotherapy — Evidence Grade B–C: 1. Manual Therapy Grade B — moderate evidence : - Thoracic spine manipulation / high-velocity thrust HVLAT : moderate evidence for short-term pain reduction in thoracic pain Briggs AM et al., 2009 - Maitland Grade III–IV mobilisation at affected levels: well-supported in clinical practice; Grade I–II for irritable presentations - Rib mobilisation for costovertebral component - Contraindications to manipulation: osteoporosis, instability, cord signs, anticoagulation, inflammatory arthritis 2. Exercise Therapy Grade B : - Thoracic extension strengthening: prone cobra, scapular retraction, rowing exercises - Flexibility: thoracic rotation stretches, foam roller extension, lateral flexion stretches - Core stability: deep thoracic/lumbar stabiliser programme - Postural strengthening: lower trapezius, rhomboids, serratus anterior 3. Electrotherapy: - TENS: short-term pain relief, Grade C evidence NICE supports for chronic pain - Therapeutic ultrasound: insufficient evidence for recommendation 4. Education and Self-Management: - Ergonomics: workstation assessment, avoid prolonged thoracic flexion, screen height, chair lumbar support - Activity modification: pace activities, graded return to exercise - Reassurance: often resolves with appropriate management Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - Topical NSAIDs first-line : Diclofenac 1% gel TDS at painful area NICE NG59 — preferred for localised MSK pain - Oral NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD + PPI; 2–4 weeks NICE NG59 - Paracetamol: Adjunct; limited evidence for back pain per NICE - Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants: Amitriptyline 10–25mg nocte for chronic thoracic pain — off-label but supported by NICE NG193 for chronic primary pain - Avoid: Prolonged opioid use, benzodiazepines NICE NG59 Interventional Pain Clinic : - Medial branch blocks: Diagnostic and short-term therapeutic; methylprednisolone 20–40mg + local anaesthetic at thoracic medial branches image-guided - Radiofrequency denervation RFD / thermocoagulation: For confirmed facet joint pain ≥80% relief from dual medial branch blocks — evidence: Manchikanti L et al. 2012 — significant pain/function improvement at 1–2 years vs sham Level II evidence, Pain Physician - Intraarticular steroid injection: Moderate short-term benefit; less evidence than RFD for long-term relief Onward Referral Criteria Urgent: - Any red flag identified see above - Progressive neurological deficit → emergency To Pain Management Elective : - Failure of ≥8–12 weeks physiotherapy - High pain/disability burden suitable for diagnostic medial branch blocks - For consideration of RFD if blocks confirm diagnosis To Rheumatology: - Suspected inflammatory arthropathy bilateral, morning stiffness, elevated inflammatory markers Surgical: - Rarely indicated for isolated facet joint pain - Occasionally: spinal decompression if co-existing stenosis or spondylolisthesis --- Key References 1. Manchikanti L, Singh V, Pampati V, et al. 2007 . Prevalence of thoracic facet joint pain in chronic thoracic pain. Pain Physician , 10 4 , 521–532. 2. Atluri S, Datta S, Falco FJE, Lee M. 2011 . Systematic review of diagnostic utility and therapeutic effectiveness of thoracic facet joint interventions. Pain Physician , 14 5 , E241–E264. 3. Manchikanti L, Kaye AD, Boswell MV, et al. 2012 . A systematic review and best evidence synthesis of effectiveness of therapeutic facet joint interventions in managing chronic spinal pain. Pain Physician , 15 4 , E349–E404. 4. Bogduk N. 2011 . Practice Guidelines for Spinal Diagnostic and Treatment Procedures 2nd ed. . International Spine Intervention Society. 5. Schwarzer AC, Aprill CN, Derby R, Fortin J, Kine G, Bogduk N. 1994 . The false-positive rate of uncontrolled diagnostic blocks of the lumbar zygapophyseal joints. Pain , 58 2 , 195–200. 6. Pneumaticos SG, Chatziioannou SN, Hipp JA, Moore WH, Esses SI. 2006 . Low back pain: prediction of short-term outcome of facet joint injection with bone scintigraphy. Radiology , 238 2 , 693–698. 7. Briggs AM, Smith AJ, Straker LM, Bragge P. 2009 . Thoracic spine pain in the general population: prevalence, incidence and associated factors in children, adolescents and adults. A systematic review. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders , 10, 77. 8. NICE guideline NG59 2016, updated 2020 . Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s: assessment and management . NICE. 9. NICE guideline NG193 2021 . Chronic pain primary and secondary . NICE. 10. Dreyfuss P, Tibiletti C, Dreyer SJ. 1994 . Thoracic zygapophyseal joint pain patterns: a study in normal volunteers. Spine , 19 7 , 807–811.

title: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome
summary: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic Outlet Syndrome TOS refers to a group of disorders caused by compression of the neurovascular structures brachial plexus, subclavian artery, subclavian vein as they pass through the thoracic outlet — the space between the clavicle, first rib, and scalene muscles.
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic Outlet Syndrome TOS refers to a group of disorders caused by compression of the neurovascular structures brachial plexus, subclavian artery, subclavian vein as they pass through the thoracic outlet — the space between the clavicle, first rib, and scalene muscles. Subtypes - Neurogenic TOS nTOS : ~95% of cases. Compression of the brachial plexus most commonly lower trunk C8–T1 . Presents with pain, paraesthesia, and weakness in the upper limb. - Venous TOS vTOS : ~4%. Subclavian vein compression; Paget-Schroetter syndrome effort thrombosis . Presents with arm swelling, cyanosis, distended veins. - Arterial TOS aTOS : ~1%. Subclavian artery compression; typically associated with a cervical rib. Presents with ischaemic symptoms, pallor, cold limb. Relevant Anatomy - Thoracic outlet consists of three potential compression zones: 1. Interscalene triangle anterior and middle scalene + first rib 2. Costoclavicular space clavicle + first rib + subclavius 3. Subpectoral/retropectoralis minor space Prevalence & Risk Factors - Estimated prevalence: 3–80 per 1,000 in the general population wide range due to diagnostic variability - Female:male ratio approximately 3.5:1 for nTOS - Peak onset: 20–50 years - Risk factors: cervical rib present in ~0.5–1% of population , anomalous first rib, scalene muscle hypertrophy, poor posture, repetitive overhead activity, trauma especially whiplash , and breast hypertrophy Mechanism Compression results in either direct mechanical compression of neural/vascular structures or ischaemic neuropathy. In nTOS, the lower trunk and medial cord of the brachial plexus C8, T1 are most commonly affected, producing ulnar-distribution symptoms. --- Special Tests > Note: Provocative tests for TOS have historically poor diagnostic accuracy. They are best interpreted in combination cluster approach with patient history. No single test is pathognomonic. Many studies are limited by lack of reference standard. Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Adson's Test 0.79 0.76 3.29 0.28 Low–Moderate High false-positive rate; tests interscalene triangle; reproduces symptoms or abolishes radial pulse Wright's Hyperabduction Test 0.70 0.53 1.49 0.57 Low Tests subpectoral space; pulse obliteration unreliable as occurs in 60–70% asymptomatic individuals Roos Stress Test EAST – Elevated Arm Stress Test 0.82 0.59 2.00 0.30 Moderate 3-minute arm elevation with repeated hand opening/closing; reproducing symptoms more specific than pulse obliteration Costoclavicular Manoeuvre 0.53 0.68 1.66 0.69 Low Tests costoclavicular space; shoulders drawn back and downward Upper Limb Tension Test ULTT1/ULTT4 0.97 0.22 1.24 0.14 Low–Moderate for nTOS High sensitivity; poor specificity; useful for ruling OUT neurogenic component Spurling's Test 0.50 0.86 3.57 0.58 Moderate Differentiates cervical radiculopathy from TOS References: Hooper TL et al. 2010 . J Man Manip Ther ; Gillard J et al. 2001 . J Hand Surg ; Nord KM et al. 2008 review data. Recommended Test Cluster nTOS A positive diagnosis of nTOS requires ≥3 of the following Consensus criteria — Illig KA et al., 2010 : 1. Symptoms consistent with brachial plexus compression 2. Positive provocative testing EAST or ULTT 3. Response to scalene muscle block 4. Exclusion of other diagnoses --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Sudden severe arm pain + pallor + coldness Arterial TOS / acute limb ischaemia Emergency vascular referral 999/A&E Arm swelling + cyanosis + distended veins after exertion Venous TOS / Paget-Schroetter Urgent same-day vascular referral Horner's syndrome ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis Pancoast tumour / apical lung malignancy Urgent CXR + oncology referral Progressive neurological deficit Space-occupying lesion, cord compression Urgent MRI and neurology/neurosurgery Night sweats, unintentional weight loss, haematoptysis Malignancy Urgent GP referral / 2WW pathway Bilateral symptoms with spasticity Cervical myelopathy Urgent neurosurgical referral Cervical rib with pulsatile mass Subclavian artery aneurysm Emergency vascular review --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Assess accessory and physiological movements of the cervicothoracic junction C7–T1, T1–T4 , first rib mobility, and clavicular movement - Pain mapping: distinguish local thoracic outlet tenderness from peripheral neurological patterns - Grade III–IV mobilisations of the first rib posteroanterior, longitudinal caudad may decompress the interscalene triangle - Reassess neurodynamic sensitisation using ULTT after joint mobilisation McKenzie/MDT Framework - Postural assessment: forward head posture, rounded shoulders, thoracic kyphosis increase scalene tension and reduce outlet volume - McKenzie posture correction and extension exercises may reduce compression in costoclavicular and subpectoral spaces - Classify: postural syndrome vs dysfunction vs derangement though TOS rarely fits classical MDT subgroups - Sustained extension/retraction exercises as home exercise programme Pattern Recognition - Lower trunk brachial plexus pattern C8–T1 : medial forearm, ring/little finger paraesthesia, intrinsic hand weakness especially first dorsal interosseous - Differentiate from ulnar neuropathy at the elbow no neck/shoulder component, positive elbow provocation tests - Vascular pattern: positional symptoms, effort-induced, colour/temperature changes --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in TOS --------- ------------- ------ ------------ NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Primary pain outcome DASH / QuickDASH Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder and Hand 10.2 points DASH / 15.9 QuickDASH Upper limb function — well validated for TOS PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 3–5 activities 2.0 points Individualised functional goals UEFI Upper Extremity Functional Index 20-item self-report 9 points Alternative to DASH Global Rating of Change GRC –7 to +7 Likert scale +2 to +3 Perceived overall recovery Grip Strength dynamometry Hand dynamometry kg Variable Objective functional measure for nTOS --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic Criteria There is no validated gold-standard diagnostic test. The Consensus Statement Illig et al., 2010; endorsed by Society for Vascular Surgery recommends a clinical diagnosis based on: 1. Symptoms consistent with brachial plexus compression 2. Positive provocative test battery 3. Exclusion of other diagnoses cervical radiculopathy, rotator cuff pathology, carpal tunnel syndrome Imaging - CXR/Plain X-ray: First-line to identify cervical rib, elongated C7 transverse process, clavicle/first rib anomalies - MRI brachial plexus: Useful to exclude disc prolapse, Pancoast tumour; poor sensitivity for dynamic compression in TOS - CT angiography / Duplex ultrasound: For arterial/venous TOS with positional manoeuvres - Nerve Conduction Studies NCS / EMG: May show medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve abnormality in nTOS ~77–95% sensitivity in true nTOS per Machanic & Bhatt, 2017 ; however, many nTOS cases have normal NCS - Scalene Muscle Block diagnostic : Considered quasi-gold standard for nTOS; >50% symptom relief supports diagnosis Key Systematic Reviews - Povlsen B et al. 2014 . Cochrane Database : Insufficient RCT evidence to determine superiority of any intervention. - Hooper TL et al. 2010 . J Man Manip Ther 18 2 :74–83: Comprehensive review of diagnostic accuracy of clinical tests. --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Cervical radiculopathy C8/T1 Positive Spurling's, cervical movement provocation, dermatomal pattern; MRI cervical spine Ulnar neuropathy at elbow Positive elbow flexion provocation test, Tinel's at cubital tunnel; NCS localises lesion Carpal tunnel syndrome CTS Positive Phalen's/Tinel's at wrist; median nerve distribution; nocturnal symptoms typical Rotator cuff pathology Localised shoulder pain, positive impingement tests Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer , no neurological symptoms Cervical myelopathy Bilateral, lower limb involvement, Lhermitte's sign, pathological reflexes, Hoffman's sign Pancoast tumour Weight loss, haemoptysis, Horner's syndrome, CXR abnormality; urgent investigation required CRPS Type I Autonomic features sweating, colour change , allodynia; follows injury without nerve lesion Peripheral arterial disease Claudication, ankle-brachial index 15 mmHg between arms --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Community Physiotherapy Primary Care : - First-line management for suspected nTOS - Referral via GP or self-referral where available to community MSK physiotherapy - Initial assessment to exclude red flags and vascular/arterial TOS - Waiting times vary: typically 6–18 weeks community MSK in NI check local BHSCT/SEHSCT/NHSCT/SHSCT/WHSCT directory Secondary Care: - Refer to vascular surgery for arterial/venous TOS urgent if acute vascular compromise - Refer to neurology/orthopaedics/spinal surgery if myelopathy suspected - Consider referral to pain management if conservative management fails at 3–6 months - Scalene block may be arranged via pain clinic or vascular surgery NI — typically at RVH Belfast or Altnagelvin Occupational Health: - Workplace assessment and modification for occupational TOS repetitive overhead work, keyboard posture Conservative Management First-line Physiotherapy Evidence Grade B–C : 1. Postural re-education: Correct forward head posture, rounded shoulders, thoracic kyphosis. Evidence shows postural correction reduces outlet narrowing. Lindgren KA, 1997 2. Stretching: Scalene stretching anterior and middle , pectoralis minor stretching, levator scapulae. Hold 30–45 seconds, 3–5 repetitions, 2–3x/day. 3. Strengthening: Scapular stabiliser strengthening lower trapezius, serratus anterior . Progressive resistance programme over 6–8 weeks. 4. Neural mobilisation ULTT-based : Slider and tensioner techniques for brachial plexus. Evidence from Sanders RJ et al. 2010 . 5. First rib mobilisation/manipulation: PA mobilisations of first rib Grade III–IV Maitland . May improve interscalene space. Lindgren, 1997 6. Breathing retraining: Diaphragmatic breathing to reduce accessory breathing muscle scalene overuse. 7. Education: Activity modification, ergonomic advice, avoidance of provocative postures. Programme Duration: Minimum 6–8 weeks conservative physiotherapy before reassessment for further management. Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - NSAIDs: Short-term up to 4 weeks for pain management — ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD with PPI cover. NICE NG59 musculoskeletal pain - Neuropathic agents: Amitriptyline 10–25mg nocte or gabapentin 300mg TDS titrating for neurogenic symptoms — NICE NG173 neuropathic pain in adults - Muscle relaxants: Diazepam 2–5mg TDS short-term only, maximum 4 weeks for scalene spasm — use with caution - Anticoagulation: For venous TOS / Paget-Schroetter — managed by vascular team typically LMWH → warfarin or DOAC - Thrombolysis/anticoagulation: For acute vTOS — vascular surgery decision Onward Referral Criteria Urgent same-day/within 24 hours : - Acute limb ischaemia arterial TOS — 6 Ps: pallor, pulselessness, pain, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold - Acute axillo-subclavian vein thrombosis with significant swelling Urgent within 2 weeks : - Suspected Pancoast tumour Horner's + shoulder/arm pain + weight loss/haemoptysis - Progressive neurological deficit Elective Referral 6–12 weeks : - Failure of ≥3 months conservative physiotherapy - Confirmed cervical rib with ongoing symptoms — vascular surgery for consideration of rib resection/first rib resection - Diagnostic scalene block — pain clinic/vascular surgery referral Surgical Options vascular surgery decision : - First rib resection transaxillary or supraclavicular approach - Scalenectomy - Cervical rib resection - Venous decompression + thrombolysis for vTOS --- Key References 1. content: Overview & Pathophysiology Thoracic radiculopathy refers to pain and/or neurological dysfunction attributable to irritation or compression of a thoracic nerve root as it exits the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramen. It is significantly less common than cervical or lumbar radiculopathy, partly because the thoracic spine has less mobility and is stabilised by the rib cage, resulting in less disc degeneration and foraminal narrowing. Prevalence - Thoracic radiculopathy is rare in isolation — estimated at Critical note: There are very limited validated clinical tests specifically for thoracic radiculopathy. The thoracic spine lacks equivalent validated provocative tests to the SLR lumbar or Spurling's cervical . Diagnosis is primarily clinical dermatomal distribution + symptom pattern supported by MRI and nerve conduction studies. Available Clinical Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level Notes ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- ------- Thoracic Slump Test Limited data one small study Limited data — — Expert opinion Neural tension test for thoracic nerve roots; overpressure in slump + thoracic extension/rotation reproducing dermatomal symptoms Kemp's Test Thoracic Not formally validated Not formally validated — — Expert opinion Extension + ipsilateral rotation + compression at thoracic level; reproduces radicular pain Deep Tendon Reflexes abdominal Limited data Limited data — — Expert opinion Upper abdominal T7–T9 , lower abdominal T10–T12 reflexes — assessed by skin stimulation; loss suggests root pathology Dermatomal Sensation Testing Not validated as standalone Not validated — — Standard practice Pinprick and light touch in thoracic dermatomal pattern; lateralisation and level identification Intercostal Rib Palpation tender nerve in groove Not validated Not validated — — Expert opinion Palpation along inferior rib border reproducing radicular pain in dermatomal distribution Chest Expansion / Deep Breath Provocation Not validated Not validated — — Expert opinion Exacerbation of band-like pain with deep inspiration suggests intercostal nerve/root irritation Key diagnostic tool: MRI thoracic spine — assesses nerve root compression, foraminal stenosis, disc herniation, cord signal change. Nerve conduction studies / EMG: Limited utility for thoracic radiculopathy intercostal muscles technically difficult to assess ; however, paraspinal EMG may show denervation at affected level. NCS for associated limb pathology useful for differential diagnosis. --- Red Flags Red Flag Concern Action ---------- --------- -------- Bilateral band-like thoracic pain + leg weakness + spasticity Myelopathy cord involvement, not purely radiculopathy Emergency MRI + neurosurgical referral Bowel/bladder dysfunction Cord or conus medullaris involvement Emergency neurosurgical referral Thoracic dermatomal pain + known malignancy Metastatic nerve root compression Same-day oncology/MSCC coordinator NICE NG23 Thoracic pain + fever + immunosuppression Herpes zoster, epidural abscess, discitis Urgent: antiviral if vesicular rash; MRI if no rash Vesicular rash in thoracic dermatome Herpes zoster — refer to GP for antiviral within 72 hours GP same-day Thoracic radiculopathy + unexplained weight loss, night sweats Malignancy 2WW GP referral + urgent imaging Thoracic pain + postural hypotension + abdominal pain Aortic aneurysm / dissection 999 Uncontrolled diabetes + thoracic pain + abdominal wall weakness Diabetic thoracic radiculopathy GP referral; exclude other causes first Severe, rapidly progressive neurological deficit Space-occupying lesion; vascular Emergency neurosurgery Thoracic pain in child/adolescent Scheuermann's, tumour, infection Paediatric orthopaedic referral --- Clinical Frameworks Maitland Framework - Assess thoracic spine segmentally: PAIVMs central and unilateral at suspected root level s and adjacent levels - Identify comparable sign: movement or pressure reproducing concordant radicular symptoms - Rib mobility: assess costovertebral/costotransverse joints — may contribute to foraminal narrowing via rib head position - Neural tension: Thoracic Slump test — assess neural mechanosensitivity; distinguish peripheral sensitisation from local mechanical compression - Treatment: Grade I–II oscillatory mobilisations to reduce pain and neural sensitivity; Grade III–IV for foraminal mobility once irritability assessed - Caution: avoid mobilisations that peripheralise symptoms McKenzie/MDT Framework - Perform systematic assessment of directional preference - Thoracic extension commonly reduces discogenic radiculopathy centralisation - Lateral shift correction if present lateral disc herniation with nerve root displacement - If symptoms centralise with extension: progressive extension programme McKenzie Protocol - If extension worsens/peripheralises: flexion or lateral bias assessment; may indicate foraminal pathology - Education: avoidance of sustained flexion postures increase disc/nerve pressure Neurodynamic Framework Butler/Shacklock - Thoracic radiculopathy produces mechanosensitivity of the thoracic nerve roots and intercostal nerves - Slump Sliders grade I : Gentle rhythmic neural mobilisation — alternating cervical flexion/extension with knee extension to create sliding motion of neural tissue - Tensioners: Held-end-range for more established mechanical adherence use with caution in acute phase - Combined with spinal mobilisation to address the joint component --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Use in Thoracic Radiculopathy --------- ------------- ------ ------------------------------- NPRS 0–10 Numeric Pain Rating Scale 2.0 points Primary pain outcome PSFS Patient-Specific Functional Scale 2.0 points Individualised activities affected by radiculopathy ODI Oswestry Disability Index 10 items 10% Disability measure — validated for spinal pain Neuropathic Pain Scale NPS 10-item scale for neuropathic qualities burning, electric, etc. Variable Characterises neuropathic component DN4 Questionnaire 7-item neuropathic screening tool Score ≥4 suggests neuropathic Identifies neuropathic pain component sensitivity 0.83, specificity 0.90 Global Rating of Change GRC –7 to +7 +2 to +3 Recovery perception EQ-5D-5L Generic HRQoL 0.037 NICE-recommended for cost-effectiveness monitoring --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic Approach 1. History: Band-like, dermatomal chest/abdominal pain; unilateral; aggravated by thoracic movement, deep inspiration, cough; may have history of disc herniation, fracture, herpes zoster, diabetes, or malignancy 2. Neurological Examination: Dermatomal sensory change hypoaesthesia/hyperaesthesia , abdominal reflex loss, focal muscle wasting rare 3. MRI Thoracic Spine: Primary investigation — identifies structural cause disc, osteophyte, fracture, tumour ; cord signal change indicates myelopathy change management 4. EMG/NCS: Limited but paraspinal EMG can show denervation at affected levels; rules out more distal nerve pathology 5. Serological: HbA1c diabetic radiculopathy , ESR/CRP infection/inflammatory , PSA/protein electrophoresis malignancy , VZV serology/PCR herpes zoster Herpes Zoster — Critical Consideration - Herpes zoster shingles reactivation in thoracic ganglia is the most common cause of acute thoracic dermatomal pain in adults - Pain typically precedes the vesicular rash by 3–7 days — during this window, presentation is identical to mechanical thoracic radiculopathy - Always ask: previous chickenpox, immunocompromised state, age >60 - If suspected: Same-day GP referral for antiviral prescription aciclovir 800mg 5x/day or valaciclovir 1g TDS for 7 days — most effective within 72 hours of rash onset NICE CKS Shingles - Post-herpetic neuralgia PHN : Persistent pain >3 months after rash resolution; gabapentin/amitriptyline first-line NICE NG173 Diabetic Thoracic Radiculopathy Diabetic Truncal Neuropathy - Rare; presents as unilateral or bilateral abdominal/thoracic pain and weakness - Associated with abdominal wall bulge muscle atrophy T6–T12 - Often presents in middle-aged males with poorly controlled diabetes - Diagnosis: clinical + EMG; MRI normal - Management: glycaemic control; neuropathic pain agents; physiotherapy --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Distinguishing Features ----------- ------------------------ Herpes zoster shingles Dermatomal burning pain ± vesicular rash; VZV serology; older/immunocompromised Thoracic disc herniation MRI confirms; may present with myelopathy cord signs Intercostal neuralgia post-herpetic Post-rash chronic pain; allodynia in dermatomal distribution Costochondritis Anterior chest wall, costo-sternal tenderness, no neurological signs Cardiac ischaemia Central, crushing; ECG/troponin changes; exertional Pulmonary embolism Pleuritic; dyspnoea; tachycardia; D-dimer/CTPA Aortic dissection Sudden severe tearing pain; BP differential; haemodynamic instability Biliary colic / cholecystitis Right upper quadrant, post-prandial; Murphy's sign; ultrasound Peptic ulcer disease Epigastric, food-related; H. pylori; endoscopy Renal colic Loin-to-groin pain; haematuria; non-positional; CT-KUB Pleuritis / pneumonia Fever, cough, reduced air entry; CXR abnormality Thoracic facet joint pain Paraspinal, localised; no dermatomal neurological signs; not true radiculopathy Diabetic truncal neuropathy Diabetes history; abdominal wall weakness; EMG confirms Metastatic spinal disease Night pain; weight loss; bone destruction; known primary Multiple sclerosis Lhermitte's; relapsing-remitting; MRI brain/spine plaques --- Management & Treatment HSC Northern Ireland Pathway Primary Care / Community: - GP assessment to exclude herpes zoster, cardiac, and pulmonary causes — mandatory - Herpes zoster → same-day antiviral prescription from GP - Mechanical thoracic radiculopathy → community physiotherapy referral self-referral or GP referral - Diabetic radiculopathy → GP/diabetology for glycaemic optimisation + physiotherapy - Malignancy/MSCC → NICE NG23 pathway; contact MSCC coordinator NI: Belfast City Hospital oncology Secondary Care: - MRI ordering GP or secondary care : consider for persistent radiculopathy >6 weeks unresponsive to conservative management - Neurosurgical referral: for confirmed compressive pathology on MRI with significant neurological deficit or myelopathy - Pain management: referral for thoracic epidural, nerve root injection, or management programme if conservative management fails at 3 months - NI Pain Management: Belfast City Hospital, Altnagelvin, Daisy Hill Conservative Management Physiotherapy — Evidence Grade C extrapolated from cervical/lumbar radiculopathy evidence : 1. Patient Education: - Natural history: most mechanical radiculopathies improve within 6–12 weeks - Pain neuroscience education PNE : address fear-avoidance, catastrophising - Activity modification: avoid sustained thoracic flexion, heavy lifting during acute phase - Positioning advice: pain-relieving positions, sleep posture 2. Neural Mobilisation: - Thoracic slump sliders — Grade I–II rhythmic neural mobilisation - Intercostal nerve mobilisation: side-lying ipsilateral lateral flexion away + rib spacing - Progress to tensioners when acute irritability settles - Butler DS 2000 — Mobilisation of the Nervous System: neural sliding techniques 3. Manual Therapy: - Grade I–II Maitland mobilisations at affected level pain-dominant/acute phase - Grade III–IV mobilisation for foraminal restriction subacute/chronic phase - Rib mobilisation: costovertebral joints may contribute to foraminal dynamics - Avoid Grade V manipulation in acute radiculopathy with neurological signs 4. Exercise Therapy: - McKenzie extension programme if directional preference confirmed - Thoracic stabiliser strengthening progressive — avoid painful loading - Postural correction: scapular retractors, thoracic extensors 5. TENS / Electrotherapy: - TENS for pain relief in acute neuropathic pain Grade C - Acupuncture: NICE NG193 supports for chronic primary pain Pharmacological NICE-Aligned - NSAIDs: Short-term 2–4 weeks — ibuprofen 400mg TDS or naproxen 500mg BD + PPI NICE NG59 - Neuropathic Pain first-line per NICE NG173 : - Amitriptyline 10mg nocte titrating to 25–75mg — evidence Grade B - Duloxetine 60mg daily titrate from 30mg — evidence Grade B - Gabapentin 300mg TDS titrate — evidence Grade B; note 2019 controlled drug scheduling Schedule 3 - Pregabalin 75–300mg BD — evidence Grade B; also Schedule 3 controlled drug - Antiviral Herpes Zoster : Aciclovir 800mg 5x/day × 7 days OR valaciclovir 1g TDS × 7 days — most effective within 72 hours of rash; reduces PHN risk NICE CKS - Corticosteroids: Oral prednisolone 40mg/day 5-day reducing course — acute severe radiculopathy; limited evidence; off-label - Topical: Lidocaine patches or capsaicin cream 0.025–0.075% for localised neuropathic thoracic pain — NICE NG173 supports as adjunct Interventional Pain Clinic : - Thoracic nerve root injection TNRI / epidural: Methylprednisolone 40–80mg + local anaesthetic — image-guided fluoroscopy or CT ; short-to-medium term pain reduction; limited RCT evidence at thoracic level; risk of cord trauma → high expertise required - Pulsed radiofrequency PRF of dorsal root ganglion: Emerging evidence for refractory radiculopathy NICE IPGS; specialist pain service decision Onward Referral Criteria Emergency: - Myelopathy bilateral signs, cord compression - Bowel/bladder dysfunction - MSCC per NICE NG23 Urgent within 2 weeks : - Progressive neurological deficit - Severe refractory pain with MRI-confirmed compressive lesion - Suspected malignancy Elective 3–6 months : - Failure of conservative management with confirmed compressive pathology - Pain management referral for nerve root injection / PRF consideration - Post-herpetic neuralgia >3 months → pain management NICE NG173 --- Key References 1. title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
summary: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Overview & Pathophysiology Carpal tunnel syndrome CTS is the most common peripheral entrapment neuropathy, affecting 3–6% of the general population and up to 15% of specific occupational groups. It results from compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tu
content: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Overview & Pathophysiology Carpal tunnel syndrome CTS is the most common peripheral entrapment neuropathy, affecting 3–6% of the general population and up to 15% of specific occupational groups. It results from compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel — a rigid fibro-osseous canal bounded by the carpal bones posteriorly and the flexor retinaculum anteriorly. Pathophysiological mechanisms: - Elevated intracarpal tunnel pressure normal ~7 mmHg; symptomatic CTS typically >30 mmHg - Ischaemia of the median nerve epineurium → demyelination → axonal degeneration in severe cases - Mechanical deformation of axons with repetitive wrist flexion/extension - Inflammatory oedema of tenosynovium especially in secondary CTS Risk factors: - Female sex 3:1 female:male ratio ; peak incidence 40–60 years - Pregnancy transient, resolves postpartum in ~50% - Obesity BMI >30 doubles risk - Diabetes mellitus metabolic neuropathy compounds compression - Hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly - Repetitive hand/wrist use vibrating tools, keyboard work — moderate evidence - Previous distal radius fracture Colles' fracture - Haemodialysis amyloid deposition Anatomical variants: Bifid median nerve and persistent median artery increase compression risk and complicate surgical release. --- Special Tests > All values referenced against nerve conduction studies NCS as gold standard unless otherwise stated. Test How to Perform Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ --------------- ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Phalen's Test Passive wrist flexion ≥60° for 60 sec; positive = symptom reproduction 0.68 0.73 2.52 0.44 High meta-analysis, Wilder 2010 Tinel's Sign Percussion over carpal tunnel at wrist crease; positive = paraesthesia in median distribution 0.50 0.77 2.17 0.65 High meta-analysis, Wilder 2010 Durkan's Carpal Compression Test Direct thumb pressure over carpal tunnel for 30 sec; positive = symptom reproduction 0.87 0.90 8.70 0.14 High Durkan 1991; replicated Gonzalez 2002 Hand Elevation Test Both hands elevated above head for 2 min; positive = symptom reproduction 0.75 0.98 37.5 0.26 Moderate Ahn 2001 Flick Sign Patient reports relief of nocturnal symptoms by flicking/shaking the hand 0.93 0.96 23.3 0.07 Moderate Pryse-Phillips 1984 Two-Point Discrimination Static 2PD >6 mm on volar fingertip median distribution 0.33 0.99 33.0 0.68 Moderate severe/advanced CTS Thenar Wasting Visual/palpable atrophy of APB 0.19 0.99 19.0 0.82 Low late sign — indicates axonal loss Clinical note: Durkan's compression test has the best combination of sensitivity and specificity among physical examination tests. The Hand Elevation Test has exceptional specificity 0.98 — a positive result is strongly predictive. The Flick Sign, while poorly studied, has high reported accuracy and is highly patient-specific. Sensory distribution to confirm: Thumb, index, middle finger, radial half of ring finger palmar surface . Dorsal surface of distal phalanges. Sparing of thenar eminence palmar cutaneous branch exits proximal to carpal tunnel . --- Red Flags > Immediate escalation required if any present - Thenar muscle wasting — indicates chronic axonal loss; urgent NCS + surgical referral - Complete median nerve motor loss APB weakness, inability to oppose — urgent referral - Bilateral acute onset — consider cervical myelopathy, systemic neuropathy - Night pain with constitutional symptoms weight loss, fever — exclude malignancy - Rapidly progressive neurological deficit — acute compression e.g., post-fracture haematoma ; surgical emergency - Vascular compromise — pallor, pulselessness — exclude thoracic outlet syndrome or vascular pathology - Signs inconsistent with CTS — consider double crush, brachial neuritis, MS --- Clinical Frameworks CTS-6 Clinical Prediction Rule Graham et al., 2006 — validated diagnostic prediction tool Score 1 point for each present: Item Points ------ -------- Nocturnal numbness 1 Shaking relieves symptoms Flick sign 1 Thenar atrophy 1 Positive Phalen's test 1 Loss of 2-point discrimination >6mm 1 Wrist ratio >0.67 AP:ML diameter 1 Interpretation: - ≥4 points: CTS highly likely LR+ = 18.3 — NCS may be deferred; treat clinically - 3 points: Uncertain — NCS recommended - ≤2 points: CTS unlikely LR– = 0.09 — consider alternative diagnosis NCS/EMG Diagnostic Criteria American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine — AANEM Diagnostic threshold for abnormal NCS: - Median sensory distal latency >3.5 ms 14 cm distance - Median motor distal latency >4.2 ms to APB - Median-ulnar sensory latency difference >0.4 ms ring finger comparison - Median-radial sensory latency difference >0.5 ms thumb comparison Severity grading Stevens 1997 : Grade NCS Findings ------- ------------- Mild Sensory latency prolonged only Moderate Both sensory and motor latency prolonged Severe Absent sensory response ± reduced motor amplitude Extreme Absent sensory and motor responses; denervation on EMG HSC NI NCS Referral: NCS arranged via neurology/neurophysiology; await results before surgical referral in non-urgent cases. Urgent track for progressive motor loss. USS Criteria - Cross-sectional area CSA of median nerve at pisiform level ≥10 mm² = abnormal sensitivity 0.87, specificity 0.83 - CSA ≥12 mm² has higher specificity 0.94 — useful in equivocal cases - USS preferred in pregnancy avoids NCS ; also useful for anatomical variants pre-surgery --- Outcome Measures Measure Description MCID Administration --------- ------------- ------ ---------------- Boston CTS Questionnaire BCTQ 19 items; Symptom Severity Scale SSS, 11 items + Functional Status Scale FSS, 8 items ; 1–5 scale SSS: 1.14 points; FSS: 0.74 points Self-report; 5–10 min DASH Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder, Hand 30-item upper limb disability scale; 0–100 10.2 points Self-report; 10–15 min QuickDASH 11-item abbreviated DASH 15.9 points Self-report; 5 min PRWE Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation 15-item wrist-specific; pain + function subscales; 0–100 14 points Self-report; 5 min Global Rating of Change Single-item; –7 to +7 or similar N/A Clinician/self Recommended for CTS: BCTQ condition-specific, validated for surgical and conservative outcomes + QuickDASH upper limb function . Collect at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, discharge. --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Diagnostic algorithm adapted from NICE NG54 and AANEM guidelines : 1. Clinical diagnosis first — history + physical examination sufficient in classic presentation - Nocturnal paraesthesia, flick sign, median nerve distribution symptoms → high pre-test probability 2. Apply CTS-6 — score ≥4: treat clinically; score 3: NCS; score ≤2: reconsider diagnosis 3. NCS indicated when: - Diagnosis uncertain after clinical assessment - Atypical features e.g., whole-hand numbness, proximal symptoms - Surgical planning baseline severity grading - Medicolegal / occupational health documentation - Failed conservative treatment reassess severity 4. USS as adjunct when: - NCS unavailable or inconclusive - Pregnancy - Anatomical variant suspected - Space-occupying lesion possible lipoma, ganglion, amyloid Diagnostic accuracy of clinical assessment alone: - Experienced clinician with classic history: sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.80 Fowler 2002 - Combined test battery ≥2 positive tests improves specificity substantially --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features Investigation ----------- ---------------------------- --------------- Cervical radiculopathy C6 Neck pain, shoulder/arm radiation, positive Spurling's, symptoms in thumb/index but also dorsal MRI cervical spine; NCS normal distal latencies Pronator teres syndrome Proximal forearm pain, reproduction with resisted pronation, positive Tinel's at pronator, palmar cutaneous branch involved NCS abnormal proximal ; USS forearm Thoracic outlet syndrome Bilateral, positional, Adson's/ROOS test, vascular component Vascular duplex; chest X-ray cervical rib Ulnar neuropathy cubital tunnel Little/ring finger numbness, intrinsic weakness, Froment's sign, Tinel's at elbow NCS ulnar motor/sensory De Quervain's tenosynovitis Radial-sided wrist pain, Finkelstein's positive, no sensory change Clinical; USS Raynaud's phenomenon Colour change white → blue → red , cold trigger, bilateral, no neurological deficit Nailfold capillaroscopy; ANA if secondary suspected Diabetic peripheral neuropathy Stocking-glove distribution, bilateral, distal symmetrical HbA1c; NCS Double crush syndrome CTS + proximal nerve compression C6 radiculopathy ; amplified symptoms Full NCS; MRI spine --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Pathway Conservative Management Splinting strong evidence — Cochrane 2012 : - Wrist splint in neutral position 0° worn nocturnally - 3–6 months trial recommended - Full-time wear more effective than night-only in early stages - Custom thermoplastic vs prefabricated: equivalent outcomes at 1 year Brininger 2007 - NNT for symptom relief: ~3 at 3 months Exercise emerging evidence : - Nerve gliding exercises: equivocal evidence; may reduce need for surgery in mild CTS - Tendon gliding: reduces tendon adhesion, improves flexor tendon excursion - Programme: 5 × daily, 10 repetitions each exercise Activity modification: - Avoid sustained wrist flexion/extension >30° - Vibrating tool exposure reduction - Ergonomic keyboard/mouse assessment HSC OT referral if occupational LLLT/Ultrasound therapy: - Therapeutic ultrasound: some evidence for short-term symptom relief Ebenbichler 1998 ; effect modest - LLLT: insufficient evidence; not routinely recommended Pharmacological Management Corticosteroid injection strong evidence : - Methylprednisolone 20–40 mg + 1% lidocaine, palmar approach at carpal tunnel - NNT for symptom relief at 1 month: 2.0 Armstrong 2004 - Benefit wanes at 3 months; 50% recurrence by 6 months - Maximum 2 injections recommended risk of median nerve damage, tendon rupture - Diagnostic role: short-term response predicts good surgical outcome - Technique: Needle insertion at proximal wrist crease, ulnar to palmaris longus, directed 30° distally; USS-guided preferred to avoid median nerve injury Oral corticosteroids: - Short-term relief prednisone 20 mg/day × 2 weeks : evidence limited - Not recommended for long-term management; significant systemic side effects NSAIDs: No significant evidence for benefit over placebo in CTS; may address coexisting tendinopathy Diuretics in pregnancy : Not recommended; limited evidence Vitamin B6: Insufficient evidence; not recommended Surgical Management Referral Criteria Indications for surgical referral: - Failed ≥6 weeks conservative management splinting ± injection - Moderate–severe NCS findings - Thenar wasting or progressive motor deficit urgent - Patient preference after informed discussion of risks/benefits Surgical options: - Open carpal tunnel release OCTR : gold standard; recurrence <5% at 5 years - Endoscopic carpal tunnel release ECTR : equivalent outcomes; faster return to work; higher risk of transient nerve injury - Mini-open: intermediate approach Post-operative physiotherapy: - Scar desensitisation, grip strengthening, oedema management - Return to light work: 2–4 weeks; heavy manual work: 6–12 weeks NICE Pathway NG54 / CKS - Diagnose clinically; NCS if uncertainty or surgical planning - Offer splinting and/or steroid injection first-line - Refer for surgery if conservative measures fail after 3 months or if motor involvement - Refer urgently if thenar wasting or severe NCS --- Key References 1. The fibro-osseous tunnel at the radial styloid become
content: De Quervain's Tenosynovitis Overview & Pathophysiology De Quervain's tenosynovitis is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, affecting the tendons of abductor pollicis longus APL and extensor pollicis brevis EPB . The fibro-osseous tunnel at the radial styloid becomes thickened and constrictive, producing friction, pain, and swelling with thumb and wrist movement. Pathological mechanism: - Repetitive radial/ulnar deviation with thumb use → mechanical irritation of the tendon sheath - Fibrosis and thickening of the extensor retinaculum - Oedema and mucoid degeneration within the tendon sheath - Anatomical variant: EPB subcompartment present in ~33–50% of patients — missed subcompartment is the most common cause of treatment failure Epidemiology: - Incidence: ~0.5 per 1,000 person-years - Female:male ratio approximately 6–10:1 - Peak age: 30–50 years - Strong association with new mothers infant lifting , repetitive manual work, and racket sports - Prevalence in postpartum women estimated at 17–30% --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Finkelstein's test original: ulnar deviation with thumb adducted in fist 0.89 0.14 1.03 0.79 Moderate Kutsumi et al., 2005 Eichhoff's test patient makes fist around thumb, examiner deviates ulnarly ~0.89 ~0.14 — — Low-moderate commonly conflated with Finkelstein Modified Finkelstein / Wrist Stretch Test WST examiner-administered: passive thumb flexion + ulnar deviation Higher specificity reported — — — Limited Goubau et al., 2014 Tenderness over radial styloid ~0.85 0.55 1.89 0.27 Low Palpable crepitus 0.40 0.90 4.0 0.67 Low > Clinical note: Finkelstein's and Eichhoff's tests are frequently conflated in the literature. The true Finkelstein 1930 involves the examiner grasping the thumb and sharply deviating the wrist ulnarly — this is the higher-sensitivity version. The Eichhoff patient-performed has similar sensitivity but poorer specificity. Both are positive if pain is reproduced over the first dorsal compartment. A positive test in isolation has poor specificity; clinical context is essential. > Modified Finkelstein/WST Goubau et al., 2014 : Passive thumb CMC and MCP joint flexion combined with wrist ulnar deviation — may improve specificity compared to standard Eichhoff. Useful when standard tests produce equivocal results or when differentiating from intersection syndrome. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Urgent onward referral if any of the following are present: - Rapidly progressive swelling with systemic features fever, erythema tracking, rigors → Septic tenosynovitis — surgical emergency - Inability to straighten/bend fingers + fever → septic flexor tenosynovitis Kanavel's signs - Traumatic mechanism with bony tenderness → scaphoid fracture / radial styloid fracture - Suspected inflammatory arthropathy bilateral, symmetrical, morning stiffness >1 hour, raised ESR/CRP - Rapidly enlarging mass at radial wrist → consider ganglion, lipoma, or rarely tumour - Neurovascular compromise paraesthesia, colour change, absent pulse --- Clinical Frameworks Anatomical Variants — Surgical Relevance - EPB subcompartment 33–50% : failure to release this separate compartment = most common surgical failure - Multiple APL slips up to 6 reported : associated with higher recurrence - Ultrasound can identify subcompartmentalisation pre-procedure Intersection Syndrome Differential - Pain 4–6 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle at crossover of APL/EPB and ECRB/ECRL - Palpable/audible crepitus at crossover point - Often seen in rowers, weightlifters Diagnostic Framework 1. Clinical diagnosis history + special tests sufficient for initial management 2. USS confirms if clinical uncertainty or prior to corticosteroid injection 3. MRI reserved for complex/refractory cases or suspected concurrent pathology --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- QuickDASH 16 points Preferred for upper limb function; 11 items; validated in hand/wrist conditions DASH 10–15 points Full 30-item version; higher ceiling for complex cases PRWE Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation 14 points Wrist-specific; pain + function subscales; highly responsive to change in wrist conditions NRS Pain 0–10 2 points Simple, rapid; use alongside functional measure Grip strength Jamar dynamometer 6–7 kg Compare with contralateral; use at baseline and discharge --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Ultrasound USS Findings - First-line imaging when diagnosis uncertain - Findings: thickened tendon sheath >3 mm , hyperaemia on Doppler, peritendinous fluid, EPB subcompartment identification - Sensitivity ~0.87, specificity ~0.89 for confirming de Quervain's Klauser et al., 2002 - USS-guided injection significantly improves corticosteroid placement accuracy vs anatomical landmark injection MRI - Not routinely indicated - Demonstrates tendon sheath thickening, fluid, and tendon changes - Useful if concurrent intra-articular pathology suspected SLAC, STT OA --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Intersection syndrome Pain 4–6 cm proximal; crepitus at crossover point; common in rowers Thumb CMC osteoarthritis Grind test positive; bony enlargement at base of thumb; Eaton-Littler staging Scaphoid fracture Trauma history; anatomical snuffbox tenderness; X-ray ± MRI Wartenberg's syndrome Radial sensory nerve entrapment; burning/paraesthesia dorsal thumb; Tinel's over radial forearm FCR tendinopathy Pain at volar wrist; tenderness over FCR tendon Trigger thumb A1 pulley Triggering/locking; palmar MCP tenderness Extensor tendon tear/subluxation Sudden deformity; localised swelling; positive subluxation test --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Primary care → Physiotherapy/Hand Therapy → Surgical/Injection if required Step 1 — Initial assessment physiotherapy/hand therapy : - Confirm diagnosis; screen red flags - Baseline QuickDASH/PRWE + grip strength - Advise activity modification; avoid provocative loading Step 2 — Conservative management first-line; 4–6 weeks : - Thumb spica splint see below - Activity modification and ergonomic advice - Hand therapy graded loading programme when acute phase resolves Step 3 — Corticosteroid injection if inadequate response at 4–6 weeks, or severe at presentation : - USS-guided injection strongly preferred - Refer to physiotherapist with injection qualification or GP/MSK interface clinic - Document EPB subcompartment injection if USS confirms separate compartment Step 4 — Surgical referral if 2 injections fail, or persistent >6 months : - HSC NI Trauma & Orthopaedics / Hand Surgery waiting list - Include EPB subcompartment status in referral --- Conservative Management Thumb Spica Splinting: - Cochrane Peters-Veluthamaningal et al., 2009 : Low-quality evidence; splinting reduces symptoms in short-term but no RCT demonstrates superiority over other conservative treatments - Thermoplastic thumb spica immobilising wrist in slight extension and CMC in palmar abduction; IP joint free - Wear: 24 hours for acute phase; wean to activity-only as symptoms improve - Duration: 4–6 weeks; reassess at 2–4 weekly intervals Exercise therapy: - Limited high-quality evidence; tendon-gliding exercises, graded loading - Eccentric loading of APL/EPB not well-studied; clinical consensus supports gentle tendon mobilisation post-acute phase Acupuncture/dry needling: Insufficient evidence; not routinely recommended in HSC NI pathway --- Pharmacological Corticosteroid Injection CSI : - Cochrane Peters-Veluthamaningal et al., 2009 : One small RCT 20 participants — CSI superior to splinting alone; combination of CSI + splint may not be superior to CSI alone - Evidence base non-Cochrane : Pooled data suggests ~62–83% success rate with single CSI; second injection adds limited additional benefit - Methylprednisolone acetate 20–40 mg with 1 mL lidocaine; USS-guided - Complication awareness: Skin depigmentation, fat atrophy, and tendon rupture risk rare ; counsel patient NSAIDs: Topical diclofenac gel or oral for acute symptom management; short-course only; follow NICE/HSC NI prescribing guidance --- Onward Referral Criteria Trigger Referral Destination --------- --------------------- Diagnosis unclear / USS required MSK USS radiology Failed conservative 4–6 weeks Injection service qualified physiotherapist / GP-with-SI / MSK interface clinic Failed 2 corticosteroid injections HSC NI Hand Surgery / T&O Red flags septic tenosynovitis Emergency Department — same day Inflammatory arthropathy suspected Rheumatology --- Key References 1. J Hand Surg Am. 2005;30 1 :130–135. 3. Goubau JF, Goubau L, Van Tongel A, et al.
