title: Dupuytren's Contracture
summary: Dupuytren's Contracture Palmar Fibromatosis Overview & Pathophysiology Dupuytren's contracture is a benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar and digital fascia, characterised by progressive thickening and shortening of the palmar aponeurosis, resulting in fixed flexion contractures of the MC
content: Dupuytren's Contracture Palmar Fibromatosis Overview & Pathophysiology Dupuytren's contracture is a benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar and digital fascia, characterised by progressive thickening and shortening of the palmar aponeurosis, resulting in fixed flexion contractures of the MCP and PIP joints. Named after Baron Guillaume Dupuytren 1831 , though Plater described it earlier in 1614. Pathological mechanism: - Myofibroblast proliferation within palmar fascia Skoog's pretendinous bands, spiral bands, natatory ligaments, Grayson's ligaments - Three histological phases: proliferative → involutional → residual - Pretendinous cord → MCP contracture; spiral cord Cleland's, Grayson's, pretendinous, lateral digital sheet → PIP contracture + neurovascular bundle displacement - Spiral cord displaces NVB medially, superficially, and proximally — critical surgical consideration Epidemiology: - Prevalence: ~2–30% in Western European populations; highest in Northern Europe Scandinavia, Scotland, Ireland, Northern England - Northern Ireland prevalence estimated 10–15% in those >65 years — clinically significant for HSC NI - Male:female ratio 6–10:1 young ; equalises with age - Peak presentation: 50–60 years males ; 60–70 years females - Ring finger most commonly affected 70–80% , followed by little finger Risk Factors Established : Risk Factor Evidence Notes ------------- ---------- ------- Northern European ancestry Strong genetic Autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance Age >50 years Strong Risk increases linearly with age Male sex Strong — Diabetes mellitus Moderate OR ~3–4 Bilateral; radial digits; more aggressive Epilepsy / anticonvulsant use Moderate phenobarbitone historically Possibly drug-mediated Alcohol use disorder Moderate Liver fibrosis association Smoking Moderate Microvascular ischaemia proposed Manual labour / vibration Weak-moderate Contested; some evidence for repetitive hand trauma HIV infection Emerging — Diathesis Hueston : Aggressive phenotype — bilateral disease, ectopic involvement Peyronie's, Ledderhose/plantar , radial digit involvement, strong family history, early onset. Higher recurrence post-treatment. --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Hueston tabletop test patient cannot lay palm flat on table ~0.95 ~0.90 ~9.5 ~0.06 Low-moderate widely used; limited formal validation Passive joint angle assessment goniometry Reference standard — — — Moderate Palpable cord in palm/digit ~0.90 ~0.85 6.0 0.12 Low Skin pitting/tethering ~0.70 ~0.90 7.0 0.33 Low > Diagnosis is clinical — history of progressive painless contracture + palpable cord + skin changes. Imaging not required for diagnosis. > Hueston tabletop test: Positive when patient cannot simultaneously lay palm and fingers flat on a table surface. Indicates ≥30° combined MCP/PIP contracture and is commonly used as the surgical referral threshold . --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Expedited onward referral if: - Rapidly progressive contracture weeks, not months/years → consider rare desmoplastic fibroma or sarcoma; request USS ± MRI - Painful, inflamed cord with systemic features → exclude infection or acute inflammatory condition - Neurovascular compromise digital paraesthesia, colour change, absent pulse → urgent surgical assessment - Locked digit in acute flexion with trauma history → exclude fracture/dislocation - Child/adolescent with progressive hand contracture → consider knuckle pads alone vs juvenile Dupuytren; rare — paediatric orthopaedic referral --- Clinical Frameworks Tubiana Staging System Stage Total Passive Extension Deficit TPED Description ------- --------------------------------------- ------------- N 0° Palmar nodule/cord only; no contracture Stage I 0–45° Mild; MCP predominantly Stage II 45–90° Moderate; MCP + PIP involvement Stage III 90–135° Severe; significant PIP contracture Stage IV >135° Very severe; fixed contracture; DIP may be involved > TPED = sum of extension deficit at MCP + PIP + DIP for the affected ray. Guides surgical planning and outcome benchmarking. Surgical Referral Threshold HSC NI - MCP contracture ≥30° or PIP contracture ≥15° any degree of PIP contracture is functionally significant - Positive tabletop test - Progressive disease documented over 3–6 months Anatomorphological Types - Nodular: Early; may be painful; proliferative phase - Cord: Band-like; main driver of contracture - Diffuse: Skin involvement; poor prognosis; higher recurrence --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- QuickDASH 16 points Primary functional outcome measure DASH 10–15 points Full version for complex presentations URAM scale Unité Rhumatologique des Affections de la Main 5 points Dupuytren-specific PRO; validated; 9 items Goniometry passive extension deficit 10° Primary objective measure; document per joint, per digit Hueston tabletop test Pass/fail Binary; document at each review PRWE 14 points Less Dupuytren-specific; use QuickDASH/URAM preferentially --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging - USS: Not required for diagnosis; useful to identify cord anatomy, NVB position pre-procedure needle aponeurotomy - MRI: Reserved for atypical cases or suspected malignancy aggressive/rapidly progressive - No routine imaging indicated for established Dupuytren's Histopathology - Rarely required; if diagnosis uncertain e.g., excludes fibrosarcoma - Alpha-smooth muscle actin α-SMA positive myofibroblasts — hallmark --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Palmar ganglion Fluctuant; transilluminates; no contracture; USS confirms Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath Firm, lobulated nodule; USS — vascular; no cord Fibroma/fibrosarcoma Rapidly progressive; painful; USS ± MRI Trigger finger Active triggering/locking; A1 pulley tenderness; no palmar cord Ulnar nerve palsy Intrinsic minus hand; clawing 4th/5th digits; motor/sensory deficit Camptodactyly Congenital; painless PIP flexion; no palmar cord; young onset Knuckle pads Thickening over PIP/MCP dorsum; no contracture; Dupuytren diathesis association Ledderhose disease plantar fibromatosis Ectopic manifestation; plantar nodules; part of Dupuytren diathesis --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Monitoring → Hand therapy conservative → Procedural/Surgical intervention when threshold met Step 1 — Baseline Assessment: - Tubiana staging + goniometry per joint/digit - Hueston tabletop test document pass/fail - QuickDASH + URAM scale - Risk factor screening; document diathesis features Step 2 — Watchful waiting Stage N–I; not functionally limiting : - Reassure re: benign nature; lifestyle advice alcohol, smoking - Review at 6–12 months or if progression - Educate: "not cured by treatment; recurrence is expected" Step 3 — Hand therapy pre- and post-procedural : - Pre-procedural: Serial static night extension splinting NOT evidence-based as standalone; do not delay referral - Post-procedural: Extension splinting + hand therapy exercise programme is essential for all interventions - Post-collagenase/NA: Immediate hand therapy; night splinting 3–6 months Step 4 — Procedural Intervention MCP ≥30° or PIP ≥15°, or functionally significant : - Discuss all options; patient choice and comorbidities guide selection - Refer HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery --- Conservative Management Splinting alone, non-post-procedural : - No high-quality RCT evidence that splinting alone alters disease progression or prevents contracture recurrence - Night extension splinting is appropriate post-procedure; not as primary disease-modifying treatment - Radiotherapy low-dose, <30 Gy : May slow progression at nodular stage Stage N–I ; limited UK availability; experimental in HSC NI --- Interventional Options — Comparative Evidence Intervention Procedure Initial Correction Recurrence at 5 years Notes --- --- --- --- --- Needle fasciotomy NA/PNA Percutaneous needle division of cord; outpatient; LA 75–80% MCP; 50–60% PIP ~50–65% MCP ; higher PIP Rapid recovery; lowest cost; office procedure; suitable elderly/comorbid Collagenase injection Xiapex / CCH Clostridium histolyticum collagenase; 2-visit: inject Day 1, manipulate Day 2 ~75–90% MCP; ~40–60% PIP ~47–66% at 5 years CORDLESS study NICE-approved; withdrawn UK market 2020 commercial ; may return; discuss if available Limited fasciectomy LF Surgical excision of diseased fascia; regional/GA; day case ~85–95% MCP; ~70–80% PIP ~20–40% at 5–10 years Gold standard; higher complication rate 10–15% ; nerve/vessel risk; longer recovery Dermofasciectomy Fasciectomy + skin graft Z-plasties ; recurrent/diathesis cases Similar to LF ~8–10% at 5 years Lowest recurrence; highest morbidity; reserved for recurrence or severe diathesis Key comparative evidence: - CORD-I & CORD-II RCTs Hurst et al., 2009; Gilpin et al., 2011 : Collagenase CCH vs placebo — CCH significantly superior; 64% achieved full correction MCP - CORDLESS study Peimer et al., 2013 : Long-term follow-up — 47% recurrence ≥20° contracture at 5 years post-CCH - Cochrane Zhao et al., 2022 : Needle fasciotomy vs limited fasciectomy — LF achieves superior correction; NA has shorter recovery and fewer complications; recurrence higher with NA - van Rijssen et al. 2012 : RCT — NA vs LF; at 5 years, recurrence 85% NA vs 21% LF for MCP joints --- Onward Referral Criteria Trigger Referral Destination --------- --------------------- MCP ≥30° contracture HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery Any PIP contracture affecting function HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery Positive tabletop test HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery Diathesis features + progressive disease HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery early discussion Rapidly progressive / atypical mass MSK Radiology USS ± MRI → Orthopaedics --- Key References 1. Dupuytren G. Leçons orales de clinique chirurgicale. Paris; 1832. 2. Tubiana R, Michon J, Thomine JM. Scheme for the assessment of deformities in Dupuytren's disease. Surg Clin North Am. 1968;48 5 :979–984. 3. Hueston JT. The table top test. Hand. 1982;14 1 :100–103. 4. Hurst LC, Badalamente MA, Hentz VR, et al. Injectable collagenase clostridium histolyticum for Dupuytren's contracture. N Engl J Med. 2009;361 10 :968–979. 5. Peimer CA, Blazar P, Coleman S, et al. Dupuytren contracture recurrence following treatment with collagenase clostridium histolyticum CORDLESS study . J Hand Surg Am. 2013;38 12 :2333–2340. 6. van Rijssen AL, ter Linden H, Werker PM. Five-year results of a randomized clinical trial on treatment in Dupuytren's disease: percutaneous needle fasciotomy versus limited fasciectomy. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012;129 2 :469–477. 7. Zhao JZ, Hadley S, Floyd E, et al. The impact of collagenase clostridium histolyticum introduction on Dupuytren treatment trends. J Hand Surg Am. 2016;41 10 :1007–1012. 8. Nanchahal J, Ball C, Davidson D, et al. Intervention to reduce the development and progression of Dupuytren's disease: SMART Small Manipulation And Radiotherapy Trial multicentre RCT. Health Technol Assess. 2022;26 26 . 9. Hindocha S, McGrouther DA, Bhatt R. The prevalence of Dupuytren's disease in patients with diabetes mellitus versus without diabetes. title: Scaphoid Fracture

headings: Ottawa Wrist Rules Derived Criteria — Scaphoid Application
content: Overview & Pathophysiology Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal bone fractures, accounting for approximately 60–70% of all carpal fractures and 2–7% of all fractures. They typically result from a fall on an outstretched hand FOOSH with the wrist in dorsiflexion and radial deviation, transmitting compressive force through the thenar eminence to the scaphoid waist. Anatomical Vulnerability The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply predominantly from the radial artery entering distally through the dorsal ridge. The proximal pole receives no direct blood supply, making proximal pole fractures particularly vulnerable to avascular necrosis AVN . AVN occurs in up to 30–40% of untreated or delayed-diagnosis fractures of the proximal pole. Fracture Classification Herbert & Fisher - Type A: Stable acute fractures A1: tubercle fracture; A2: incomplete waist fracture - Type B: Unstable acute fractures B1: distal oblique; B2: complete waist; B3: proximal pole; B4: trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation - Type C: Delayed union - Type D: Established non-union D1: fibrous; D2: pseudarthrosis Epidemiology - Peak incidence: males aged 20–30 years - Annual incidence: ~5 per 10,000 population UK - Up to 20% of scaphoid fractures are occult on initial plain X-ray - Delayed diagnosis is associated with non-union up to 12% waist fractures if missed and AVN --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Anatomical snuffbox tenderness 0.90 0.40 1.50 0.25 Moderate Parvizi et al. 1998; Duckworth et al. 2012 Scaphoid compression test longitudinal compression of thumb 0.80 0.48 1.54 0.42 Moderate Parvizi et al. 1998 Scaphoid tubercle tenderness 0.82 0.57 1.91 0.32 Moderate Grover 1996 Pain on supination against resistance 0.74 0.76 3.08 0.34 Low–Moderate Freeland 1989 Combined 3-test rule snuffbox + compression + tubercle 0.98 0.40 1.63 0.05 Moderate Unsworth et al. 2020 Clinical Notes on Tests Anatomical Snuffbox Tenderness: High sensitivity 0.90 makes it an excellent screening test — a negative test is clinically useful −LR 0.25 . However, poor specificity 0.40 means many false positives; should not be used in isolation to confirm fracture. Scaphoid Compression Test: Apply longitudinal compression along the axis of the thumb toward the scaphoid. Positive = pain at the anatomical snuffbox or radial wrist. Lower sensitivity than snuffbox tenderness; adds specificity when combined. Combined 3-Test Rule: If all three tests are negative, fracture is unlikely −LR 0.05, post-test probability ⚠️ Urgent / Do Not Miss - Perilunate dislocation / trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation — Carpal malalignment on X-ray; median nerve compromise; requires emergency orthopaedic referral - Open fracture — Requires same-day surgical review - Median nerve symptoms acute carpal tunnel syndrome post-injury — Sensory loss in median nerve distribution, thenar weakness; urgent decompression may be required - Vascular compromise — Skin changes, absence of digital pulses post-injury - Pathological fracture — Low-energy mechanism; consider bone metastasis, primary bone tumour, or metabolic bone disease osteoporosis workup in older patients - Child/adolescent — Growth plate involvement; paediatric orthopaedic referral Non-union risk factors refer urgently : - Proximal pole fracture - Displaced fracture >1 mm gap or >10° humpback deformity - Delayed presentation >4 weeks - Previous non-union --- Clinical Frameworks Ottawa Wrist Rules Derived Criteria — Scaphoid Application The original Ottawa Wrist Rules were developed for wrist fracture detection post-FOOSH. Validated sensitivity for any wrist fracture: ~98%. For scaphoid specifically: Image if ANY of the following: 1. Point tenderness over anatomical snuffbox 2. Point tenderness over scaphoid tubercle 3. Painful supination against resistance 4. Age 65 years with mechanism of FOOSH 5. Neurovascular deficit Clinical Prediction Rule Duckworth et al. 2012 — BSSH guidance : - Negative snuffbox + negative compression + negative tubercle → fracture extremely unlikely NPV ~98–100% - Any positive → proceed to imaging regardless of plain X-ray result Injury Grading — DISI Deformity A scapholunate angle >60° on lateral wrist X-ray suggests DISI Dorsal Intercalated Segment Instability associated with ligamentous instability — requires specialist review. --- Outcome Measures Measure Full Name MCID Notes --------- ----------- ------ ------- DASH Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand 10.2 points 30-item PRO; validated for wrist fractures QuickDASH Quick DASH 11 items 15.9 points Strong correlation with DASH; preferred in busy clinical settings PRWE Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation 11.5 points Wrist-specific; highly responsive to change post-fracture; recommended for monitoring scaphoid outcomes VAS Pain Visual Analogue Scale 1.5–2.0 cm Use alongside functional measures Grip strength Dynamometry Jamar ≥10% deficit vs contralateral Functional endpoint; target ≥80% contralateral at discharge PRWE is recommended as the primary outcome measure for scaphoid fractures in research and clinical audit settings MacDermid et al. 1998 . --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Imaging Pathway MRI: - Gold standard for occult scaphoid fracture detection - Sensitivity 0.88–1.00; Specificity 0.97–1.00 Yin et al. 2010 — systematic review - Recommended within 72 hours if X-ray negative but clinical suspicion high - NICE guidance NG38, 2016 : Offer MRI within 72 hours; if unavailable, CT acceptable; bone scintigraphy third-line CT: - Sensitivity 0.72–0.93; Specificity 0.99 Brydie & Raby 2003 - Superior to MRI for cortical detail and surgical planning - Preferred for fracture characterisation once diagnosed displacement, comminution, union monitoring Bone Scintigraphy: - High sensitivity ~1.00 but low specificity ~0.60 — significant false-positive rate - Reserved for when MRI and CT are both unavailable NICE NG38 Plain X-ray Limitations: - Sensitivity for scaphoid fracture: 0.54–0.70 on initial films Yin et al. 2010 - Up to 20% missed on day 1; repeat X-ray at 10–14 days improves but does not replace MRI --- Differential Diagnosis Condition Key Distinguishing Features Investigation ----------- ---------------------------- --------------- Distal radius fracture Tenderness over distal radius not snuffbox ; visible on X-ray Plain X-ray Scapholunate ligament injury Scapholunate gap >3 mm on PA X-ray "Terry Thomas sign" ; stress views X-ray stress views; MR arthrography De Quervain's tenosynovitis Positive Finkelstein's test; tenderness over 1st extensor compartment Clinical; USS Radial styloid fracture Tenderness at radial styloid; fracture on X-ray Plain X-ray Trapezium fracture Tenderness at CMC joint; rare CT Carpal tunnel syndrome acute Median nerve symptoms; Tinel/Phalen positive Clinical + nerve conduction TFCC injury Ulnar-sided pain; fovea sign positive; piano key test MRI / MR arthrography Wrist sprain Diffuse tenderness; no specific bony point tenderness; normal imaging Diagnosis of exclusion --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Pathway Emergency Department ED : 1. Clinical assessment + Ottawa Wrist Rules application 2. Plain X-ray scaphoid series: PA, lateral, oblique, scaphoid view 3. If fracture confirmed: immobilise in thumb spica plaster/splint; refer to fracture clinic next available, within 5 working days 4. If X-ray negative but clinical suspicion high: - Immobilise in thumb spica backslab - Refer urgently for MRI within 72 hours via fracture clinic or radiology direct access - Written safety-netting advice return if symptoms worsen 5. If perilunate dislocation suspected: same-day orthopaedic review Fracture Clinic HSC NI Trust : - Review with MRI/CT results - Classify fracture Herbert & Fisher - Decision: conservative vs surgical management - Physiotherapy referral: post-immobilisation rehabilitation Conservative Management Evidence-Based Indications: Non-displaced 1 mm step-off or >10° humpback deformity on CT - Proximal pole fracture high AVN risk - Non-union at 12 weeks - Athlete/manual worker preference for earlier return to activity - Perilunate fracture-dislocation emergency Procedure: Percutaneous or open cannulated headless compression screw fixation e.g., Herbert screw, Acutrak Post-surgical physio: As conservative Phase 1–3, typically commencing 2 weeks post-op Onward Referral Criteria Physiotherapy → Orthopaedics - Failure to progress with conservative management at 12 weeks - Development of AVN pain, restricted ROM, X-ray/MRI changes - Non-union on imaging - Complex regional pain syndrome CRPS signs --- Key References 1. Yin ZG, Zhang JB, Kan SL, Wang XG. Diagnosing suspected scaphoid fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2010;468 3 :723–734. doi:10.1007/s11999-009-1106-6 2. Duckworth AD, Ring D, McQueen MM. Assessment of the suspected fracture of the scaphoid. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 2011;93 6 :713–719. 3. Dias JJ, Dhukaram V, Abhinav A, Bhowal B, Bhatt RA. Clinical and radiological outcome of cast immobilisation versus surgical treatment of acute scaphoid fractures at a mean follow-up of 93 months. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 2008;90 7 :899–905. 4. NICE Guideline NG38. Fractures non-complex : assessment and management. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. 2016. Available at: www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng38 5. title: TFCC Injury (Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex)
summary: TFCC Injury Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex Overview & Pathophysiology The Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex TFCC is the primary stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint DRUJ and the ulnocarpal joint , and acts as a load-transmitter distributing approximately 20% of axial load across the ulnar si
content: TFCC Injury Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex Overview & Pathophysiology The Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex TFCC is the primary stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint DRUJ and the ulnocarpal joint , and acts as a load-transmitter distributing approximately 20% of axial load across the ulnar side of the wrist Palmer & Werner, 1984 . Injury is a common cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain. Anatomical components: - Articular disc fibrocartilage : Central avascular zone; periphery is vascular - Dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments: Deep fibres insert at fovea primary DRUJ stabilisers ; superficial fibres insert at ulnar styloid - Ulnotriquetral UT ligament - Ulnolunate UL ligament - Extensor carpi ulnaris ECU subsheath - Meniscus homologue Vascular anatomy surgical relevance : - Central disc = avascular; poor healing potential; debridement is treatment of choice - Peripheral 1–2 mm = vascular; repair is feasible - Deep fibres at fovea = critical stabilisers; foveal detachment = DRUJ instability Mechanism of injury: - Traumatic Palmer Type I : Fall on outstretched hand; forceful forearm rotation; axial loading with ulnar deviation; DRUJ dislocation; distal radius fracture associated - Degenerative Palmer Type II : Repetitive loading; ulnar impaction syndrome; abutment of ulnar head against TFCC/lunate/triquetrum - Ulnar variance: Positive ulnar variance increases load through TFCC; associated with degenerative tears Epidemiology: - Common cause of ulnar wrist pain; exact incidence unclear - Wrist arthroscopy series: TFCC tears found in ~35% of arthroscopies for wrist pain; 53% in distal radius fractures - Degenerative Type II tears increasingly common >40 years; frequent incidental finding --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Fovea sign deep palpation between FCU tendon and ulnar styloid in anatomical snuffbox equivalent; positive if reproduces deep ulnar wrist pain 0.95 0.87 7.3 0.06 Moderate Tay et al., 2007 Press test patient presses up from chair arms using wrists; positive if ulnar wrist pain reproduced 1.00 0.64 2.8 0.00 Moderate Lester et al., 1995 — caution: high sensitivity, poor specificity Ulnar grind test axial compression + rotation of wrist in ulnar deviation; positive if pain reproduced at DRUJ/ulnocarpal ~0.54 ~0.67 1.6 0.69 Low Nakamura et al. DRUJ ballottement piano key test dorsopalmar stress of ulnar head vs radius; positive if laxity, pain, or crepitus vs contralateral ~0.66 ~0.64 1.8 0.53 Low-moderate Ulnocarpal stress test maximal ulnar deviation + axial compression + forearm rotation; positive = ulnar pain ~0.64 ~0.65 1.8 0.55 Low ECU synergy test resisted index finger abduction while palpating ECU; positive if ECU pain/weakness ~0.82 ~0.81 4.3 0.22 Low-moderate differentiate ECU > Clinical interpretation: The fovea sign has the best combined sensitivity/specificity and should be the primary provocative test. Press test is highly sensitive rules out if negative but non-specific. Use a cluster: fovea sign + press test + piano key for DRUJ stability + active forearm rotation assessment. > DRUJ instability assessment: Compare ballottement laxity bilaterally in neutral, pronation, and supination. Laxity in all positions = physiological; laxity in only one = pathological. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Urgent onward referral if: - Acute DRUJ dislocation inability to pronate/supinate; prominent ulnar head; post-trauma → Emergency Department / Orthopaedics same day - Galeazzi fracture-dislocation distal radius fracture + DRUJ disruption → Orthopaedic emergency - Essex-Lopresti injury radial head fracture + interosseous membrane disruption + DRUJ injury → Orthopaedic emergency - Vascular compromise absent ulnar pulse; Allen's test positive for ulnar artery → Vascular surgery - Acute ulnar nerve deficit → Urgent neurological assessment - Suspected carpal instability perilunate dislocation; scapholunate dissociation on plain X-ray → Urgent orthopaedic referral --- Clinical Frameworks Palmer Classification Type I — Traumatic: Subtype Lesion --------- -------- IA Central perforation articular disc — avascular; debridement IB Ulnar avulsion ± ulnar styloid fracture — peripheral; can repair; foveal detachment = DRUJ instability IC Volar avulsion ulnocarpal ligaments ID Radial avulsion ± sigmoid notch fracture Type II — Degenerative Ulnar Impaction Syndrome : Subtype Lesion --------- -------- IIA TFCC wear — no perforation IIB TFCC wear + lunate/ulnar chondromalacia IIC TFCC perforation + chondromalacia IID TFCC perforation + chondromalacia + LT ligament tear IIE TFCC perforation + chondromalacia + LT tear + ulnocarpal arthritis > Palmer classification guides arthroscopic management — Type IA: debridement; Type IB: repair; Type IIE: ulnar shortening osteotomy may be required. Diagnostic Algorithm 1. Ulnar-sided wrist pain + mechanism + provocative tests 2. Plain X-ray bilateral neutral PA : assess ulnar variance; exclude fracture 3. If diagnosis unclear: MRI wrist ± arthrography 4. If surgical management planned: MR arthrography gold standard non-invasive ; wrist arthroscopy definitive --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- PRWE Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation 14 points Best validated wrist-specific PRO; recommended for TFCC QuickDASH 16 points Upper limb function; validated DASH 10–15 points Full version for complex cases Grip strength Jamar dynamometer 6–7 kg Compare bilaterally; DRUJ injury commonly reduces grip ~25–30% Forearm rotation goniometry 10° Pronation/supination; document degrees NRS Pain 2 points Baseline and review MAYO wrist score — Surgeon-used; pain, function, ROM, grip; 100-point scale --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Plain Radiography - Bilateral neutral PA wrists: Assess ulnar variance positive >2 mm associated with degenerative TFCC - Assess DRUJ congruence; carpal alignment Gilula's arcs - Pronated-grip PA view increases positive variance by ~1–2 mm MRI Wrist - Standard MRI: Sensitivity 0.71–0.86, specificity 0.67–0.89 for TFCC tears meta-analysis, Saupe et al. - 3T superior to 1.5T; dedicated wrist coil essential - Identifies peripheral vs central tears, associated pathology LT ligament, ulnocarpal MR Arthrography MRA - MRA: Sensitivity ~0.84–0.93, specificity ~0.93–0.95 for full-thickness TFCC tears - Gold standard non-invasive investigation — preferred pre-arthroscopy - Intra-articular gadolinium radiocarpal injection ; contrast leak into DRUJ confirms perforation - Differentiates partial from full-thickness; better assessment of foveal detachment CT / CT Arthrography - DRUJ geometry assessment pre-operative; instability evaluation - CT arthrography: comparable sensitivity to MRA; useful when MRI contraindicated Wrist Arthroscopy Definitive - Gold standard for diagnosis and treatment - Allows direct visualisation of all TFCC components; dynamic assessment; treatment in same setting - Trampoline test probe bounce on articular disc evaluates tension; abnormal if disc lax --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- ECU tendinopathy/subluxation ECU synergy test; pain dorsal ulnar; ECU groove tenderness; USS Lunotriquetral LT ligament tear Shuck test LT ballottement ; ulnar dorsal pain; MRA Ulnocarpal impaction syndrome Positive ulnar variance; degenerative; X-ray; axial loading pain Pisotriquetral arthritis Pisiform tenderness; pain on radial deviation + compression; X-ray Ulnar styloid non-union Post-fracture; X-ray; tenderness at styloid Hypothenar hammer syndrome Vascular; repetitive hypothenar trauma; abnormal Allen's test; duplex USS Guyon's canal syndrome Ulnar nerve compression; sensory loss 4th/5th digits; Tinel's De Quervain's tenosynovitis Radial-sided pain; Finkelstein positive Distal radius malunion Post-fracture; radiological --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Primary care / Physiotherapy → MSK imaging → Specialist Hand Surgery referral for surgical cases Step 1 — Initial Assessment: - Confirm ulnar-sided wrist pain; mechanism; provocative tests fovea sign, press test, piano key - Palmer classification clinical working diagnosis - Baseline PRWE + QuickDASH + grip strength + forearm rotation goniometry - Plain X-ray bilateral PA wrists — request if not done Step 2 — Conservative management 6–8 weeks; appropriate for most Type I uncomplicated, Type II non-surgical : - DRUJ immobilisation Munster cast or rigid DRUJ orthosis 6–8 weeks for acute peripheral tears - Activity modification: avoid forearm rotation under load; gripping - Graded hand therapy after immobilisation Step 3 — Physiotherapy programme post-immobilisation or degenerative : - DRUJ stabilisation exercises; ECU strengthening - Forearm rotation restoration; proprioception training - Theraband graded resisted pronation/supination - Typical programme: 6–12 weeks physiotherapy post-immobilisation Step 4 — MRI/MRA if not improving at 8–12 weeks conservative, or acute high-energy mechanism : - Request via MSK interface / T&O outpatient - Guide surgical decision-making Step 5 — Surgical Referral DRUJ instability; failed conservative; acute Type IB foveal detachment : - HSC NI Hand Surgery / Trauma & Orthopaedics - Include ulnar variance, Palmer type clinical , MRI findings in referral --- Conservative Management Immobilisation: - Acute peripheral tears Type IB : Below-elbow Munster cast or custom rigid DRUJ orthosis in neutral rotation × 6–8 weeks - Evidence: Minimal RCT data; case series demonstrate 60–75% satisfactory outcomes with conservative management of peripheral tears - Type IA central : Conservative has lower success; shorter immobilisation 2–4 weeks then physiotherapy; arthroscopic debridement if persistent Physiotherapy: - ECU subsheath repair / DRUJ stabilisation via dynamic muscle exercise - Evidence limited case series ; consensus recommends graded loading programme - Duration: 6–12 weeks post-immobilisation Corticosteroid Injection: - USS-guided injection into radiocarpal joint ± DRUJ - Limited specific evidence; may reduce pain in degenerative Type II - Refer to qualified injection physiotherapist / GP-with-SI --- Surgical Options Procedure Indication Outcomes Evidence Level ----------- ------------ ---------- ---------------- Arthroscopic debridement Type IA central tear ~78–88% good/excellent at 2 years Moderate case series Arthroscopic peripheral repair Type IB peripheral tear; DRUJ stable ~80–85% good/excellent; return to sport/work Moderate case series Foveal reattachment open or arthroscopic Type IB with foveal detachment + DRUJ instability ~80–90% DRUJ stability restored Moderate Ulnar shortening osteotomy USO Type II degenerative + positive ulnar variance ~75–90% pain improvement Moderate DRUJ reconstruction Chronic instability; failed repair; salvage Variable Low --- Onward Referral Criteria Trigger Referral Destination --------- --------------------- Acute DRUJ dislocation / Galeazzi / Essex-Lopresti Emergency Department — same day DRUJ instability confirmed clinical HSC NI Hand Surgery — urgent 2 weeks Failed conservative ≥8–12 weeks MSK Radiology MRA → Hand Surgery Positive ulnar variance + degenerative symptoms Hand Surgery / MSK interface discussion Vascular compromise Vascular Surgery — urgent --- Key References 1. title: Thumb CMC Osteoarthritis (Trapeziometacarpal OA)
summary: Thumb CMC Osteoarthritis Trapeziometacarpal / First CMC OA Overview & Pathophysiology Thumb carpometacarpal CMC osteoarthritis — also termed trapeziometacarpal TMC or basal joint OA — is the second most common site of symptomatic OA in the hand after the DIP joint. It results from progressive articu
headings: Thumb CMC Osteoarthritis Trapeziometacarpal / First CMC OA
content: Thumb CMC Osteoarthritis Trapeziometacarpal / First CMC OA Overview & Pathophysiology Thumb carpometacarpal CMC osteoarthritis — also termed trapeziometacarpal TMC or basal joint OA — is the second most common site of symptomatic OA in the hand after the DIP joint. It results from progressive articular cartilage degeneration at the trapeziometacarpal joint, with secondary involvement of the scaphotrapezial joint in advanced cases. Anatomy & Biomechanics: - The trapeziometacarpal joint is a biconcave-convex saddle joint with inherent bony incongruity - Primary stabiliser: anterior oblique ligament beak ligament / volar AOL — deep fibres critical - Instability of the beak ligament allows dorsoradial subluxation of the 1st metacarpal — characteristic finding in Eaton Stage II+ - Pinch loads generate joint reactive forces of 12× applied force at the CMC joint — explains vulnerability with repetitive fine grip Pathological sequence: 1. Volar AOL laxity → dorsoradial subluxation of 1st MC 2. Progressive cartilage loss → subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation 3. Adduction contracture of 1st web space adaptive shortening of adductor pollicis 4. Compensatory MCP hyperextension "shoulder sign" or "Z-deformity" 5. Advanced: scaphotrapezial involvement; STT OA Epidemiology: - Radiographic prevalence: ~25–35% women and ~10–15% men >50 years Haara et al., 2004 - Symptomatic OA: ~7–15% in adults >40 years - Female predominance 5–10:1 vs males - Strong correlation with age, female sex, post-menopausal status, prior thumb injury, hypermobility, occupational pinching --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Grind test axial compression + circumduction of 1st MC at CMC; positive = pain ± crepitus 0.53 0.80 2.65 0.59 Moderate Merritt et al., 2010; Kalichman & Hernández-Molina, 2011 Distraction test axial distraction of 1st MC; positive = pain relief or joint laxity ~0.70 ~0.55 1.6 0.55 Low Shoulder sign Z-deformity MCP hyperextension + CMC flexion on lateral X-ray/inspection — — — — Diagnostic sign; not a provocation test CMC grind + crepitus combined ~0.65 ~0.78 2.95 0.45 Moderate Pinch grip pain key pinch or 3-jaw chuck; positive if basal pain reproduced ~0.80 ~0.50 1.6 0.40 Low Radial ABduction stress passive radial abduction stress; positive = pain at CMC ~0.70 ~0.60 1.75 0.50 Low > Clinical note: No single test has high sensitivity and specificity. Grind test has best specificity 80% — positive result is more useful than negative for ruling in OA. Combine with plain radiography for diagnostic confirmation; X-ray is essential for Eaton-Littler staging and surgical planning. > Grind test technique matters: The examiner applies firm axial compression to the 1st MCP joint while simultaneously circumducting the metacarpal. Reproducing the patient's typical pain at the CMC base is a positive result. Crepitus alone without pain is less significant degenerative crepitus common in asymptomatic elderly . --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Expedited onward referral if: - Rapidly progressive joint destruction in young patient → seronegative or psoriatic arthropathy; refer Rheumatology - Hot, swollen, erythematous CMC → gout podagra pattern may affect hand ; septic arthritis rare at CMC ; aspirate and send for MCS/crystals - Suspected scaphoid fracture anatomical snuffbox tenderness + trauma → X-ray ± MRI; do not conflate with CMC OA - Median nerve compromise carpal tunnel syndrome often co-exists; BCTQ screening → neurophysiology ± CTS pathway - Inflammatory arthropathy bilateral symmetric; MCP/PIP swelling; morning stiffness >1 hour → Rheumatology - Bone pain at night / unremitting → exclude malignancy uncommon; rare at carpus --- Clinical Frameworks Eaton-Littler Classification Radiographic Staging Stage Radiographic Findings Joint Space Clinical Correlation ------- ---------------------- ------------- --------------------- Stage I Normal or widened joint space; no osteophytes; possible laxity/subluxation Normal Ligamentous laxity; synovitis; normal/near-normal X-ray Stage II Joint space narrowing; osteophyte 2 mm; >1/3 MC subluxation Markedly narrowed Established OA; surgical discussion; STT usually spared Stage IV Pantrapezial OA CMC + STT joint ; sclerosis; cysts Obliterated Advanced; trapeziectomy + STT involvement; arthroplasty > Staging requires X-ray — bilateral stress views Robert view / AP with thumb extended are standard. Eaton-Littler Stage guides surgical planning: Stage I–II → conservative/injection; Stage III → injection/surgery; Stage IV → surgery trapeziectomy ± arthroplasty . Z-Deformity / Shoulder Sign - MCP joint hyperextension compensates for CMC adduction contracture - Visible on clinical inspection and lateral X-ray - Functionally significant: MCP hyperextension >30° requires concomitant MCP fusion/capsulodesis at time of trapeziectomy to prevent post-operative swan-neck deformity --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- DASH 10–15 points Preferred for thumb OA; validated QuickDASH 16 points Rapid screening; validated PRWE 14 points Wrist-specific; less thumb-specific but widely used AUSCAN Australian/Canadian OA Hand Index 5–7 points pain subscale Hand OA-specific; pain, stiffness, function subscales; 15 items FIHOA Functional Index for Hand OA — 10 items; validated in hand OA Pinch strength lateral pinch / 3-jaw chuck ~1–2 kg Baseline and follow-up; Jamar or Pinch gauge Grip strength Jamar dynamometer 6–7 kg Compare bilaterally NRS Pain 2 points Quick; use alongside functional measure --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis Plain Radiography - Essential for diagnosis and staging — AP Roberts/stress view , lateral, and oblique views - Bilateral comparison recommended - Roberts view true AP of thumb CMC : hyperpronate hand on cassette with beam perpendicular — best assessment of CMC joint USS - Not primary diagnostic tool for CMC OA - Useful: synovitis assessment, USS-guided injection improves accuracy and reproducibility - Demonstrates joint effusion, osteophytes, synovial thickening, Doppler signal MRI - Not routine for CMC OA - Indications: suspected concurrent pathology scaphoid pathology, adjacent ligament injury, avascular necrosis of trapezoid/scaphoid ; diagnostic uncertainty Laboratory - Not required for uncomplicated CMC OA - If inflammatory arthropathy suspected: FBC, ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP, uric acid --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- De Quervain's tenosynovitis First dorsal compartment; Finkelstein/Eichhoff positive; no bony change on X-ray Scaphoid fracture Trauma; anatomical snuffbox tenderness; X-ray ± MRI Scaphotrapezial STT OA Radial wrist pain; X-ray shows STT involvement; often co-existent Stage IV Flexor carpi radialis FCR tendinopathy Volar wrist pain; FCR tendon tenderness; USS confirms Wartenberg's syndrome Radial sensory nerve; burning; Tinel's; no X-ray changes Carpal tunnel syndrome Median nerve territory; Phalen/Tinel; BCTQ; nerve conduction Trigger thumb Triggering/locking; A1 pulley; palmar MCP crease Gout/pseudogout at CMC Acute hot swollen joint; raised uric acid; crystals on aspiration Inflammatory arthropathy Bilateral; MCP/PIP; morning stiffness; raised inflammatory markers --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Primary care → Hand therapy conservative first-line → Injection → Surgical referral Step 1 — Initial Assessment: - Eaton-Littler stage X-ray essential — request if not available - Baseline DASH/QuickDASH + AUSCAN + pinch/grip strength - Assess MCP hyperextension Z-deformity - Screen for carpal tunnel syndrome BCTQ Step 2 — Conservative management all stages first-line; ongoing in Stage I–II : - Hand therapy referral for splinting + exercise programme - Activity modification; ergonomic advice; adaptive equipment Step 3 — Corticosteroid injection Stage I–III; failed conservative 6–8 weeks; acute flare : - USS-guided intra-articular injection CMC joint - Refer injection physiotherapist / GP-with-SI / MSK interface clinic Step 4 — Surgical referral Stage III–IV; failed conservative + 2 injections; significant functional limitation : - HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery / T&O - Include Eaton-Littler stage, MCP hyperextension status, patient functional demands --- Conservative Management Splinting: - Cochrane Bertozzi et al., 2015; Moe et al., 2021 : Evidence supports hand orthoses for pain relief and function improvement; short opponens/CMC stabilisation splint superior to no splinting for pain low-moderate quality evidence - Custom thermoplastic CMC stabilisation orthosis: Most evidence; immobilises CMC in functional position; MCP and IP joints free; worn during activity and at night - Soft neoprene splint: Less immobilisation; improves compliance; suitable for milder cases - Duration: Minimum 3 months; review at 4–6 weeks - Evidence: Berggren et al. 2001 — splinting equivalent to corticosteroid injection at 6 months; combination not superior Exercise therapy: - Cochrane Moe et al., 2021 : Exercise + splinting superior to splinting alone for pain and function at short-term; exercises should target thenar muscle strengthening and CMC stability - Exercises: opposition, abduction/adduction against resistance; web space stretching - Graded theraband / putty; avoid painful pinching initially - Duration: 6–12 weeks supervised; home programme Thermal modalities / Manual therapy: - Weak evidence; adjunct only; paraffin wax, heat, joint mobilisation CMC traction/mobilisation - Joint mobilisation Maitland/accessory : Small RCTs suggest short-term pain benefit; insufficient for standalone recommendation --- Pharmacological Corticosteroid Injection CSI : - Evidence: Joshi et al. 2019 meta-analysis — CSI provides significant short-term pain relief 4–8 weeks ; effect wanes at 6 months; no strong evidence for structural modification - USS-guided recommended small joint; improves accuracy vs landmark - Methylprednisolone 20–40 mg or triamcinolone 20 mg + 1 mL lidocaine - Frequency: Maximum 2–3 per year; evidence supports benefit of repeated injections; structural caution with frequent use - Hyaluronic acid viscosupplementation : Multiple small RCTs — comparable to CSI at 6–12 months; not NICE-recommended as standard; available at some centres Topical NSAIDs diclofenac gel : - NICE-recommended first-line pharmacological treatment for hand OA - Evidence: Hunter et al.; Cochrane Derry et al., 2017 — significant pain reduction vs placebo; fewer systemic effects than oral NSAIDs Oral NSAIDs / Analgesics: - Short-term use for acute flares; follow NICE/MHRA guidance; consider GI/CV/renal risk - Paracetamol: limited efficacy in OA Machado et al., 2015 meta-analysis ; may still provide modest benefit --- Surgical Options Procedure Indication Outcomes Recurrence / Notes ----------- ------------ ---------- ------------------- Trapeziectomy simple Stage III–IV; failed conservative 80–90% good/excellent at 5 years; thumb shortening Gold standard; strong evidence base Trapeziectomy + LRTI ligament reconstruction tendon interposition Stage III–IV No evidence of superiority over simple trapeziectomy Cochrane, Wajon et al., 2015 Longer procedure; similar outcomes CMC arthroplasty prosthetic Stage II–III; younger, higher demand patients Good short-term; concern for long-term implant survival Limited UK uptake; pyrocarbon available CMC arthrodesis Young active patients; Stage II–III Eliminates pain; reduces motion; useful in manual workers Motion sacrifice Metacarpal extension osteotomy Stage I–II; young; delayed surgery Modest evidence; alters load distribution Niche; not widely used Trapeziectomy CMC arthroplasty criteria for HSC NI : - Eaton-Littler Stage III–IV - Failed conservative management ≥6 months - Failed ≥2 corticosteroid injections - Significant functional limitation QuickDASH >40 or equivalent - MCP hyperextension >30° — note for surgeon may need concurrent MCP procedure Cochrane evidence Wajon et al., 2015 : No significant difference in outcomes between trapeziectomy alone vs trapeziectomy + LRTI vs trapeziectomy + K-wire stabilisation. Simple trapeziectomy is therefore the evidence-based standard, avoiding the morbidity of tendon harvest. --- Onward Referral Criteria Trigger Referral Destination --------- --------------------- Suspected inflammatory arthropathy Rheumatology Acute hot swollen CMC suspected gout/septic Emergency Assessment / Rheumatology urgent Stage III–IV; failed conservative/injection HSC NI Hand Surgery / Plastic Surgery Carpal tunnel syndrome co-existing HSC NI CTS pathway / Nerve conduction studies Diagnostic uncertainty / unusual presentation MSK Radiology USS/MRI --- Key References 1. Eaton RG, Littler JW. Ligament reconstruction for the painful thumb carpometacarpal joint. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1973;55 8 :1655–1666. 2. Eaton RG, Glickel SZ. Trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis: staging as a rationale for treatment. Hand Clin. 1987;3 4 :455–471. 3. Merritt MM, Roddey TS, Costello C, et al. Diagnostic value of clinical grind test for carpometacarpal osteoarthritis of the thumb. J Hand Ther. 2010;23 3 :261–267. 4. Kalichman L, Hernández-Molina G. Hand osteoarthritis: an epidemiological perspective. Semin Arthritis Rheum. 2010;40 2 :166–173. 5. Wajon A, Vinycomb T, Carr E, et al. Surgery for thumb trapeziometacarpal joint osteoarthritis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015; 2 :CD004631. 6. Bertozzi L, Valdes K, Vanti C, et al. Investigation of the effect of conservative interventions in thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis: systematic review and meta-analysis. Disabil Rehabil. 2015;37 22 :2025–2043. 7. Moe RH, Kjeken I, Uhlig T, et al. There is inadequate evidence to determine the effectiveness of non-pharmacological and non-surgical interventions for hand osteoarthritis. J Clin Epidemiol. 2009;62 8 :843–845. 8. Joshi R, Hadzic A, Kalava A, et al. Corticosteroid injections for basal thumb osteoarthritis — a meta-analysis. J Hand Surg Am. 2019;44 4 :314–323. see also: Meenagh et al. 9. Haara MM, Heliövaara M, Kröger H, et al. Osteoarthritis in the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb. Prevalence and associations with disability and mortality. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2004;86 7 :1452–1457. 10. Derry S, Conaghan P, Da Silva JA, et al. Topical NSAIDs for chronic musculoskeletal pain in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016; 4 :CD007400.

title: Trigger Finger (Stenosing Tenosynovitis)
summary: Trigger Finger Stenosing Tenosynovitis Overview & Pathophysiology Trigger finger stenosing tenosynovitis results from a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and the A1 pulley at the level of the MCP joint. Repetitive microtrauma causes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and hypertrophy of the A1 pulle
content: Trigger Finger Stenosing Tenosynovitis Overview & Pathophysiology Trigger finger stenosing tenosynovitis results from a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and the A1 pulley at the level of the MCP joint. Repetitive microtrauma causes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and hypertrophy of the A1 pulley, while the flexor tendon develops a fusiform nodule proximal to the pulley. This produces the characteristic catching, triggering, or locking of the digit in flexion. Anatomy: - A1 pulley overlies the MCP joint; most commonly affected - Flexor digitorum superficialis FDS and profundus FDP pass through the fibro-osseous canal - Tendon nodule forms proximal to A1 pulley; catches on pulley margins during gliding Epidemiology: - General population incidence: 28 per 100,000 person-years - Peak age: 55–60 years; females > males 2:1 - Ring finger most commonly affected, followed by thumb trigger thumb - Strong association with: - Diabetes mellitus 10× increased risk; 10–20% of diabetics affected - Rheumatoid arthritis - Hypothyroidism - Carpal tunnel syndrome co-occurrence ~10–20% - Repetitive gripping activities Trigger thumb A1 pulley of thumb flexor behaves similarly; note distinction from paediatric trigger thumb congenital form with Notta's node . --- Special Tests Test Sensitivity Specificity +LR -LR Evidence Level ------ ------------- ------------- ----- ----- ---------------- Triggering/locking on active flexion/extension ~0.92 ~0.95 18.4 0.08 Moderate Palpable nodule at A1 pulley MCP palmar crease ~0.75–0.80 ~0.90 7.5 0.25 Low-moderate Tenderness over A1 pulley ~0.90 0.65 2.6 0.15 Low Crepitus on tendon gliding ~0.50 ~0.80 2.5 0.63 Low > Diagnosis is predominantly clinical — active triggering or locking of the digit during flexion/extension, combined with palmar MCP tenderness and a palpable nodule, is sufficient for diagnosis. Imaging is not routinely required. > USS can confirm nodule size, pulley thickening, and tendon morphology — useful pre-injection or when diagnosis is uncertain. Characteristic USS finding: hypoechoic nodule proximal to A1 pulley with restricted tendon glide on dynamic assessment. --- Green Classification Severity Grade Description Clinical Features ------- ------------- ------------------- Grade I Pre-triggering Pain; history of catching but no demonstrable triggering on examination; tenderness over A1 pulley Grade II Active triggering Demonstrable triggering/snapping on active flexion-extension; patient can actively extend digit Grade III Locked Digit locked in flexion; patient cannot actively extend; requires passive correction IIIa or cannot be corrected passively IIIb Grade IV Contracture Fixed flexion contracture at PIP joint in addition to locking > Clinical relevance: Grade I–IIIa respond well to corticosteroid injection. Grade IIIb–IV typically require surgical intervention. Grade IV may require additional PIP joint contracture release. --- Red Flags > ⚠️ Urgent/priority onward referral if: - Acute locked digit unable to extend passively + fever/erythema → Septic flexor tenosynovitis — surgical emergency Kanavel's cardinal signs: fusiform swelling, flexed posture at rest, pain on passive extension, tenderness over tendon sheath - Traumatic mechanism with locked digit → exclude volar plate injury, fracture, or dislocation - Rapidly progressive, bilateral triggering with joint swelling → inflammatory arthropathy RA - Paediatric locked thumb → congenital trigger thumb — paediatric orthopaedic referral - Firm, fixed nodule not consistent with tendon — consider giant cell tumour of tendon sheath GCT ; USS ± referral --- Clinical Frameworks Diagnostic Framework 1. History: Catching, triggering, locking; worse in morning; pain at palm/MCP 2. Examination: Active triggering; palpable nodule; A1 pulley tenderness; assess for locked digit 3. Green classification to guide management 4. Comorbidity screen: Diabetes, RA, hypothyroidism 5. Imaging: USS if diagnosis uncertain or pre-procedural planning Special Considerations - Diabetic patients: Lower injection success rates 50–60% vs ~75% in non-diabetics ; higher recurrence; may require earlier surgical referral - Multiple digits: USS of all affected digits; injection of all at one visit appropriate - Paediatric trigger thumb: Different pathology Notta's node at A1 pulley ; spontaneous resolution possible up to age 3; refer paediatric orthopaedics --- Outcome Measures Measure MCID Notes --------- ------ ------- QuickDASH 16 points Validated in hand conditions; preferred for upper limb function DASH 10–15 points Full version; appropriate for complex or multi-digit cases PRWE 14 points Wrist-specific; less appropriate for isolated finger; use QuickDASH preferentially Quinnell grading N/A Surgeon-used severity grading I–IV ; similar to Green NRS Pain 2 points Baseline and outcome tracking Grip / pinch strength 6–7 kg grip Compare bilaterally; Jamar dynamometer --- Evidence-Based Diagnosis USS Findings if performed - Hypoechoic nodule in flexor tendon proximal to A1 pulley - A1 pulley thickening normal: 2 mm - Restricted tendon glide on dynamic USS with active flexion/extension - Power Doppler: peritendinous hyperaemia in active inflammation - USS-guided injection improves accuracy and may improve outcomes Laboratory - No routine bloods required for diagnosis - If inflammatory arthropathy suspected: FBC, ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP - Diabetes screen if not known: HbA1c / fasting glucose --- Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features ----------- ---------------------------- Septic flexor tenosynovitis Kanavel's signs; fever; systemic illness; surgical emergency Volar plate injury / PIP dislocation Trauma; localised PIP tenderness; X-ray Dupuytren's contracture Progressive painless contracture; palmar cord; no triggering Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath Firm, fixed, non-tender nodule; USS — lobulated, vascular Flexor tendon rupture RA Inability to flex; RA history; Mannerfelt syndrome Locked MCP joint Sesamoid entrapment; X-ray shows sesamoid between metacarpal heads Camptodactyly Congenital or juvenile; painless PIP flexion deformity; no triggering --- Management & Treatment HSC NI Hand Therapy Pathway > Primary care → Physiotherapy/Hand Therapy → Injection → Surgical referral Step 1 — Initial Assessment: - Confirm diagnosis + Green grade - Screen for comorbidities diabetes, RA - Baseline QuickDASH + grip/pinch strength Step 2 — Conservative Grade I–II; trial 4–6 weeks : - Night extension splinting of MCP joint PIP/DIP free — reduces morning locking - Activity modification; avoid sustained gripping/vibration - Gentle tendon-gliding exercises - Refer to hand therapist for splint fabrication and exercise programme Step 3 — Corticosteroid Injection Grade I–IIIa; preferred first-line for active triggering : - USS-guided into tendon sheath at A1 pulley level - Refer to qualified physiotherapist injection / GP-with-SI / MSK interface clinic - Second injection if inadequate response at 6–8 weeks Step 4 — Surgical Referral Grade IIIb–IV; failed 2 injections; diabetic recurrence : - Percutaneous A1 pulley release or open surgical release - HSC NI Hand Surgery / T&O referral --- Conservative Management Night Extension Splinting: - MCP joint in 0–15° extension; PIP and DIP joints free - Reduces triggering by preventing full flexion at rest - Evidence: Patel & Bassini 1992 — 66% resolution with splinting alone grade I–II - Thermoplastic custom splint via hand therapy or off-the-shelf MCP extension splint Tendon Gliding Exercises: - Hook fist, straight fist, composite fist positions - Purpose: maintain tendon excursion, reduce adhesion formation - Limited high-quality RCT evidence; clinical consensus supports use --- Pharmacological Corticosteroid Injection CSI : - Cochrane Peters-Veluthamaningal et al., 2009 : CSI produces short-term resolution in up to 93% of cases at 4 weeks; effect diminishes at 6 months ~57% sustained ; recurrence rate ~50% at 1 year - Best evidence: Triamcinolone acetonide 10–20 mg or methylprednisolone 20–40 mg + 1 mL lidocaine into tendon sheath - USS-guided injection: higher accuracy, similar outcomes to landmark-guided RCT evidence limited - Diabetic patients: ~50–60% short-term success; earlier recurrence; monitor glucose post-injection - 2nd injection: Additional 50–60% resolution in those not responding to first - 3rd injection: Diminishing returns; proceed to surgical referral NSAIDs: Topical or oral for pain; limited specific evidence in trigger finger; adjunct only --- Surgical Options Procedure Description Recurrence Rate Notes ----------- ------------- ----------------- ------- Percutaneous A1 pulley release Needle or blade via palmar approach;
